how-to-use-this-book:
How to use this book & pick your path

This book is one chapter pool shared across three reader tracks — Beginner, Engineer, and Automator. Each track is a curated sequence through those chapters, ordered to match your starting point and goals. By the end of this short orientation you will know which track fits you, how the book saves your progress, and how to switch paths any time.

Three tracks, one pool

Every chapter belongs to one or more tracks. When you choose a track the sidebar reorders itself to show only the chapters that matter for your path, in the right sequence. A chapter that appears in all three tracks — like this one — contains notes pitched at each audience, but you only ever see it once.

Here is how the tracks differ:

| Track | Who it is for | Depth |
|---|---|---|
| Beginner | Curious people with little or no coding background | Plain language, no APIs, small wins |
| Engineer | Developers integrating Claude into software | API details, tool use, production concerns |
| Automator | Power users wiring Claude into workflows | Step-by-step, integration-first, minimal code |

Answer two questions below and the widget will recommend a track and drop you at your first chapter. You can always switch later — your progress carries over.

How the tracks share chapters

Think of each track as a reading list, not a separate book. The same underlying chapters are shared; what changes is which ones appear and in what order.

When you switch tracks mid-way, the chapters you have already marked done stay marked. If a completed chapter also exists on your new track it shows as done there too. Nothing is lost.

How progress and resume work

Progress is stored entirely in your browser's  under the key . There is no account, no login, and no server. Two practical consequences:

- Clearing browser data resets your progress. If you care about your place, note the chapter ID from the URL (e.g. ) before clearing.
- Progress does not sync across devices. Open the same URL on another machine and you start fresh.

When you return to the book the sidebar offers a Resume link that takes you to the first chapter in your current track that is not yet marked done. Marking a chapter done is a manual step — there is a button at the bottom of each page. This keeps you in control: skim a chapter you already know and tick it immediately, or sit with a hard one before marking it complete.

Your active track is also stored in  under . It persists across browser sessions until you change it.

Switching tracks

You can change your track any time from the sidebar or by retaking the two-question quiz on this page. The manifest knows which chapters belong to which track, so the sidebar updates instantly. There is no penalty for switching — treat the tracks as lenses, not locked lanes.

Engineer and Automator chapters overlap more than either overlaps with Beginner. If you write code but care most about productivity workflows, start on Automator — you can dip into Engineer chapters via the search palette whenever you want the API-level detail.

How this book is organised

Chapters are grouped into parts (shown in the sidebar as section headers):

- P0 — Orientation (you are here): mental models and navigation
- P1 — First Contact: your first real interaction with the API
- P2 — The Harness: Claude Code and the tool surface
- P3 — Context Engineering: what goes into the context window and why
- P4 — Prompting & Spec Engineering: writing instructions that hold up
- P5 — Multi-Agent Orchestration: chaining models and tasks
- P6 — The Dev Workflow: Claude in your everyday coding loop
- P7 — Extending Claude: MCP, custom tools, plugins
- P8 — Automation & Integrations: webhooks, n8n, Zapier, scripts
- P9 — Mastery & Power User: advanced patterns and edge cases
- P10 — Reference: quick-reference tables and checklists

Not every track visits every part. Beginner skips most of P5 and P7; Automator skips the API deep-dives in P1 and P6.

Your next step

The first chapter in every track is the same: What is an LLM, fundamentally? It builds the one mental model that makes everything else click — why Claude predicts tokens, what the context window actually is, and why confident-sounding wrong answers happen. Understanding that foundation pays dividends in every chapter that follows.

Once you have chosen a track above, use the Next → link at the bottom of each page to move through your sequence without thinking about navigation.
what-is-an-llm:
What is an LLM, fundamentally?

At its heart, a large language model does one surprisingly simple thing: given some text, it predicts what text should come next. That's it. Everything else — answering questions, writing code, explaining concepts, engaging in conversation — emerges from doing that one thing extremely well, at enormous scale, over enormous amounts of training data.

Understanding that core mechanic is the foundation for using Claude effectively. Once it clicks, a lot of Claude's behaviour — both its strengths and its limitations — starts to make intuitive sense.

Tokens: the atoms of language

LLMs don't read text the way you do, word by word. They work with tokens — sub-word fragments from a vocabulary built by analyzing a large text corpus before training begins. The tokenizer is a separate preprocessing step, distinct from learning the model's weights. Common short words are usually single tokens. Longer or rarer words often get split: "tokenization" might become , . Punctuation, whitespace, and numbers each have their own patterns.

A rough rule of thumb: one token is about ¾ of an English word, or roughly 4 characters.

Paste any text into the widget below to see how many tokens it uses and what it would cost to send it to each Claude model. The counts are heuristic estimates — the exact split depends on Claude's vocabulary — but the magnitude is accurate enough to plan with.

Token counts matter for two practical reasons. First, every API call is priced per token (input and output separately). Second, there is a hard ceiling on how many tokens a single interaction can involve — the context window.

Context: everything the model can see

The context window is the model's entire working memory for a conversation. It contains the system prompt, every message in the conversation so far, any documents you've pasted in, and the outputs of any tools the model called. Nothing outside the context window exists for the model — it cannot look it up, reference it, or be influenced by it.

Modern Claude models have very large context windows (hundreds of thousands of tokens), but they are still finite. When a conversation grows long enough to approach the limit, older content is compacted or summarised to make room. This is why very long sessions can lose fidelity on details mentioned hours ago.

Practically: if something matters, make sure it is in the context. Don't assume Claude "remembers" something from a previous session — each new conversation starts with a blank context.

Training vs. inference: learned once, runs by predicting

A language model is built in two distinct phases.

Training happens once (or infrequently). The model is exposed to enormous volumes of text, and through a process of repeated prediction and correction, it learns a compressed statistical model of language and knowledge. This is where Claude acquired its understanding of grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and how to be helpful. Training is expensive and slow — it runs on thousands of GPUs for weeks or months.

Inference is what happens every time you send a message. The trained model, with its fixed weights, takes your context and predicts the next token. Then the next. Then the next. There is no further learning happening during this process — the model is not updating itself based on your conversation. It is, in a precise sense, running a very sophisticated autocomplete.

This distinction matters: Claude cannot learn new facts during a conversation. Its knowledge has a cutoff date from training. What it can do is reason carefully over information you provide in context — which is why grounding Claude in fresh documents, search results, or tool outputs is so powerful.

Why Claude can be confidently wrong

This is the most important thing to understand about any LLM: it predicts plausible text, not verified truth.

When Claude generates a response, it is producing text that fits the pattern of what a correct, helpful answer looks like — based on what it learned during training. Most of the time, plausible and correct are the same thing. But sometimes they diverge. The model may produce a date, a name, a citation, or a code snippet that sounds authoritative and turns out to be wrong. This is called hallucination, and it is not a bug in the traditional sense — it is a fundamental consequence of how prediction works.

The model has no internal "fact-checker" separate from the prediction process. It does not experience uncertainty the way you do. It can be asked to express uncertainty, and it often does so appropriately, but the underlying mechanism is still prediction.

For decisions that matter — medical, legal, financial, or factual claims you'll share publicly — treat Claude's output as a knowledgeable first draft, not a ground truth. Ask Claude to reason through its answer, check sources independently, and use tool calls that return real data where possible.

So what does this mean for using Claude?

The chapters ahead explore this in depth, but here is the short version:

Claude is most powerful when you treat it as a capable reasoning partner operating over information you supply — not as an oracle that independently knows the truth. Give it clear context. Tell it what role to play and what outcome you want. Ground it in real data when accuracy matters. Use its extended thinking and tool-calling capabilities to catch its own errors.

The rest of this book is about how to do exactly that — across prompting, tool use, multi-step agents, and the full API surface. Understanding the token-predicting machine underneath everything else is where that journey begins.
what-is-claude-code:
What is Claude Code — the agentic harness

Claude Code is not a chat window bolted onto a terminal. It is a fully autonomous agent that can read files, edit code, run commands, search the web, and orchestrate other agents — all inside a loop it drives itself. This chapter explains what that loop looks like, why it matters, and how the harness shapes every interaction you will ever have with Claude Code.

From chat box to agent loop

Most people's first experience with an AI is a chat interface: you type, the AI responds, you type again. The model is passive. It answers when asked and forgets everything the moment the window closes.

Claude Code works differently. When you give it a task, it enters a loop:

1. The model reads everything in the context window and decides what to do next.
2. If it needs information or wants to change something, it requests a tool call — read a file, run a command, search the web, write an edit.
3. The tool runs. The output comes back as a new message appended to the context.
4. The model reads the updated context and decides whether it is done or needs another action.
5. Steps 2–4 repeat until the model produces a final response with no tool requests — or a configured limit is reached.

That cycle — model inference, tool dispatch, result append, repeat — is the agent loop. It is what separates an agentic harness from a chat box. The model is not just answering questions. It is taking actions in the world and observing the results, turn by turn, until the task is complete.

The context window is an append-only message array. Every user message, assistant response, tool call, and tool result is added to it — nothing is overwritten. This is the loop's entire working memory. If something is not in the context, the model cannot act on it.

Anatomy of a turn

Each full cycle of the loop is one turn. Here is what happens inside a single turn in concrete terms:

The turn count matters because it controls how long Claude can work before you review progress. In the CLI, it runs until complete by default. When you embed the Agent SDK in your own application, you set  and  explicitly — otherwise the loop runs indefinitely, which is hazardous for open-ended prompts.

The HarnessExplorer — click each phase

The widget below maps the six phases of the agent loop. Select any phase to read what it does and how it connects to the others.

What "harness" means

The word harness is deliberate. The loop itself — the scaffolding that manages context, dispatches tools, enforces permissions, tracks spend, fires hooks, and emits the final result — is the harness. The Claude model is a component inside it, not the whole system.

This distinction has practical consequences:

The harness enforces permissions, not the model. Before any tool runs, the harness checks against your permission rules ( /  in ). Six permission modes control the overall policy — from  (prompt on anything dangerous) through  (auto-approve file edits) to  (no checks at all, for isolated containers). The model has no say in this; it requests tools and the harness decides whether to run them.

Hooks intercept the loop at defined points. Thirty named hook events fire throughout the session:  can block a tool call before it runs,  can rewrite the output Claude sees,  can inject more context to keep the loop going. These are shell scripts or SDK callbacks in your configuration — not model prompts.

Context is precious and finite. Every tool result consumes tokens. A large file read can cost thousands. When the context approaches its limit, automatic compaction summarises older history (emitting a  system message). You can also trigger manual compaction with . Static content — the system prompt, tool definitions, your  — is automatically prompt-cached after the first request, so repeated-request costs stay low.

The loop terminates, not the model. The harness emits a  when the loop ends. That message carries the final text, the session ID, cumulative token counts, and total cost. Five end states exist: , , , , and . Only  means the model decided it was done.

Tools: the model's hands

The model reasons, but it cannot do anything without tools. As of the current version, Claude Code ships with over thirty built-in tools. A few worth knowing early:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
|  | Reads a file with line numbers; also handles images, PDFs, and notebooks |
|  | Exact string replacement in a file (requires a prior ) |
|  | Creates or overwrites a file |
|  | Runs a shell command (2-minute default timeout, 30 000 character output limit) |
|  | Finds files by pattern |
|  | Searches file contents via ripgrep |
|  | Queries the web and returns titles and URLs |
|  | Fetches a URL and returns extracted content (processed by a small model before Claude sees it) |
|  | Spawns a subagent — a fresh Claude instance with its own loop |

Read-only tools (, , , and MCP tools marked ) can run in parallel within a single turn. Everything that modifies state runs sequentially. You do not control this scheduling — the harness manages it automatically based on tool annotations.

Tools are gated by rules like  or . Adding these to  in  lets matching tool calls run without a prompt. The  permission mode — useful in CI — means Claude only runs tools that already have an allow rule and silently rejects everything else.

Why this mental model matters

Once you see Claude Code as a loop rather than a chat box, several things that might otherwise seem surprising start to make sense.

"Why did it do so much without asking?" Because the loop is designed to run autonomously until complete. The model requested tools, the harness approved them (per your rules), results came back, and it kept going. If you want checkpoints, set  low, use plan mode ( or ) to require approval before any edit, or add  hooks that pause on specific actions.

"Why does it sometimes lose context from earlier in the session?" Because the context window is finite and append-only. Old messages eventually get compacted away. Critical project conventions belong in  (loaded fresh every session) or in auto-memory files — not just mentioned once in a long conversation.

"How do I make it faster or deeper?" Effort levels — , , , ,  — control how much reasoning the model applies per turn. Higher effort uses more thinking tokens and costs more, but produces better results on complex tasks. Set the level with  or the  setting.

"Can it run multiple things at once?" Yes — via subagents. The  tool spawns a fresh Claude instance with its own isolated loop. Dynamic workflows can run up to sixteen subagents concurrently, with intermediate results staying in script variables rather than in the parent's context window.

The agent loop can create files, run commands, and make network requests — all without further prompts if you have approved those tool categories. Start with the  permission mode and narrow to  or  only once you understand what Claude will reach for. The harness is your enforcement layer; configure it intentionally.

CLAUDE.md: standing instructions across every loop

One practical consequence of the append-only loop: each new session starts with an empty context. Any project conventions you want Claude to follow must be loaded fresh every time.

 is the mechanism. Place one at your project root and it is injected as a user message at the start of every session — before your first prompt. Your personal  loads for every project. The harness prompt-caches these files after the first request so they do not add cost on subsequent turns within the same session.

Think of  as your standing brief to a new collaborator: what this project is, what patterns to follow, what to avoid. The loop reads it; it does not need to be repeated.

Recap

Claude Code is an agent loop: the model reads context, requests tools, gets results back, and repeats until done. The harness — not the model — manages permissions, hooks, context compaction, spend limits, and the final result. Tools are the model's only way to affect the world. Understanding the loop is the foundation for every technique in the chapters that follow.

Next: What is an LLM, fundamentally? covers the token-predicting engine inside the model — the layer underneath the harness.
what-is-claude:
What is Claude — the model family

Claude is Anthropic's family of AI assistants. In this chapter you will learn how the model tiers relate to each other, what kinds of input Claude can handle, and — just as importantly — where its limits are. By the end you will have an honest mental model of what you are working with before you write a single prompt.

One name, many models

"Claude" is not a single model — it is a product family that Anthropic releases in multiple capability tiers. Each release generation is given a number (Claude 3, Claude 4, …) and each generation ships several variants tuned for different cost / performance trade-offs.

The naming follows a consistent pattern across generations:

| Tier | Character | When to reach for it |
|---|---|---|
| Opus | Most capable, highest cost | Hard reasoning, long complex tasks, when quality matters more than speed or cost |
| Sonnet | Balanced — the everyday workhorse | The default for most tasks; strong reasoning at a reasonable price |
| Haiku | Fastest, lowest cost | High-volume pipelines, quick lookups, mechanical verification, anything that runs hundreds of times |

As of June 2026, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 ("Mythos-class") to general availability — a specialised model positioned above Sonnet and below Opus for certain agentic and creative workloads. The tier naming is not always perfectly linear across every use case; check the current model catalogue before assuming a strict hierarchy.

Source: Claude Code changelog v2.1.170, code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog, verified 2026-06-21.

The right tier for your task is almost never obvious from the name alone. Later chapters (particularly the one on cost-tiering in multi-agent orchestration) will give you concrete decision rules. For now, Sonnet is a safe starting point for anything interactive; Haiku is worth knowing for tasks that run many times per minute.

What goes in: Claude's modalities

Claude accepts several types of input within a single conversation turn.

Text is the baseline. Prompts, documents, code, structured data — if it can be expressed as a string, Claude can reason over it.

Images are natively understood. You can paste a screenshot, a diagram, a photo of a whiteboard, or a UI mockup and ask Claude to read, describe, or reason about it. This is not OCR bolted on — the model processes the image holistically as part of its context. Rough rule of thumb: one image counts for several hundred to a few thousand tokens depending on its resolution, so large image-heavy conversations fill the context window faster than text-only ones.

Documents (PDFs and similar) can be provided via Claude.ai's file upload, the API, or tool calls that read files. The model treats the document content as text in its context window.

Tool results are a special form of input: when Claude calls a tool (a web search, a file read, a bash command) the tool's output is fed back into the context and Claude reasons over it as if you had typed the result yourself.

What Claude does not currently produce natively: audio, video, or images as output. It generates text — but that text can be code that draws images, markdown that renders rich documents, or JSON that drives other systems.

The combination of text + images + tools is more powerful than any one modality alone. A common pattern: paste a screenshot of a bug or layout issue → Claude reads the visual context → Claude runs a bash command to check the relevant code → Claude suggests the fix. Each medium fills a gap the others leave.

The context window is the whole conversation

Every piece of text, every image, every tool result — all of it lives in the context window, which is Claude's working memory for that session. Modern Claude models support very large context windows (hundreds of thousands of tokens), but the window is still finite. When it fills, older content is either dropped or compacted.

Paste the text of a long document below to see how many tokens it consumes:

This matters when you are working with Claude Code on a large codebase or in a long autonomous session. Chapter 3 (Context Engineering) covers the tools for managing this deliberately. For now: if something must stay in scope, keep it in the context.

What Claude is genuinely good at

Understanding where Claude excels — not as marketing, but as a practical operating guide — helps you deploy it well.

Reasoning over text you provide. Claude is excellent at synthesising, summarising, critiquing, comparing, and re-expressing information that you give it. This is the highest-confidence use: you supply the facts, Claude supplies the reasoning.

Writing and editing. First drafts, copy edits, tone adjustments, translation of technical concepts into plain language, structure review. Claude handles all of these at a level that accelerates most writing workflows significantly.

Code. Generating, explaining, refactoring, debugging, and reviewing code across most mainstream languages. Claude Code in particular is built on top of this capability — the agentic harness gives it tools to read files, run tests, and iterate autonomously.

Structured extraction. Given a messy document, Claude can reliably extract structured data — names, dates, entities, relationships — into JSON, tables, or other formats. This is a high-value automation target because it scales to large document sets.

Planning and breaking down problems. Given a complex goal, Claude is good at producing a step-by-step plan, identifying sub-problems, and flagging dependencies. It works well as a reasoning partner before implementation begins.

Where Claude has real limits

Being honest about limits is more useful than listing capabilities.

Claude does not know what happened after its training cutoff. Its knowledge has a hard date. News events, new package versions, recent API changes, updated documentation — anything that postdates training is invisible to Claude unless you provide it in context. This is why tool calls that fetch live data (web search, file reads, API calls) matter so much in production workflows.

Claude can hallucinate. As the previous chapter explained, Claude predicts plausible text. For well-covered domains, plausible and correct almost always align. For niche facts, recent events, specific citations, or obscure details, plausible and correct can diverge — and Claude will not always signal the uncertainty. Verify anything high-stakes against a primary source.

Claude cannot take actions outside its tools. Claude itself cannot access the internet, write to your disk, or call an API unless it has a tool that does so, and you have allowed that tool. This is a feature, not a limitation — it is the basis of safe, auditable automation — but it is important to understand that Claude-in-the-chat-window and Claude-with-tools are meaningfully different operating modes.

Long-context degradation. Very long conversations, or contexts packed with many documents, can cause Claude to lose track of details mentioned early on. This is a known characteristic of attention-based models: not everything in the context window gets equal weight. The practical response is to keep context lean and put the most important instructions near the top and near the end.

Claude's tone does not reliably signal its confidence. It may state something incorrect in the same assured register it uses for things it knows well. This is not deceptive — it is a consequence of how next-token prediction works. Treat Claude's output as a smart first draft by a knowledgeable collaborator who occasionally mis-remembers facts, not as a reference that has been verified.

How the tiers fit into a real workflow

Most teams end up using all three tiers in combination, even within a single feature:

The engineering track chapter on cost-tiering (Part 5) covers when to dispatch which tier in an automated pipeline. For now, the takeaway is: Sonnet for judgment, Haiku for scale, Opus when quality is the ceiling constraint.

Recap

- Claude is a family of models, not a single thing. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus (plus Fable in the current generation) serve different cost/performance points.
- It understands text, images, documents, and tool results as input. It produces text (including code and structured data) as output.
- Its genuine strengths are reasoning over context you supply, writing, code, structured extraction, and planning.
- Its genuine limits are knowledge cutoff, hallucination risk on specific facts, scope bounded by its tools, and attention degradation over very long contexts.

Next: What is Claude Code — agentic harness vs a chat box walks through what changes when Claude gets tools and an agent loop, which is where the power (and the complexity) really starts.
first-task-e2e:
Your first real task, end to end

You have Claude Code installed and you understand permissions. Now it is time to complete something real — a task with a clear start, a middle you can watch, and a finish you can verify. By the end of this chapter you will have the loop in your fingers, not just your head, and you will know exactly what to do the next time you sit down with Claude.

Picking a task that fits

The ideal first task is small, bounded, and easy to check. Something like:

- "Summarise every TODO comment in this codebase into a single list."
- "Write a README for this project."
- "Explain what this function does and suggest a simpler version."

For this walkthrough we will use: write a  for a small project you already have on disk. It is concrete (you end up with a real file), slightly open-ended (Claude has to make sensible choices), and easy to judge (you can read the result and decide if it is right).

If you do not have a project handy, create a minimal one:

That is enough structure for Claude to work with.

Step 1 — Open a session in your project directory

Navigate to the project root in your terminal, then start Claude Code:

Claude will read any  file in the directory (there is not one yet — that is fine), load the available tool set, and show you a prompt. You are now inside a session scoped to this directory.

Claude's tools navigate relative to the directory you launched from. Starting from the project root means , , and  all work with paths you expect. If you launch from a subdirectory, Claude may miss files in parent folders.

Step 2 — Give Claude a clear, specific prompt

Type your instruction and press Enter:

A few things make this prompt work well:

- It names the output file explicitly. Claude knows to create , not something else.
- It lists the sections you expect. Claude will not have to guess what belongs in a contributing guide.
- It sets a length target. Without that, Claude might write three pages.

You do not need magic words or special formatting. Plain language instructions are what Claude is trained on.

Step 3 — Watch the agent loop run

After you press Enter, Claude does not reply immediately. Instead you will see tool calls appear:

Claude is exploring your project before writing anything. This is the agent loop in action — the same cycle from the previous chapter, but now you can watch each tool execute in real time.

Read-only tools (, , ) run silently — no permission prompt. When Claude reaches the  call to create , you will see a prompt:

Press  to approve this one write, or  to allow all file writes without asking again for this session. For a first session,  keeps you in the loop without being disruptive.

Step 4 — Read the result critically

Once Claude finishes you will see two things: the content of  in the terminal output, and a short summary of what Claude did and why it made the choices it made.

Open the file:

Read it as if you were a new contributor to your project. Ask yourself:

- Does the dev setup section match how you actually install dependencies?
- Did Claude invent a test command, or does it match what is in ?
- Is the tone right for your project?

This is the most important part of the workflow: you are the final reviewer. Claude produces a first draft, not a final document. Your judgment is what turns a good first draft into something you would actually commit.

If your project has no test runner configured, Claude will write something generic like "run your test suite before submitting a PR." That is not wrong, but it is vague. The fix is easy: tell Claude explicitly what to put there, or update  yourself afterward. Do not assume Claude's first pass is complete just because it looks polished.

Step 5 — Iterate in the same session

If something is off, do not start over. The existing context — the files Claude already read, the draft it already wrote — is still in the session. Use it:

Claude will call  to make a targeted change to the file it already wrote. You will see exactly which lines change before they are applied:

One short follow-up and the doc is tighter. This is the normal rhythm: prompt → review → refine → done.

Step 6 — Verify and close out

Once you are happy, do a final check:

You should see  listed as a new file. Check that no other files were modified — Claude should have only created that one file. If something unexpected changed,  will show you exactly what.

When everything looks right, commit:

You have completed the loop. You gave Claude a clear task, watched the tool calls run, approved the write, reviewed the output, iterated once, and verified the result before committing. That sequence — prompt → watch → approve → review → iterate → verify — is the same workflow you will follow for tasks ten times more complex.

What made this work

Looking back at what you just did, a few things kept it on track:

| Practice | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Specific prompt with named output | Claude did not have to guess the file name or structure |
| Watching tool calls | You knew what Claude read before it wrote, so surprises were rare |
| Approving writes one at a time | You stayed in control of what hit your filesystem |
| Reading the output critically | You caught the vague test section before it was committed |
| Iterating in the same session | Claude reused existing context — faster and cheaper than starting over |

Everything Claude read and wrote in this session is still in its context window. A follow-up prompt like "now turn CONTRIBUTING.md into a PR template" would not require re-reading the project files — Claude already has them. Long sessions reuse this context efficiently; static parts such as the system prompt, tool definitions, and CLAUDE.md are prompt-cached after the first request, while file reads remain in the append-only conversation history and count toward the context limit.

Recap

You completed a real task end to end: a bounded prompt, a watched agent loop, a write approval, a review, one iteration, and a verified commit. The workflow is the same regardless of task size — the loop just runs more turns for harder problems. In the next part we look at the full tool surface available to Claude and how to shape which tools it can reach.
install-first-session:
Install & first session

By the end of this chapter you will have Claude Code running on your machine, understand the three main ways to reach it (CLI, desktop app, and IDE extension), and have completed a real first session — not a toy "hello world," but an interaction that shows you what the tool actually does. Nothing in here requires prior AI experience; if you can open a terminal and install a package, you are ready.

Ways to run Claude Code

Claude Code is fundamentally a CLI tool — a process you launch in your terminal that can read files, run shell commands, and talk to the Claude API on your behalf. That CLI is also the engine underneath two other surfaces: a native desktop app and IDE extensions for VS Code and JetBrains. All three share the same agent loop and the same configuration system, so skills you learn in one transfer directly to the others.

If you are new to Claude Code, start with the CLI. It shows you exactly what is happening — tool calls, permissions, token counts — with nothing hidden. Once you are comfortable, the desktop app and IDE extensions add convenience without removing any capability.

The CLI

The CLI is distributed as an npm package. You need Node.js installed (any recent LTS version works). Install it globally:

That puts the  binary on your . Verify:

You should see a version string. If you see a "command not found" error, check that your npm global bin directory is on your  —  will show you where it is.

The desktop app

The desktop app wraps the same CLI engine in a native window with a sidebar, persistent session list, and OS-level notifications. Download the installer for your platform from claude.ai/download. The app self-updates by default; you can pin it to the  channel (one week behind ) by setting  in your settings if you prefer a slower cadence.

IDE extensions

VS Code: install the "Claude Code" extension from the VS Code Marketplace. It adds a panel that opens a Claude Code session scoped to your current workspace, with inline diff previews when files are edited.

JetBrains: install the "Claude Code" plugin from the JetBrains Marketplace. Works in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, and the other JetBrains IDEs.

Both extensions are thin UI wrappers — they run the same CLI binary under the hood, so the same  file and  that you configure for the CLI apply automatically.

Authenticating

Claude Code needs credentials to call the Claude API. On first run it will prompt you:

You will be asked to choose between two auth methods:

- claude.ai login — sign in with your claude.ai account (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan). This is the easiest path if you already have a subscription.
- API key — set the environment variable  to a key from console.anthropic.com. This is the right choice for scripting, CI, or if you want direct usage control.

For a personal laptop where you are the only user, the claude.ai login is simpler. For anything automated — a CI job, a server, a script you will run headlessly — use an API key.

If you set  in your shell profile (, , etc.) before running  for the first time, the CLI will pick it up automatically and skip the auth prompt. This is the cleanest setup for API key users.

Your first session

Open your terminal, navigate to a project directory you are comfortable experimenting in (or create an empty one), and run:

You will see a prompt appear. You are now talking to a Claude model that can see your filesystem, run commands, and edit files — all subject to your permission approvals.

Let's run a real interaction, not a greeting. Ask Claude to explain the project:

What happens next illustrates the core loop. Claude will call a few read-only tools — probably  to find files and  to inspect key ones — then synthesize an answer. Watch the tool calls appear on screen as they happen. Each one is labelled with the tool name and the arguments Claude chose.

Notice that these read-only operations did not prompt you for permission. That is by design: , , and  are considered safe to run without approval. If Claude tries to do something that could modify state — run a shell command, edit a file — you will see a permission prompt and can approve or reject it.

The agent loop in one picture

Every turn follows the same cycle:

The loop terminates naturally when Claude produces a response with no further tool calls. For most questions this takes one or two turns. For larger tasks — refactoring a module, writing tests across a codebase — it may take many turns.

Key things to observe in your first session

Permission prompts. The first time Claude tries to run a shell command you will see:

-  approves once
-  adds a permanent allow rule for this command pattern
-  denies, and Claude will try a different approach
-  asks Claude to justify why it wants to run the command

You control the blast radius. Claude cannot do anything to your system that you have not approved.

The permission mode indicator. At the bottom of the CLI you will see the current mode.  cycles through three modes:  (prompt for everything dangerous),  (auto-approve file edits and common filesystem ops), and  (read-only exploration — file edits always prompt, never auto-approved). Plan mode is useful when you want to understand what Claude would do before letting it touch anything.

Slash commands. Type  to see what is available. The most useful ones to know immediately:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
|  | Lists all commands including any custom ones you've defined |
|  | Summarises older history to free up context space |
|  | Starts a fresh context (new conversation, same session) |
|  | Shows token consumption and estimated cost for this session |

Useful configuration from day one

Claude Code is highly configurable, and most of the configuration lives in  (your personal settings, applies everywhere) or  inside a project directory (project-specific, can be committed to git).

You do not need to touch configuration to get started. But two settings are worth knowing early:

 — project instructions. Create a file called  in your project root. Write anything you would tell a new team member: what the project does, conventions to follow, commands to run before making changes. Claude reads this file automatically at the start of every session. It is prompt-cached after the first request, which means repeated reads are charged at a sharply reduced rate — but the content still counts against your context window on every turn.

Auto-memory. Claude can persist facts across sessions to a local memory directory ( by default). This is enabled by default. If you prefer fully stateless sessions, add  to your user settings.

The fastest way to understand what Claude Code can do is to give it a task you would actually want done, not a demonstration. Pick something modest and bounded: "find all TODO comments in this repo and summarise them," "write a README for this library," or "explain what this function does and suggest a simpler implementation." The tool becomes intuitive quickly once you see the loop in action on real work.

How the surfaces compare

For reference, here is when each surface tends to be the right choice:

| Surface | Best for |
|---|---|
| CLI | Learning, scripting, SSH sessions, maximum transparency |
| Desktop app | Long sessions, multiple concurrent threads, push notifications, non-technical tasks |
| VS Code extension | Code-focused work where you want inline diff previews alongside your editor |
| JetBrains plugin | Same as VS Code, in JetBrains IDEs |

What you have now

You have Claude Code installed, authenticated, and have run a first session. You know where permission prompts come from and how to control them. You have seen the agent loop complete a turn. And you know the two pieces of configuration —  and user settings — that make Claude immediately useful in your project.

The next chapter covers the agent loop in depth: how turns work, what the context window contains at each step, how compaction prevents you from running out of space, and how to think about cost as you build more complex sessions.
permissions-and-safety:
Permissions, modes & safety

Claude Code can read files, run shell commands, browse the web, edit code, and spawn background agents — but it never does any of that silently without rules you set. This chapter explains the permission model that governs every tool call, the six operating modes that let you tune how much it asks vs. acts, and the practical habits that keep you safely in control.

Why permissions exist

Every action Claude takes in your session goes through a tool call. Reading a file is a  tool call. Running  is a  tool call. Creating or overwriting a file is a  or  tool call. The permission system sits between Claude's decision to use a tool and the tool actually running.

This matters because Claude operates inside your real environment — your filesystem, your shell, your git history. A single misunderstood instruction could delete the wrong files, push credentials to a public repo, or rack up unexpected API costs. Permissions are the mechanism that keeps you the decision-maker, even when Claude is moving fast.

Every capability Claude has — shell, files, web, agents, scheduling — surfaces as a named tool. Permission rules target tool names, so everything is configurable at the same level of abstraction. The interactive widget below lets you explore the full tool catalog and see which tools require approval by default.

The full tool surface at a glance

The widget below is your reference for all built-in tools: what each one does, which surface it belongs to (filesystem, shell, web, agents, …), and whether it prompts for approval before running.

A few patterns worth internalising from the catalog:

- Read-only tools are silent. , , , and  never prompt — they can only observe, not change. You'll notice these have a "silent" badge.
- State-changing tools prompt by default. , , , , and  all show an approval dialog in the default mode before they run the first time per domain or command pattern.
- Agent tools are silent. Spawning a subagent () does not itself require approval, but the subagent's own tool calls do — through the parent terminal.

The six permission modes

Claude Code ships with six modes, selectable per session. Think of them as a dial from "always ask" to "never ask."

default

The baseline. Claude prompts before every tool call that is not already covered by an explicit allow rule. If there is no allow rule and no one to ask (e.g., non-interactive CI), the call is denied. This is the safest starting point when you are exploring a new codebase or doing something irreversible.

acceptEdits

Auto-approves file edits (, , ) and common filesystem operations (, , , ). Shell commands, web fetches, and anything else still follow default rules. Good for code-writing sessions where you want flow but still care about shell commands.

plan

Read-only exploration mode. File edits are never auto-approved — you will always see a prompt before any file changes. Use this when you want Claude to research a codebase or draft a plan without touching anything on disk. Toggle with  in the CLI or the  command.

dontAsk

Never prompts. Every tool call either passes an existing allow rule or is denied silently. Designed for CI/CD pipelines and automation scripts where there is no human to approve anything. Pre-populate your allow rules carefully before switching to this mode.

auto (TypeScript SDK only)

A model-based classifier decides whether to approve or deny each tool call. This is an experimental mode for embedded applications; the CLI does not expose it by default. Administrators can prevent it from being activated via  in managed settings.

bypassPermissions

Skips every permission check. Intended only for isolated containers — sandboxed CI, Docker environments — where Claude literally cannot reach anything you do not want it to touch. It cannot run as root on Unix as an additional hard limit.

Only use  (CLI flag ) when the environment itself provides the isolation. Running it on your development laptop means a misunderstood prompt could delete files, push commits, or run arbitrary commands with no guardrail.

Switching modes in the CLI: press  to cycle through . You can also type  to toggle plan mode directly.

Allow and deny rules

Modes set the default behaviour. Rules let you carve out exceptions — specific tools or paths that should always run (or always be blocked) without a prompt.

Rules live in  under  and . The format is :

A few things to know:

- Deny beats allow. If both a deny rule and an allow rule match a tool call, deny wins.
-  implicitly allows reading the same path — you do not need a separate  rule for the same glob.
- Specifier formats vary by tool:  and  use command patterns; , , , and  use path patterns;  uses  prefixes;  has no specifier (it's all-or-nothing).
- No specifier means the entire tool.  approves every web search without prompt.

Settings scope hierarchy

Rules can live at four levels. Higher levels win:

| Level | File | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Managed (highest) | MDM / server config | IT / platform admin |
| CLI args |  /  | Session caller |
| Local |  | You, not committed |
| Project |  | Team, committed |
| User (lowest) |  | You, all projects |

The local file is gitignored by convention — it is the right place for personal overrides that should not affect teammates. Project settings are committed alongside the code, so the whole team gets the same baseline rules.

In an interactive session, type  to see which rules are currently active and what each tool's status is. It is the fastest way to audit what Claude can do right now without opening any files.

Hooks: automation beyond rules

Permission rules control whether a tool runs. Hooks let you react to events around tool calls — before they run, after they complete, or when Claude finishes responding. They are the extension point for enforcement, auditing, and automation.

The most useful hook for safety is . Any script registered there runs before the matched tool executes. Exit code 2 blocks the tool call entirely:

The  hook fires whenever a permission dialog would appear. You can auto-approve or auto-deny matching calls programmatically — useful for building custom approval UIs or headless pipelines that still need selective gating.

Hooks are covered in depth in the Hooks chapter. For now, the key mental model: rules are static filters; hooks are dynamic logic.

The sandbox

For the strongest isolation, Claude Code supports a sandboxed  tool that confines shell commands at the OS level. Unlike  rules (which only block recognised bash patterns Claude constructs), sandbox enforcement applies to every process spawned — including indirect access from Python scripts, Node programs, or shell one-liners that Claude writes.

Sandbox network rules are independent of  allow rules. Enabling the sandbox in settings does not automatically grant network access to domains already in your  allowlist; you configure them separately.

The sandbox is not available on Windows (where the  tool is used instead).

Practical habits for staying in control

Use  mode when exploring. Before you let Claude make changes to an unfamiliar codebase, spend a turn or two in plan mode. Let it read, search, and tell you what it would do. Then exit plan mode and approve the actual changes.

Commit allow rules with your code. Project-level  is committed. If your project always needs  and , add those to  so every session — and every CI run — gets the same baseline without manual approval.

Use  for things that should never happen. If your project has a directory that should never be touched (, , prod credentials), add a  rule. It costs nothing and removes the category of mistake entirely.

Check  before long runs. Before you kick off an extended agentic task, open  and verify the allow rules match what the task actually needs. An unexpected permission prompt mid-run can block automation for hours.

For CI, use  + an explicit allowlist. The pattern is: define every tool call the CI job needs in , set  in the run options, and let any unanticipated call fail fast rather than hang waiting for input.

Recap

The permission system has three layers: modes (how much Claude asks by default), rules (static allow/deny for specific tools and paths), and hooks (dynamic logic around tool events). Together they give you fine-grained control over exactly what Claude can touch — from "prompt for everything" in a new project to "fully headless" in a locked-down CI container.

Next: the The agent loop & tool calls chapter goes inside the loop to show how tool calls are sequenced, parallelised, and how results flow back to Claude.
the-chat-loop:
The chat loop

Every interaction with Claude — whether you type a question in a chat window or call the API from code — follows the same underlying rhythm. By the end of this chapter you will be able to picture exactly what happens between the moment you hit send and the moment Claude's words appear, and you will know what levers you can pull to shape that exchange.

What actually happens when you send a message

A conversation with Claude is a series of turns. Each turn has the same basic shape:

1. You send a prompt — your input for this round.
2. Claude reads the full context (everything said so far, plus your new message).
3. Claude generates a response, token by token, until it decides it is done.
4. That response is added to the shared context, and the cycle is ready for your next message.

This is often called the chat loop — though "loop" understates it slightly, because each trip around picks up everything that came before. The context is append-only: messages accumulate, and Claude sees all of them every time.

The prompt: your side of the conversation

A prompt is simply the text you send for one turn. It can be a question, an instruction, a chunk of data, a code snippet, or all of the above combined. There is no magic format — Claude interprets plain language.

That said, a few qualities consistently produce better results:

- Be specific about what you want. "Summarize this in three bullet points for a non-technical reader" beats "summarize this."
- Provide relevant context upfront. Claude cannot go looking for information that is not in the conversation — anything it needs must be in the prompt.
- State the shape of the answer. If you want a table, a numbered list, or a short paragraph, say so.

You don't need to follow a rigid template. Think of it like briefing a capable colleague: the clearer your brief, the less back-and-forth you need.

System prompts

In the API (and in most Claude-powered products), there is a special slot called the system prompt that appears before the conversation begins. It is not part of the back-and-forth — it is more like standing instructions that apply for the whole session: a persona, a set of rules, a context that the assistant should always keep in mind.

When you use Claude through a product or integration, the system prompt is usually set by that product. When you call the API directly, you control it. Either way, it is just more text that lands in the context before your first message.

Reading the response

Claude's response arrives as a stream of tokens — the same next-token prediction described in the previous chapter. The practical consequence is that you often see words appearing progressively rather than all at once, especially for longer answers.

A response can contain:

- Plain prose — explanations, analysis, creative writing.
- Structured text — markdown tables, numbered lists, fenced code blocks.
- Multiple distinct sections — Claude will naturally break longer answers into headed sections when that aids clarity.

Claude calibrates response length to the complexity of the request. A simple factual question gets a concise answer. A multi-part technical question gets a detailed one. If you need brevity, ask for it explicitly: "in one paragraph" or "in under 50 words."

How context accumulates across turns

After the first exchange, every subsequent turn includes the full prior history. Claude does not just remember your previous message — it sees the entire transcript from the start of the session. This is what makes multi-turn conversations coherent: Claude can refer back to anything said earlier without you repeating yourself.

The practical implication is that context is cumulative and finite. Claude models have a context window measured in tokens — a hard ceiling on how much text can be in play at once. Within a session you are steadily spending that budget. Very long conversations can eventually exhaust that budget; depending on the product or API setting, older content may be summarised and compacted, or simply unavailable, once the limit is approached.

There is no memory between separate conversations unless a product explicitly saves and re-injects it. If you close a chat and open a new one, Claude has no knowledge of what you discussed before. Continuity within a session is real; continuity across sessions requires explicit handling.

A minimal example

Here is the structure of a two-turn exchange expressed the way the API sees it — no special syntax required, just roles and content:

When Claude processes that last message, it reads all three entries. Its response will be consistent with what it said in the middle entry, without you having to re-explain anything.

What determines response quality?

Three things have the most leverage:

| Factor | What to do |
|---|---|
| Clarity of intent | State what you want and why |
| Context in the prompt | Include relevant background; don't assume Claude knows |
| Iteration | Treat the first response as a draft; follow up to refine |

The chat loop is designed for iteration. If Claude misunderstands, clarify in the next turn rather than restarting from scratch — the prior exchange is part of the context and can itself inform the correction.

Recap

A chat loop is: you send a prompt → Claude reads the accumulated context → Claude responds → the response joins the context → repeat. The context is append-only and finite. System prompts set standing instructions before the conversation begins. Response quality is driven by prompt clarity, available context, and willingness to iterate.

In the next chapter we look at how to write prompts that get reliable results — moving from the mechanics of the loop to the craft of shaping what comes out of it.
glossary:
Glossary

This glossary collects the key terms used throughout the book and gives each a plain-language definition. Scan it top to bottom for a quick mental map of the whole system, or jump straight to an unfamiliar word when you encounter it in a chapter. Precise technical meanings are kept, but jargon is explained, not assumed.

Each definition links back to the part of the book where the concept is introduced in full. A quick definition here is a starting point, not a substitute for the chapter itself.

A

Agent loop
The turn-based cycle at the heart of Claude Code. One cycle: Claude receives a prompt, decides which tools (if any) to call, gets the results of those calls back, then either calls more tools or produces a final text response. The loop repeats until Claude produces a response with no tool calls. The only persistent state across turns is the append-only message array — there is no hidden memory between steps. (See Part 2, Agent loop anatomy.)

Allow rule
A permission setting that pre-approves a specific tool call so Claude never needs to ask before running it. Rules use the format  — for example  pre-approves any npm script, and  pre-approves edits inside your source directory. Allow rules live in  under . Deny rules take precedence over allow rules when both match. (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

Auto-compact
A setting (, on by default) that triggers automatic context compaction when the conversation history approaches the model's context window limit. Claude summarises older parts of the conversation and emits a  marker. Manual compaction via  is more predictable and lets you direct what gets preserved. (See Part 2, Settings and environment.)

Auto-memory
A feature that lets Claude read and write structured facts to  between sessions. Enabled by default. Useful for preferences, project quirks, and recurring context that would otherwise be re-explained every session. Disable with  or the  environment variable. (See Part 2, Settings and environment.)

B

Bash tool
The built-in tool that executes shell commands in your local environment. Default timeout is 2 minutes per command (overridable up to 10 minutes). Output is capped at 30,000 characters by default. Working directory changes () carry over across Bash calls within a session; environment variable changes do not. Requires user approval by default. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

BullMQ
Not a Claude Code term — but appears in the book's worked examples: a Node.js background-job queue built on Redis. Used in the sample CRM project to dequeue webhook payloads and process leads asynchronously. Mentioned here because the book's project examples use it alongside Claude Code's automation features. (See Part 5.)

bypassPermissions
The most permissive operating mode. Skips all permission checks — no prompts, no deny rules. Intended only for isolated containers or test environments where there is nothing sensitive to protect. Cannot run as root on Unix. Activated via the  CLI flag. (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

C

CLAUDE.md
A Markdown file that Claude Code automatically loads as project context at the start of every session. Place it at the repository root (or any parent directory up to the git root) to give Claude standing instructions — coding conventions, architecture notes, team rules. Personal instructions go in . Content is injected as a user message and prompt-cached after the first request. For procedures that only need to load when invoked, prefer a Skill instead, to avoid bloating every session's context. (See Part 2, Memory and CLAUDE.md.)

Context window
The hard limit on how much text (measured in tokens) a model can hold in its active memory at once. Everything in a session — system prompt, CLAUDE.md, conversation history, tool results — counts against this budget. When the window fills, older content must be summarised or dropped. Understanding the context window is foundational to working with Claude effectively. (See Part 0, What is an LLM?)

compactboundary
A marker message emitted by Claude Code when it compacts conversation history. It signals the point before which older turns have been summarised. Visible in the SDK as a  subtype. Compaction can be triggered manually with  or automatically when the context approaches its limit.

D

Deny rule
A permission setting that blocks a specific tool call entirely — Claude is not even shown the option to run it. Deny takes precedence over allow when both rules match the same call. Use deny rules for truly off-limits operations (e.g., ) that should never run regardless of what Claude decides. (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

dontAsk mode
An operating mode for CI/CD and headless automation. In , Claude never shows permission prompts: tool calls that match an allow rule proceed; everything else is silently denied. Pre-populate your allow rules carefully before using this mode — you will not see failures unless you inspect logs. (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

Dynamic workflow
A JavaScript orchestration script that runs many subagents concurrently in the background. Claude Code writes the script; the workflow runtime executes it. Intermediate results stay in script variables rather than in Claude's context window, enabling large-scale parallel work. Triggered by the  keyword or the  setting. Saved workflows become slash commands under . (See Part 6, Workflows.)

E

Edit tool
The built-in tool for making exact string replacements in files. Requires that the file was read earlier in the same conversation, and that  appears exactly once. The  parameter replaces every occurrence. Because it is a state-modifying tool, it runs sequentially (not in parallel with other edits). (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

Effort level
A per-session or per-prompt setting that controls how many "thinking tokens" Claude allocates before responding. Levels: ,  (default), , , . Higher effort improves results on complex reasoning tasks at the cost of more tokens and higher latency. Set with  or the  settings key. Effort is distinct from Extended Thinking — they can be combined independently. (See Part 2, Settings and environment.)

Extended Thinking
A Claude capability where the model produces visible chain-of-thought blocks — intermediate reasoning steps you can read — before its final answer. Produces longer, more deliberate responses. Enabled with  in settings or by requesting it per-call via the API. Different from effort level, though both affect response depth. (See Part 3, Advanced model capabilities.)

F

File checkpointing
A safety mechanism (, on by default) that snapshots files before Claude Code edits them. The  command restores any file to its pre-edit snapshot. Disable with  if you are confident in your git workflow and want to reduce disk usage. (See Part 2, Settings and environment.)

Forked subagent
A subagent that inherits the full parent conversation context rather than starting fresh. Always runs in the background. Used when the subagent needs the history of what has already been decided. Distinguished from a named subagent, which starts with its own clean context. (See Part 6, Subagents.)

G

Glob tool
The built-in tool for finding files by pattern, with  wildcard support. Results are sorted by modification time and capped at 100 files. Unlike , Glob does not respect  by default — set  to change this. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

Grep tool
The built-in tool for searching file contents using regex, built on ripgrep. Respects  by default. Three output modes:  (default), , . Read-only, so it can run concurrently with other read-only tools in the same turn. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

H

Hook
A lifecycle event handler that runs custom code at specific moments in Claude's agent loop — before a tool call, after a tool call, when a session starts, when Claude finishes responding, and many more. Shell command hooks are defined in ; SDK hooks are callback functions. Hooks can block actions (exit code 2), inject additional context, modify tool outputs, or fire side effects. There are 30 named hook events. (See Part 2, Hooks.)

Hook event
One of the 30 named moments where a hook can be registered. Examples:  (before any tool runs),  (after a tool succeeds),  (at session open),  (when Claude finishes a response),  (when an approval dialog would appear). Blockable events (those where exit code 2 stops the action) include , , , , and . (See Part 2, Hooks.)

L

LSP tool
The built-in tool that connects to language servers for code intelligence: jump to definition, find references, type errors, call hierarchies, and symbol search. Requires a code intelligence plugin to be installed. After each file edit, LSP automatically reports type errors so Claude can fix issues without a separate build step. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

M

maxTurns
An option on the agent SDK () that caps the number of tool-use round trips in a single run. The final text-only turn does not count against this limit. When the cap is reached, the SDK emits a  with subtype . Pair with  for cost control in unattended runs. (See Part 6, Agent SDK.)

MCP (Model Context Protocol)
An open protocol for connecting Claude Code to external tools, data sources, and services. MCP servers expose tools that appear in Claude's tool list as . Servers are configured in  or in  under . The  built-in tool enables deferred loading of MCP tool schemas, keeping context overhead low. (See Part 7, MCP and integrations.)

Monitor tool
A built-in tool that runs a command in the background and feeds each output line back to Claude in real time as it arrives. Useful for watching CI logs, file watchers, or server output without polling. Uses the same permission rules as Bash. Not available on Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Foundry. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

O

Output style
A system prompt modifier that changes Claude's default behaviour and communication pattern. Four built-in styles:  (standard engineering instructions),  (acts immediately, makes assumptions),  (adds reasoning commentary),  (adds  markers for pair-programming). Custom styles are Markdown files in . Changed via . (See Part 4, Output styles.)

P

Permission mode
One of six settings that controls how aggressively Claude Code prompts for approval before running tools. In order from most restrictive to least:  (read-only, always prompts for edits),  (prompts for every non-allowed operation),  (auto-approves file edits),  (never prompts; deny unless allowed),  (model classifier decides),  (no checks at all). (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

Plan mode
A permission mode where file edits are never auto-approved — Claude can read and explore freely, but writing to disk always requires explicit confirmation. Toggle with  or . Useful when you want Claude to research a codebase or draft a plan without touching any files. (See Part 2, Permissions and modes deep dive.)

Prompt caching
An automatic optimisation where static portions of the context — the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, tool definitions — are cached after the first request. Subsequent turns do not re-pay the token cost for those sections. Happens transparently; no configuration needed. (See Part 3, Cost and performance.)

Prompt (user prompt)
The text you send to Claude for a single turn of the conversation. A prompt can be a question, instruction, code snippet, pasted document, or any combination. The entire conversation history is included as context alongside your new message every time. Quality, specificity, and context in the prompt are the primary levers for improving Claude's output. (See Part 0, The chat loop.)

R

Read tool
The built-in tool for reading file contents. Returns text with line numbers. Handles plain text, images, PDFs, and Jupyter notebooks. Read-only, so it can run in parallel with other read-only tools (, , ) within the same turn. Required before  or  can modify an existing file. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

ResultMessage
The final message the agent SDK emits at the end of a run. Contains the final text response, total token usage, session cost, and session ID. Subtypes indicate how the loop ended: , , , , or . (See Part 6, Agent SDK.)

Round-robin assignment
A scheduling strategy that distributes work (tasks, leads, API calls) evenly across a pool of targets by cycling through them in order. Not a Claude Code term, but used in the book's worked automation examples when distributing incoming leads across sales agents. (See Part 5, Automation case study.)

S

Settings scope hierarchy
The four-level priority order that determines which  value wins when the same key appears in multiple places. From highest to lowest priority: Managed settings (MDM-deployed, cannot be overridden) → CLI arguments → Local (, gitignored) → Project () → User (). Managed settings are absolute; user settings are overridden by everything above them. (See Part 2, Settings and environment.)

Skill
A Markdown file ( with YAML frontmatter) that extends Claude's capabilities as a slash command. Skills load lazily — the body content reaches Claude only when the skill is invoked, unlike CLAUDE.md which loads on every request. Skills can inject live context (via -prefixed shell commands in the file body), restrict their own tool access, specify a model, and run in a subagent context. Stored in  (project) or  (personal). (See Part 6, Skills.)

Subagent
A separate Claude instance spawned inside a session to handle a specific task in isolation. Named subagents start with a fresh context; forked subagents inherit the parent's conversation. Subagents appear in the  panel. Their tool calls flow through the parent terminal for permission prompts. Custom subagents are defined as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in  (project) or  (personal). (See Part 6, Subagents.)

System prompt
Text injected before the first user message that gives Claude standing instructions for the entire session. In Claude Code, the system prompt is set internally by the CLI and modified by output styles. In the API and SDK, you supply it directly. CLAUDE.md is injected as a user message after the system prompt — not as part of the system prompt itself. (See Part 0, The chat loop.)

T

Token
The basic unit of text that language models read and generate. Roughly 3–4 characters of English text, though the exact boundary depends on the tokeniser. Tokens are the currency of the context window: every message, tool result, and piece of injected context consumes tokens. Understanding token cost is essential for managing long-running sessions and controlling API spend. (See Part 0, What is an LLM?)

Tool call
A structured request from Claude to execute a specific capability — read a file, run a command, search the web. Each tool call has a name and typed parameters. The result is fed back into the conversation as a  before the next model turn. Read-only tool calls can run in parallel; state-modifying calls run sequentially. (See Part 2, Agent loop anatomy.)

ToolSearch
A built-in tool that dynamically loads MCP tool schemas on demand. Because MCP tools are not loaded into the context upfront (they would inflate every session),  fetches the schema for a specific tool when Claude needs it. On Google Vertex AI, or when a non-first-party  is configured,  is disabled and all MCP schemas load on every request instead. (See Part 7, MCP and integrations.)

Turn
One complete cycle of the agent loop: Claude receives the current context, produces output (tool calls and/or a text response), and the results are appended to the message array.  counts only tool-use turns — the final text-only response does not count as a turn against the limit. (See Part 2, Agent loop anatomy.)

U

ultracode
An effort level that combines  reasoning depth with automatic dynamic workflow orchestration. When you include the word  in a prompt (or set  for the session), Claude plans and executes work across many concurrent subagents rather than working sequentially in a single context. Use it for large-scale refactors, bulk processing, or multi-step research. Press  /  to suppress the trigger for a single prompt. (See Part 6, Workflows.)

W

WebFetch tool
The built-in tool for fetching a URL and converting its content to Markdown. Lossy by design: an extraction prompt runs via a small fast model before Claude sees the result, so you receive a distilled summary rather than raw HTML. HTTP is auto-upgraded to HTTPS. Results are cached for 15 minutes. Requires approval by default; preapproved documentation domains skip the prompt. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

WebSearch tool
The built-in tool for querying the web. Returns titles and URLs only — not page content. Claude follows up with  to read specific pages. May issue up to 8 backend searches per call, refining results internally. Available on the Claude API and Microsoft Foundry; available on Vertex AI only with Claude 4 models; not available on Amazon Bedrock. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

Workflow
See Dynamic workflow.

Write tool
The built-in tool for creating or overwriting files. When overwriting an existing file, the file must have been read earlier in the same conversation. Unlike ,  replaces the entire file content. State-modifying, so it runs sequentially and requires approval by default. (See Part 2, Tool surface.)

---

Quick recap

The terms above map onto three layers of the system:

If you have worked through the book sequentially, these definitions should feel familiar by now. If you landed here first, Part 0 (What is an LLM? and What is Claude Code?*) is the right starting point — the model layer definitions there give every other term a foundation to stand on.

Slash-command reference

Slash commands are the fastest way to reach Claude Code's built-in features: type  and a name, and you invoke everything from context management to permission control to bundled workflows. This chapter is a quick-lookup reference — what each command does, when to use it, and the handful of sharp edges worth knowing before you need them.

How slash commands work

When you type a slash command, Claude Code processes it before the message reaches the model. Depending on the command, it either runs a built-in action directly (like  resetting context), invokes a skill file (like  loading a bundled ), or starts an interactive configuration panel (like  opening a menu).

Custom skills and saved workflows also register as slash commands using the same  format — there is no visual distinction between a built-in and a skill you or your team wrote.  shows them all in one list.

Arguments are passed as text after the command name: , , . A special  placeholder in skill files receives everything after the command name, enabling parameterized commands.

Tool reference

Claude Code ships with a catalog of built-in tools that cover every surface it can reach — files, shell, web, agents, notebooks, scheduling, and more. This chapter gives you the full picture: what each tool does, when to reach for it, and the gotchas that bite people most often. Use the interactive catalog below to filter and search while you read.

The catalog at a glance

Every capability Claude exercises in your session is a named tool call. Reading a file is . Running  is . Creating a background subagent is . Understanding the tool names — and which ones require your approval — is the fastest way to understand what Claude can and cannot do on its own.

Tools that can only observe your environment — , , ,  — run without any approval prompt. Tools that can change state — , , , ,  — prompt before running unless you have an allow rule in place. The "perm" and "silent" badges in the catalog above reflect this distinction.

The catalog organises tools into surfaces. Here is what each surface covers and the most important things to know about each group.

Filesystem

Web

Parallelism: what runs together

Read-only tools (, , , and read-only MCP tools) can run concurrently in a single turn. State-modifying tools (, , ) run sequentially. Custom tools default to sequential; set  in tool annotations to enable parallelism.

This matters for speed: if Claude needs to read five files, it can do it in one turn. If it needs to make five edits, it takes five turns — plan accordingly when you care about latency.
