agent-loop-anatomy:
Anatomy of the agent loop

The previous part established how Claude thinks turn by turn. This chapter zooms in on what happens when Claude is given a task that requires doing something — reading files, running commands, calling services — not just talking. You will see each phase of the agent loop labelled and explained, understand how the pieces connect, and leave with a clear mental model for building on top of them.

From chat to action

A plain chat session is passive: you write, Claude writes back. An agent session adds a new capability — Claude can invoke tools and receive their results before it sends you a final answer. That turns the single loop of the chat into a tighter inner loop that keeps spinning until the work is done.

The engine driving that inner loop is called the agent harness in Claude Code. Every agent-capable Claude product shares the same underlying shape: assemble a context, call the model, dispatch any tool calls, collect results, and repeat. Only when the model produces output with no tool calls does the loop terminate and hand you the result.

Whether you are using Claude Code in the terminal, embedding the SDK in a Node.js service, or running a workflow with parallel subagents, all of them execute this same fundamental loop. The details differ; the skeleton does not.

The six phases, dissected

Click each node in the explorer above to read its role and see how it connects to its neighbours. The sections below narrate the same journey in prose.

Phase 1 — Context assembly

Before the model sees anything, the harness assembles an append-only message array. This is the conversation so far, expressed as a list of messages with roles (, , ). Every piece of information Claude will ever see in this turn must be in that array — there is no out-of-band channel.

What lands in context on turn one:

- The system prompt: standing instructions, persona, rules, output format constraints. In Claude Code this is where  content is injected, along with built-in engineering instructions.
- The tool definitions: a schema for each tool Claude is allowed to call — name, description, parameters. Claude reads these to know what actions are available.
- The user message: your task or question.

From turn two onward, the array also includes every previous assistant response and every tool result from prior turns. Context is cumulative and append-only; nothing is ever removed (unless compaction runs, which we cover in a moment).

The system prompt, tool definitions, and  are identical on every turn in a session. Claude Code automatically applies prompt caching to these static prefixes after the first request, so you are not paying full token costs to re-encode them on every loop iteration.

Phase 2 — Model call

The harness sends the assembled context to the model and begins streaming the response. The model produces tokens until it decides it is done, which can happen in two ways:

1. Text-only response. Claude writes an answer without invoking any tool. This ends the loop.
2. Tool call response. Claude writes one or more structured tool-call blocks — each naming a tool and providing the arguments — and then stops generating. This sends the loop to phase 3.

An important nuance: a single model response can contain multiple tool calls at once. Claude Code handles parallel and sequential tool dispatch differently based on what is safe:

- Read-only tools (, , , and any tool annotated ) can run concurrently in a single batch.
- State-modifying tools (, , ) run sequentially, one at a time, to avoid races.

This distinction is handled automatically by the harness — you do not need to manage it.

Effort levels affect how much reasoning the model does before producing its response. The spectrum runs from  through , , , to . Higher effort means more thinking tokens consumed per turn, which trades cost for quality on complex tasks. The effort level is set once for a session and applies to every turn in the loop.

Phase 3 — Tool dispatch

For each tool call in the model's response, the harness checks permissions and then executes:

If permission is denied — because no allow rule matches and the user declines, or because a  rule fires — the loop still continues. The harness synthesises a "permission denied" tool result and feeds it back to the model, which can then decide whether to try a different approach or surface the problem to you.

Read-only tools that were batched together all execute in parallel during this phase. Their results are collected and then all returned to the model in phase 4.

Phase 4 — Results injection

Tool results are wrapped in  blocks and appended to the context array. From the model's perspective, results look exactly like user messages — they are just another turn in the conversation, with special role markers that indicate they came from a tool rather than a human.

The full tool-result block includes the output text, any error information, and a  that correlates the result back to the specific tool call that produced it. The harness maintains this correlation automatically.

This is the phase where context growth is most acute. A single  command that produces verbose output, or a  of a large file, can cost thousands of tokens in a single turn. Managing what you ask the model to read is the primary lever for controlling session cost and longevity.

Phase 5 — Loop check

After injecting results, the harness asks: should we go around again?

The answer is yes (another model call) unless one of these is true:

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Last model response had no tool calls | Loop terminates — emit  |
| Turn count hit  | Loop terminates — emit  |
| Spend crossed  | Loop terminates — emit  |
| Unrecoverable execution error | Loop terminates — emit  |

Without explicit limits, the loop runs indefinitely. This is deliberate: autonomous tasks can be long. But it means that open-ended prompts on production systems should always carry a  or  guard.

Phase 6 — Result emission

When the loop terminates cleanly, the harness emits a  carrying:

- The final text from the last model response.
- Token usage — input tokens, output tokens, and cache hit/miss breakdown.
- Cost — computed from usage, useful for logging.
- Session ID — a stable identifier you can use to resume or fork the session later.

The five  subtypes are: , , , , and . Your code (or Claude Code itself) surfaces these differently — success shows the answer; error subtypes show an explanation and, where possible, what partial work completed.

The compaction escape hatch

There is one more mechanism that can interrupt the loop without ending it: automatic compaction.

As context grows toward the model's limit, the harness summarises older parts of the conversation into a compact representation and replaces them with that summary. A  system message is emitted to mark where the summarisation occurred. The loop continues from that boundary with a smaller context.

Compaction is intentionally transparent — the loop keeps running, and the model receives a coherent-enough summary to continue the task. The trade-off is that fine details from early turns are lossy after compaction. For tasks where exact earlier outputs matter, it is worth structuring work so that key results are written to files (which persist on disk) rather than kept only in the message array (which can be compacted away).

After compaction the model can no longer see the literal text of early tool outputs — only the summary. If a later step needs an exact value from an early step, write it to a file or return it as a structured result before the context fills up.

Seeing the loop in practice

Here is a minimal SDK snippet (TypeScript) that shows the loop from the outside. The  call drives the loop; your code just iterates the emitted messages:

Internally, on a task like this, the loop would look roughly like:

Two model calls, one tool call, one result. The loop ran once and exited.

What engineers control

The loop itself is fixed. What you can tune:

| Knob | Effect |
|---|---|
|  | Hard cap on tool-use round trips (default: unlimited) |
|  | Hard cap on spend per run |
|  | Reasoning depth per model call ( → ) |
|  | How aggressively to auto-approve tool calls |
| Tool allow/deny rules | Which tools can run without user confirmation |
|  | Whether auto-compaction fires near the context limit |

For beginners: the default values are sensible for interactive use. You only need to reach for these when building automated pipelines or long-running tasks.

For engineers embedding the SDK: set  and  on every production  call. Unlimited loops are a correctness hazard (infinite tool retry) and a cost hazard (runaway spend). Add them first, tune later.

Recap

The agent loop has six phases: context assembly (build the message array) → model call (produce text or tool calls) → tool dispatch (execute, respecting permissions and parallelism rules) → results injection (append results to context) → loop check (repeat or terminate based on exit conditions) → result emission (return final text, usage, cost, session ID).

The loop terminates naturally when the model produces a response with no tool calls. Safety valves (, ) terminate it early. Compaction can shrink the context mid-run without stopping the loop.

The next chapter turns from structure to strategy — how to write system prompts and task descriptions that steer the loop toward reliable, predictable behaviour.
hooks:
Hooks — automating harness behavior

Hooks let you wire deterministic behavior into the Claude Code harness itself — scripts that run when sessions start, before a tool fires, after Claude responds, or at a dozen other moments in the agent lifecycle. By the end of this chapter you will know what hook events exist, how to configure them, and how to use them to enforce policies, inject context, and automate repetitive setup without relying on Claude's attention or memory.

The problem hooks solve

Claude Code is good at reasoning about what to do. It is less suited to mechanically enforcing that something always happens — log every shell command, block  before it runs, or populate an environment variable the moment a session opens. Those tasks need code that runs reliably regardless of what Claude decides to do next.

Hooks are that code. They are scripts (or SDK callback functions) that the harness executes at named lifecycle events. The harness calls them, not Claude. They can read context about what is happening, react to it, and in some cases block the action entirely before Claude ever sees a result.

Permission rules answer a yes/no question: is this tool call allowed? Hooks answer a richer question: what should happen around this event? A hook can approve or deny, but it can also inject extra context, log to a file, send a Slack message, mutate a tool's input before it runs, or replace its output before Claude reads it. Think of rules as static filters and hooks as dynamic logic.

The thirty hook events

The harness exposes thirty named events, organized into six phases. Every event delivers a JSON payload to your script on stdin, containing at minimum , , and .

Which events can block

Most events are observational — the hook runs, does whatever it likes, and the harness continues regardless of what it returns. A handful of events are blockable: exit with code 2 and the harness stops the action, using your script's stderr as the error message shown to the user.

| Blockable event | What gets blocked |
|---|---|
|  | Entire prompt — Claude never sees it |
|  | The tool call — Claude is told it was denied |
|  | The permission dialog — auto-deny or auto-allow |
|  | Claude finishing — inject more context to continue |
|  | Subagent completing — validate output before returning it |

Every other event: exit 2 shows stderr as a warning, but execution continues.

Configuring a hook

Shell-command hooks live in  under the  key. The structure is:

Each entry under an event name is a matcher group: a  pattern that filters which tool calls (or agents, etc.) this hook applies to, plus a  array of command entries to run when matched.

Matcher rules

The  field follows a three-way rule:

- Omitted, empty, or  — matches everything
- Letters, digits, underscores, and pipe characters only — treated as an exact string or pipe-separated list ()
- Anything else — treated as a JavaScript regular expression ( matches all MCP tools)

MCP tools are always named , so the regex pattern  is the idiomatic way to gate all MCP tool calls at once.

The  field (optional) adds a permission-rule condition — evaluated only on tool events. For example,  means the hook fires only when the  matcher has already matched and the command matches .

Exit codes and stdout

Your script communicates back to the harness through exit codes and stdout:

| Exit code | Meaning |
|---|---|
|  | Success — parse stdout for a JSON control object |
|  | Blocking error — stop the action, show stderr |
| Anything else | Non-blocking — show stderr, continue |

When you exit 0, stdout is parsed as JSON. The universal fields are:

On :

Four patterns worth knowing

1. Audit log every shell command

A  hook on  can write every command to a structured log before it runs. This is observational — exit 0, return nothing — so it never blocks Claude:

Register it once in  and every session on this machine logs shell commands automatically.

2. Block dangerous commands

A  hook can enforce a blocklist. Exit 2 to reject:

Pattern matching on shell commands is useful but not a security boundary. A sophisticated prompt can construct blocked commands indirectly (via a script file, for example). For genuine isolation, combine hooks with the OS-level sandboxed Bash tool, which enforces constraints at the process level regardless of how the command arrives.

3. Inject project context at session start

The harness passes this JSON back to Claude as session context. Claude starts every session already knowing the branch and recent PR state, without needing to run  or  itself.

4. Persist environment variables across Bash calls

Claude Code's Bash tool does not persist environment variables between calls by default. The  environment variable (available to all hooks) points to a file whose contents are sourced before each Bash invocation. A  hook can pre-populate it:

Any  lines written to  by a , , , or  hook persist for the rest of that session's Bash calls — no need to  manually on every turn.

Where to put hook configuration

Hooks follow the same scope hierarchy as all settings:

| Location | File | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
| Managed (org) | MDM / policy server | Everyone in the org |
| Local (yours only) |  | You, not committed |
| Project (shared) |  | Whole team |
| User (personal) |  | You, all projects |

A common split: audit logs and personal blocklists in ; project-specific context injection in  (committed, so the whole team gets it).

The  settings key disables every hook for a session — useful when debugging whether a hook is causing unexpected behavior.  (Managed-only) prevents project or user settings from adding hooks on top of the org baseline.

Hooks in the Agent SDK

If you are embedding the agent loop in an application via the TypeScript or Python SDK, hooks are callback functions rather than shell commands. You pass them via  in the  call:

SDK callback hooks run in your application process, not in Claude's context, so they carry no token cost. The most restrictive result wins when multiple hooks match the same event: if any hook returns , the tool is denied regardless of what others return.

A few SDK-specific notes grounded in the official docs:

-  and  are TypeScript-only SDK events — they do not exist as shell hook events.
- The Python SDK does not support  and  as callback hooks; use shell command hooks via  instead.
- Mark a hook  (TypeScript) or  (Python) to fire-and-forget side effects without blocking the agent.

Recap

Hooks are the harness's event bus. Thirty named events span the full session lifecycle — from  to , from  to , from  to . Shell scripts get the event payload on stdin, communicate back via exit codes and JSON on stdout, and can block actions by exiting with code 2. The SDK surfaces the same events as in-process callbacks with no token cost.

The four most immediately useful patterns are: audit logging (exit 0, write a log), blocking dangerous commands (exit 2 on match), injecting project context at session start ( from ), and persisting environment variables via .

Permissions & modes deep dive

The six permission modes are a single dial on a much richer control surface. This chapter peels back the layers: how each mode actually decides what to run, where  mode gets its read-only guarantee, what the Bash sandbox enforces that deny rules cannot, and how to wire CI pipelines that never hang on a permission prompt.

The control surface as a stack

Before going mode-by-mode, it helps to see all the pieces together. Every tool call Claude makes passes through this decision stack, top to bottom, stopping at the first match:

The implication: deny rules and blocking hooks win before the mode even matters. Mode is the fallback policy for calls that no rule has claimed.

The  branch in the diagram uses a model classifier to approve or deny each tool call. It is available only in the TypeScript Agent SDK — not in the CLI. CLI sessions use , , , , or .

Plan mode — the read-only guarantee

Plan mode's promise is that nothing on disk changes without your approval. The mechanism is precise: in plan mode, file-edit tool calls (, , ) are never auto-approved — they always surface a prompt. Every other tool still follows the normal mode rules.

, , , and  run silently in plan mode just as they do everywhere else. The restriction is specifically on writes, not on observation. Claude can — and does — read extensively while building a plan.

Claude Code ships a built-in  subagent that plan mode uses when you invoke  explicitly. That subagent skips CLAUDE.md files and git status to keep research fast, running on the parent model. The  tool surfaces the finished plan for your approval before file changes are allowed.

Switching plan mode: press  in the CLI to cycle . The  slash command toggles it directly. There is no settings key to persist plan mode across sessions — it is intentionally session-scoped.

When to use plan mode

| Situation | Why plan mode helps |
|---|---|
| Exploring an unfamiliar codebase | Claude reads broadly; you see the findings before any edits land |
| Architectural decision first | Forces a plan review before implementation begins |
| Shared / prod filesystem | Hard guarantee that nothing touches disk during the recon phase |
| Teaching or code review | You want Claude's analysis without its changes |

Plan mode pairs well with a high effort level. Set  before entering plan mode on a complex refactor and Claude will reason more carefully about its proposed approach before it ever asks to write a file.

acceptEdits — the right default for coding sessions

 auto-approves:

- , ,  — all file mutations
- Common filesystem shell commands: , , , 

Everything else —  with arbitrary commands, ,  — still follows default rules and prompts.

This is the mode most engineers settle into for active coding sessions. You still see a prompt for shell commands (which is where accidental  territory lives), but you avoid clicking through every incremental file save.

In , Claude can be stopped at any  command it decides to run. In , even shell commands pass silently — or fail silently if they lack an allow rule. Choose  when a human is watching; choose  only in fully automated pipelines with an explicit allowlist.

Interaction with allow rules in acceptEdits

Allow rules layer on top of mode. If you have  in , those npm commands run without a prompt even in  mode —  adds nothing for them. Where  adds value is the long tail of file operations Claude generates that you have not pre-defined rules for.

dontAsk — CI and headless pipelines

 is the mode for automation. It never shows a prompt. The decision rule is binary: if there is a matching allow rule, the tool runs; if not, the call is denied silently.

The consequence: every tool call your pipeline needs must be in  before you activate . Anything not listed fails — not with an error Claude can retry, but with a silent deny that blocks progress without explanation.

Wiring a dontAsk CI run

maxTurns and maxBudgetUsd as safety bounds

In  + headless contexts there is no human to stop a runaway loop. Set both:

bypassPermissions — last resort for truly isolated environments

Two hard limits remain even in this mode:
- Cannot run as root on Unix.
- It is the caller's responsibility to ensure the environment provides actual isolation.

The flag exists for containers where the OS itself is the boundary — a Docker image with only your repo mounted, a fresh VM with no credentials on it. Using it on a developer workstation removes every guardrail simultaneously. A misread instruction can delete files, commit secrets, or run arbitrary shell code with no intervention point.

The canonical pattern is to run  inside an ephemeral container job — one that mounts only the working directory and has no access to production credentials, SSH keys, or cloud IAM roles.

The Bash sandbox — OS-level confinement

Permission rules work at the text level: deny  blocks that exact pattern. But Claude can write a Python script that calls  — and a deny rule on  does not stop what Python does internally.

The Bash sandbox is a different layer. It applies OS-level enforcement to every process spawned by the  tool, including child processes, interpreted scripts, and anything those scripts execute. It cannot be sidestepped by writing an intermediary.

Key properties sourced from the tools reference:

- Sandbox network rules are independent of  allow rules. A domain allowed in  does not automatically get network access inside the sandbox — you configure network permissions separately.
- The sandbox is not available on Windows (where the  tool preview is used instead).
- Unlike  rules, sandbox restrictions apply to indirect file access — e.g., a Python script that opens a file Claude did not name directly.

Think of deny rules as "what Claude is allowed to ask the shell to do" and the sandbox as "what the shell is actually capable of doing." They are complementary. For maximum confinement you want both: deny rules block the obvious paths, the sandbox blocks the indirect ones.

The PermissionRequest hook — programmable approval

Rather than showing a dialog to the user,  lets a hook script decide. This is the mechanism for custom approval UIs, policy engines, or headless pipelines that need selective gating without going full .

The hook receives the tool name and input via stdin as JSON. Its exit code and JSON stdout determine the outcome:

| Exit code | stdout  | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 0 |  | Tool runs, no prompt |
| 0 |  | Tool blocked |
| 0 |  | Falls through to normal dialog |
| 0 |  | Next hook in chain decides |
| 2 | (any) | Tool blocked, stderr shown as error |

When multiple  hooks are attached to the same event, precedence is: deny > defer > ask > allow. A single deny hook beats all the allows.

Precedence in practice

This lets you build a layered policy:

Managed settings — locking the control surface itself

For teams and enterprises, managed settings sit above everything else in the hierarchy:

Managed settings cannot be overridden. The ones most relevant to permission control:

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
|  | Prevents user and project settings from adding any permission rules |
|  | Removes the  mode option |
|  | Only hooks defined in managed settings can run |
|  | Allowlist of URL patterns for HTTP-based hooks |

The  key (v2.1.136+) goes further: it points to an executable that generates dynamic managed settings at session start — a policy server that can produce different rules per-user, per-repo, or per-time-of-day without re-deploying static config.

Choosing a mode: the decision matrix

| Context | Recommended mode | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Exploring unfamiliar code |  | No writes; full read access |
| Active coding, human watching |  | Edits flow; shell still prompts |
| Trusted task, human available |  | Full control; prompted on everything risky |
| CI/CD pipeline |  + explicit allowlist | No hangs; predictable |
| Isolated container |  | OS provides the boundary |
| Custom policy engine |  +  hook | Programmable per-call decisions |

Recap

Permission modes are the fallback policy, not the whole system. Deny rules and blocking hooks fire before the mode matters. Plan mode's guarantee is scoped precisely to file writes — reads are always allowed.  fills the coding-session sweet spot between  and full headless automation.  requires a complete allowlist up front and pairs with / bounds in any long-running job. The Bash sandbox adds OS-level confinement that text-based deny rules cannot provide. The  hook makes the entire approval decision programmable.

Next: the Hooks — intercepting the agent loop chapter covers the full 30-event hook surface and the patterns for auditing, blocking, and injecting context at every stage of Claude's execution.
settings-env:
Settings, env & config

Claude Code's behaviour is shaped by a layered configuration system: a structured  file for persistent preferences and rules, environment variables for one-off or deployment-specific overrides, and a scope hierarchy that lets user, project, and managed (org-wide) settings coexist without conflict. This chapter maps that system precisely so you know exactly where to put a setting, when a variable takes precedence, and how to debug unexpected behaviour when something is not working as expected.

The two knobs: settings vs. environment variables

Claude Code distinguishes between two kinds of configuration:

- * — the persistent, structured store for preferences, permission rules, hooks, MCP server declarations, and any key/value environment pairs you want injected at startup. Lives at known paths; committed or not depending on scope.
- Environment variables — classic shell-level overrides. Some are consumed by the Claude Code process itself; others are forwarded into every  tool call Claude makes. Variables take effect at process start and do not survive between shell sessions unless you set them in your shell profile or the  block of .

The relationship is largely orthogonal: most settings have no environment-variable equivalent, and many environment variables have no settings counterpart. The exceptions (where both exist) follow a predictable rule — the environment variable wins for the current invocation, the settings value is the persistent default.

The scope hierarchy

Claude Code merges settings from five layers in a fixed priority order. A key present at a higher priority wins; lower-priority values are ignored for that key.

Managed sits at the top and cannot be overridden by any user or project setting. It is distributed via MDM or a server configuration endpoint — the mechanism enterprises use to enforce org-wide policy. When  is set there, users and projects cannot add their own permission rules at all.

CLI arguments (, , , ) apply for a single invocation. They are useful in scripts and CI where you want a per-run override without touching any file.

Local () is gitignored by convention. Use it for personal tweaks — your own allow rules, your preferred effort level — that should not affect teammates.

Project () is committed alongside the code. Every session that opens this project directory — yours, your teammate's, CI — gets the same project-level settings. This is the right place for permission rules that reflect what the codebase legitimately needs.

User () is the baseline for all your projects. Think of it as your personal global defaults: preferred model, editor mode, language preference.

If a Bash command is always safe for a specific project (e.g., ), commit it in  so the whole team benefits and CI does not prompt. If it is only safe for you personally (e.g., ), put it in  or your user settings. If a command is unsafe for anyone, add a  rule in the project settings.

The  file structure

The file is plain JSON. All keys are optional — you only need the keys you actually want to change. Here is a representative project-level file showing the most commonly needed sections:

A few structural notes:

- The  object takes  and  arrays. Deny beats allow when both match a given tool call.
- The  object is keyed by event name (e.g., , , ). Each event maps to an array of matchers.
- The  object injects key/value pairs into the Claude Code process environment at startup — making them available both to Claude's reasoning and to every  command that runs.

Key settings categories

Claude Code exposes more than 80 settings keys. Rather than enumerate them all, the table below groups the most practically important ones by area:

| Area | Key examples | What they control |
|---|---|---|
| Model | , , ,  | Which model runs, fallbacks when overloaded, reasoning depth |
| Display | , , ,  | Vim keys, preferred response language, accessibility |
| Memory & files | , ,  | Auto-memory read/write,  snapshots, session file retention |
| Permissions | ,  | Allow/deny rules, prevent auto mode |
| MCP servers | , ,  | Which MCP servers load from  |
| Hooks | ,  | Lifecycle event handlers |
| Features | , ,  | Toggle major subsystems |
| Auth | , ,  | Scripts that produce credentials dynamically |
| Attribution | ,  | Commit authorship, git workflow instructions |
| Org (Managed only) | , , ,  | Org-wide CLAUDE.md, startup messages, settings merge behaviour |

Two settings deserve extra attention because they are subtle:

The default  means managed keys shadow any project/user equivalent.  allows the managed layer to extend rather than replace arrays like  — useful when you want to enforce some org rules while still allowing projects to add their own.

The executable runs at session start and returns a settings JSON blob. This enables conditional policies — e.g., different rules for engineers vs. contractors — without redeploying configuration.

Environment variables

Environment variables are the escape hatch for one-off or system-level control. Some act before  is even read (e.g., credential variables); others fine-tune tool behaviour deep in the runtime:

Unlike  in  (which sets variables in the Claude Code process environment),  is specifically designed for variables that need to be present inside  subshells — think tokens that expire and need refreshing, or project-specific shell state. A  hook can write fresh  lines to this file, and Claude Code will source them into every subsequent  call for the session. This is the correct pattern for dynamic credentials.

This makes them visible to Claude's reasoning and to tool calls.  injects variables specifically into  subshells, and it can be updated mid-session (e.g., by a hook) so refreshed credentials are picked up without restarting. Use  for static values; use  for values that need to refresh.

Config layering end to end

To make layering concrete, consider what happens when Claude Code resolves the  setting at session start:

If no managed settings exist, the CLI arg would win. Remove the CLI arg and local settings win. The user settings at the bottom act as the fallback when nothing above specifies the key.

The same priority chain applies to , , , and every other key.

Debugging config problems

When Claude is behaving unexpectedly — prompting when it should not, refusing a tool call, running with the wrong model — the diagnosis usually lives in the settings chain. Three commands help:

-  — opens the interactive configuration UI. Shows the current effective value for every key and lets you change most of them in place.
-  — lists every active allow and deny rule along with which scope each came from (user, project, local, managed). Run this before a long agentic task to confirm the allow list matches what the task needs.

A common trap: you add an allow rule to  and the prompt still appears. Check whether  is set in managed settings — if so, your project-level rule is silently ignored. Another: you set  in your user settings but a different model runs. Check whether the project or local file overrides it (they take priority).

The  block as a convenience pattern

For teams who want a repeatable local dev environment without requiring developers to set shell variables manually, the  block in the project  is a clean solution:

Every session that opens the project gets these variables automatically — no shell profile edits required. Because the file is committed, new team members get the same environment as everyone else on the first .

For values that differ per developer (personal access tokens, local port overrides), put the  block in  instead — same structure, personal scope.

Recap

Claude Code's configuration system has two instruments —  for structured, persistent preferences and environment variables for process-level and dynamic overrides — resolved through a five-level priority chain: Managed > CLI args > Local > Project > User.

The practical rules:
- Commit project-appropriate allow rules and  values in .
- Use  for personal overrides and per-developer env vars.
- Use  for dynamic credentials that need to refresh mid-session.
- Use CLI args for one-off per-invocation overrides (CI is a natural home for this).
- Use , , and  to inspect the effective resolved state when something does not behave as expected.

slash-commands:
Slash commands & built-ins

Claude Code ships with a set of slash commands that let you control the session, manage context, and trigger complex workflows — all without leaving the conversation. By the end of this chapter you will know which built-in commands exist and what each one does, how to create your own reusable shortcuts with a simple Markdown file, and how bundled skills extend the command palette with ready-made workflows.

What a slash command is

A slash command is a  shortcut you type at the Claude Code prompt. Some commands configure the session (switch model, set effort level). Some manage context (compact history, rewind file edits). Some launch multi-step workflows (deep research, code review). Under the hood each command is either a built-in that ships with the binary or a Markdown file on disk that Claude reads and executes when you invoke it.

Typing  at any time shows the full list available in your current session — built-ins, bundled skills, your custom commands, and any prompts exposed by connected MCP servers.

Built-in commands

The table below covers the most commonly used built-ins. This is not exhaustive —  is always the source of truth — but it represents the commands you will reach for daily.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|

|  | Reset conversation to an empty context (drops all history) |
|  | Summarise older history in place to free context space |

|  | Show token and cost usage for the current session |

Claude's context window is append-only — every file read, tool output, and response accumulates. When a long session starts to feel sluggish or you notice Claude losing track of earlier details,  summarises the older history in place and hands back significant headroom. The summary is injected as a  system message so the timeline is preserved.

Effort levels and 

Effort controls how much reasoning Claude applies per turn. Higher effort means more thinking tokens, higher cost, and noticeably better results on complex tasks. The levels are:

-  — the default; balanced for everyday work

Set it for a session with , or persist it in  via .

and file checkpoints

Every time Claude edits a file, Claude Code snapshots the previous version.  lets you pick a checkpoint and restore the file to that state — no git required. Checkpointing is on by default (controlled by  in settings). This is the fastest recovery path when Claude takes a wrong turn on a refactor.

Bundled skills

Beyond the built-in commands, Claude Code ships with a set of bundled skills — pre-installed slash commands that each encapsulate a complete workflow. They appear in  alongside built-ins.

| Skill | What it does |
|---|---|
|  | Review the current diff for bugs, simplification opportunities, and efficiency wins |
|  | Systematic diagnosis loop: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, verify |
|  | Infer how to launch this project and start it (reads README, package.json, Makefile) |
|  | Launch the app and observe its behaviour to confirm a change works |
|  | Run a prompt against many targets in parallel |
|  | Fan out web searches, cross-check sources, synthesise a cited report |
|  | Repeat a prompt or skill on an interval |

The key difference from built-ins: skills load lazily. Their instructions only reach Claude's context when you invoke them, so they cost no tokens when you are not using them. A project skill with the same name as a bundled skill takes precedence — you can override any bundled behaviour at the project level.

Writing your own slash commands

This is where the system becomes genuinely powerful. Any Markdown file you drop in the right directory becomes a slash command with no additional wiring.

Where to put the file

| Location | Scope | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
|  | Personal | Only you, in every project |
|  | Project | Everyone on the team |
|  | Personal (preferred format) | Only you, in every project |
|  | Project (preferred format) | Everyone on the team |

Both the  and  layouts work identically as slash commands. The skills format is preferred because it supports a richer frontmatter and slots into the same system as bundled skills.

A minimal custom command

Now  is a real command in your session.

Frontmatter fields

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
|  | One-line summary shown in ; also the phrase Claude matches when deciding to auto-invoke the skill |
|  | Comma-separated list of tools this command may use (e.g., ) |
|  | Hint shown next to the command name in autocomplete |

|  | Set  to make the skill manual-only (Claude will not auto-trigger it) |
|  | Set  to run the command in a background subagent |

Dynamic context injection

Any line in the skill body that starts with a backtick-wrapped  command is executed at load time and replaced with its output before Claude sees the content:

When you invoke this command, Claude receives the actual diff inline — it does not need to run a separate tool call to fetch it. This keeps the skill fast and keeps the tool call count down.

Claude Code watches your skill directories for changes. Adding, editing, or deleting a skill takes effect immediately in the running session. The one exception: creating a brand-new skill directory for the first time requires a restart to register the directory watcher.

Organising commands in a team repo

For a project with more than a handful of commands, subdirectory organisation keeps things tidy. A file at  becomes the slash command . The directory prefix acts as a namespace, avoiding name collisions across areas of the codebase.

How slash commands reach the SDK

If you are embedding Claude Code in an application via the Agent SDK, slash commands are dispatched the same way a user would type them — by including the  string in the prompt. The  message that arrives at the start of every SDK session carries a  field listing every command available in the current configuration, which lets your application dynamically surface the right options.

A handful of built-in commands (like , which opens a TUI panel) require an interactive terminal. They are not useful from code. Stick to commands whose output is plain text or that perform well-defined actions; check the  list to confirm a command is present before relying on it programmatically.

Recap

Slash commands are the control surface for a Claude Code session. Built-in commands handle context, modes, and session management. Bundled skills wrap complete workflows — code review, debugging, research — into single invocations. Custom commands let you encode your team's workflows as Markdown files that anyone on the project can invoke instantly.

The rule of thumb: if you find yourself giving Claude the same multi-step briefing more than twice, it belongs in a skill file. Write it once, invoke it forever.

Next up: the chapter on hooks shows you how to run your own code around Claude's tool calls — before they execute, after they finish, and at every other lifecycle event in a session.
tool-surface:
The tool surface

Claude Code ships with a catalogue of built-in tools that give the agent loop its hands. By the end of this chapter you will know what each major tool does, why the groupings matter, and — most importantly — which tool to reach for in a given situation. Use the interactive map below as a living reference as you read.

Tools are the only way Claude acts

When Claude is working as an agent it cannot produce side-effects by thinking harder. Every concrete action — reading a file, running a test, fetching a page — happens through a named tool call. The agent loop feeds the result of that call back into the context, and Claude continues reasoning with it.

This architecture has a practical consequence: if you understand the tool surface, you understand exactly what Claude can and cannot do. There is no hidden action channel. The full catalogue, organised by surface area, is filterable in the widget below.

The "perm" badge (amber) means the tool shows an approval prompt before running the first time in a session, unless you have an allow rule for it. The "silent" badge means no prompt — the tool only observes and cannot change anything. This maps directly to the permission system covered in the previous chapter.

Reading and finding files

The three file-discovery tools form a natural hierarchy.

* loads a file's contents into the context with line numbers. It handles plain text, source code, images, PDFs, and Jupyter notebooks. It requires no permission prompt because it only observes. The catch: every byte read costs context tokens, so reading a 10,000-line file when you need three lines is wasteful. Claude will prefer targeted reads when it can.

 finds files by path pattern, returning results sorted by modification time, capped at 100 entries. It does not respect  by default. Use it when you need a list of files matching a shape — ,  — before deciding which ones to read.

 searches file contents using ripgrep, and unlike  it does respect . Three modes:  (default, just filenames),  (matching lines with context),  (occurrences per file). If you know what text you are looking for,  is almost always faster than reading many files.

The typical search flow is:

 is a step further: code intelligence powered by a language server. It understands types, not just text — jump to definition, find all references, list type errors, walk call hierarchies. After every file edit,  automatically reports any new type errors so Claude can fix them without a separate build step. It requires a code intelligence plugin installed alongside Claude Code.

Writing and editing files

Three tools, three use cases.

 creates a file or completely overwrites an existing one. Because overwriting is destructive, it requires a prior  in the same session — Claude must have seen the current contents before it can replace them. Use this when creating new files or doing a full rewrite.

 does exact string replacement within a file. The  must appear exactly once (use  for repeated occurrences). It is more precise and less risky than  for targeted changes because Claude can only touch the strings it explicitly names. Most code edits happen via  rather than .

 modifies Jupyter notebook cells by cell ID — replace, insert, or delete — without touching the notebook format boilerplate. This is the right tool for  files; using  on raw notebook JSON is fragile.

Claude Code runs , , , and  concurrently within a single turn when it needs results from multiple files. , , and  run sequentially to avoid race conditions. This is automatic — no configuration needed. Structuring prompts to front-load information-gathering lets the parallelism do useful work.

Running shell commands

 is the general escape hatch: run any shell command, pipe results, chain commands with . A few constraints worth knowing:

- Default timeout is 2 minutes per command (raise it with the  parameter, up to 10 minutes).
- Output is capped at 30,000 characters. Commands that produce more need to pipe through , , or  before Claude sees the result.
- Environment variables do not persist between separate  calls in the same session. Working directory changes (via ) do persist, provided the target is within the project directory or a directory you have explicitly added to the session.
- Shell aliases from your  or  are available — Claude Code sources your profile at session start.

Because  can do almost anything, it requires a permission prompt by default. The pattern for automating this safely is to add specific command patterns to  in your project's :

 is  for streaming output. It runs a command in the background and feeds each output line back to Claude in real time — useful for tailing logs, watching a test runner, or reacting to a CI webhook. Claude can take action on each line as it arrives rather than waiting for the command to finish.

Searching the web

Two tools, two distinct jobs — and they are not interchangeable.

 queries a search backend and returns titles and URLs. It does not return page content. It may issue up to 8 backend searches internally per call, refining results before returning them. Use it to discover sources, not to read them.

 fetches a URL and runs an extraction prompt on the page before returning anything to Claude. This is intentionally lossy: rather than dumping raw HTML into the context, a small fast model extracts what is relevant and passes that summary. There is a 15-minute response cache. Cross-host redirects return redirect information rather than following automatically — Claude needs to issue a second call with the new URL.

The two tools compose naturally:  locates the right page, then  reads it. Claude does this automatically when asked a question that requires live information.

The extraction model decides what from a page reaches Claude's context. If you need a specific table, API signature, or code block from a documentation page, say so explicitly in the prompt alongside the URL. Vague extraction prompts produce vague results.

Tasks and scheduling

Task tools (, , , , ) replaced the older  as of v2.1.142. They manage a structured task list within the session — Claude uses this to track multi-step plans, update progress, and signal completion. You can inspect the live task list with  in an interactive session.

, , and  schedule prompts to run on a recurring or one-shot basis within the session. A cron task that fires every 5 minutes, re-checks a CI status, and notifies you when it goes green is a typical use case.

 is a narrower primitive: it tells Claude when to resume the current  iteration. The gap between  (external schedule) and  (self-paced loop) lets you choose whether the clock or Claude's own judgment drives the rhythm.

Agents and subagents

 spawns a subagent — an independent Claude instance that runs its own agent loop and returns a summary to the parent. Subagents start with a fresh context (only their own system prompt, not the parent's conversation history), which is both their strength and their limitation: they are cheap on the parent's context budget but know only what you explicitly give them.

The  tool does not itself require a permission prompt. The subagent's tool calls surface in the parent terminal and follow the same permission rules. A subagent running in the background () gets its own git worktree and cannot interfere with the parent's working directory.

 executes a named skill — a reusable instruction set defined in a Markdown file. Skills are lazy-loaded: their body content only enters the context when the skill is invoked, unlike  which is always present. Think of them as packaged procedures that Claude knows how to call by name.

A decision guide for common situations

| I want to… | Reach for… |
|---|---|
| Read a specific file |  |
| Find files matching a name pattern |  |
| Find files containing specific text |  |
| Check types / find references |  |
| Create a new file |  |
| Change a few lines in an existing file |  |
| Run a test, build, or any shell command |  |
| Watch streaming output (logs, CI) |  |
| Find pages about a topic |  then  |
| Fetch a specific known URL |  |
| Parallelize work across multiple files |  (subagents) |
| Run a reusable procedure |  |
| Schedule a recurring check |  |

Recap

The tool surface divides into five surfaces: filesystem (, , , , , , ), shell (, ), web (, ), agents (, ), and scheduling/tasks (, , ). Read-only tools are silent and can run in parallel; state-changing tools prompt by default and run sequentially. Every concrete action Claude takes flows through one of these tools — there is no other path.

Next: the agent loop** chapter goes inside the loop itself — how turns sequence, how tool results flow back, how context fills up, and when the loop ends.
compaction-autocompact:
Compaction & autocompact

Every Claude Code session runs on a fixed-size context window. As turns accumulate, that window fills up — and when it does, something has to give. This chapter explains the mechanics of compaction: why it triggers, what it actually costs you, and the practical techniques that keep context lean enough to work in long or repeated sessions.

Why context has a ceiling

A Claude session is an append-only message array. Every prompt you write, every tool result that comes back, every file Claude reads — all of it lands in that array and stays there for the rest of the session. Nothing is ever removed. The array only grows.

This is intentional. The model needs prior turns to reason coherently about the task. But it creates an inescapable constraint: the array cannot grow forever. Every model has a maximum context size, and once the session crosses it, the loop cannot continue.

Try the simulator above. Switch between Lean and Bloated presets, then drag the turn count upward. Notice that the bloated session — larger , more tools, file reads returned as tool results — hits the compaction threshold in far fewer turns. The system block alone (2 K vs 18 K tokens) makes an enormous difference before any conversation has even started.

The system block is the static prefix of every request: your  files, the tool schemas for every built-in and MCP tool registered to the session, and Claude Code's own engineering instructions. It is prompt-cached after the first request in a session, which avoids paying full encoding cost on every turn — but it still occupies space in the window on every call. A large  or many registered MCP tools can consume tens of thousands of tokens before you have typed a single word.

When autocompact triggers

Claude Code monitors the fill ratio of the context window continuously. When context approaches the limit, the autocompact mechanism fires automatically. You did not have to ask; the session did not crash; the loop simply continues from a summarised starting point.

The sequence looks like this:

The  system message is the observable marker. If you are watching session events with the Agent SDK, you will see a  with subtype  at this moment. The loop itself does not stop — it keeps running, picking up from the summary.

The  slash command triggers the same mechanism manually, before the threshold is reached. This is useful when you can tell that early turns have become dead weight and you want to recover headroom proactively.

You can also disable autocompact entirely:

- Settings key:  in 
- Env var: 

Disabling it means the session will eventually hit the hard context limit and terminate with an error rather than gracefully summarising. This is useful in automated pipelines where you need deterministic, unmodified context — but it is risky for long interactive sessions.

What compaction actually costs you

Compaction is lossy by design. The compactor produces a summary, and summaries omit detail. After a compaction boundary, the model can no longer see the literal text of any tool output or message that was compacted away — only the distilled version.

The practical failure modes:

Exact values disappear. If a tool returned a specific value — a file hash, an ID, a port number, an exact error message — and you did not write it somewhere durable, it may be gone after compaction. The summary might say "the build produced a binary" without recording where it was placed.

Reasoning chains compress. Multi-step arguments constructed over many turns compress into conclusions. Claude may remember the conclusion ("use approach X") without the reasoning ("because Y and Z were ruled out in turns 3–7"). If something goes wrong, the debugging context is thinner.

File state and disk state diverge. Compaction has no visibility into what is on disk. If Claude read a file in turn 4 and the file has since changed on disk, the compacted context will contain only the old version in summary form. Claude may not know to re-read it.

Any value you will need after a compaction boundary should be written to a file before it disappears. This is not just good hygiene — it is the correct architectural pattern for long sessions. Disk is persistent; context is ephemeral. Write results to files, commit them to git, save them to structured output. Do not rely on the message array as your only record.

The token cost of common operations

Understanding which operations are expensive helps you structure sessions to last longer before compaction. The simulator's presets reflect real-world proportions:

| Operation | Approximate token cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Short user message | ~100–200 | Cheap; doesn't accumulate fast |
| Assistant reply | ~300–1,200 | Varies with task complexity |
| Reading a small file | ~500–2,000 | Depends on file length |
| Reading a large file | 5,000–20,000+ | A 1,000-line file at ~5 tokens/line |
| Search results (many files) | 2,000–6,000 | Can be large when Grep returns many matches |
| MCP tool result | 500–10,000+ | Highly variable; JSON responses balloon fast |

These are illustrative ranges, not official benchmarks. The key insight is the order of magnitude difference: a file read can cost as much as dozens of plain messages. A session that reads ten large files in the first few turns has consumed a substantial fraction of the window before the conversation has even properly started.

Strategies for keeping context lean

Keep  focused

The system block is paid on every single turn in the session. Every kilobyte you add to  is a recurring cost that slightly shrinks the space available for actual conversation. This does not mean  should be short — it means it should be focused. Architecture overview, sharp edges, critical conventions: yes. Step-by-step procedural instructions that only apply sometimes: better moved to a Skill, which loads lazily only when invoked.

Skills are the correct alternative for "instructions I need sometimes." They are not injected into the system block on every turn; they are loaded on demand. Moving procedural content from  to Skills directly reduces your baseline token burn.

Prefer targeted reads over full-file reads

When Claude needs information from a file, it is worth asking: do you need the whole file, or just a portion? The  tool accepts  and  parameters for exactly this reason.  returning matching lines rather than full-file content is another approach.

A pattern that works well for large codebases: use  first (returns filenames and matching lines, not full content), then  only the files and line ranges that are relevant. This replaces a potential 15,000-token full-file read with a 300-token grep result plus a targeted 500-token partial read.

Write results to files early

Long-running tasks often produce intermediate results — IDs, generated content, computed values — that will be needed again later. If those results exist only in tool-result messages, they are compaction victims. Write them to files as you go: a , a , a simple text file in a scratch directory. The file persists across compaction boundaries; the message array does not.

This maps to a broader principle in packet research (F-09): across 76 primary sessions observed in a real project,  was invoked manually only once. Session continuity came not from carefully managing the context window, but from a dedicated memory system — automated per-session summaries written to disk and injected at the next session start. The context window is not the right place to store durable knowledge; disk is.

Manage MCP tool registrations

Every MCP tool schema registered to a session adds to the system block. If you have fifteen MCP servers connected but only ever use three tools from them, the schemas for the other twelve are consuming tokens on every turn. Claude Code supports deferred tool loading (via ) precisely to avoid this: tools that are not immediately needed are not loaded into context until you ask for them. When configuring MCP servers, prefer fine-grained enablement over connecting everything at once.

Use  before a predictable expensive phase

If you know a task is about to enter a phase that will consume a lot of tokens — reading many files, running a large search sweep — and your context is already well-used, running  first is a sound move. It resets the fill counter and gives you headroom for the expensive work ahead. The cost is the same information loss as autocompact, but you choose the timing rather than letting it happen mid-task.

What engineers can observe and hook

The Agent SDK exposes two hook events for compaction:

- * fires before the compaction begins. You can use this to write a snapshot of any in-context state you want to preserve before summarisation.
-  fires after compaction completes, with access to the new context. You can log the boundary, inject additional context for the fresh session, or notify your infrastructure.

Neither hook is blocking — compaction will proceed regardless. But they are the right place to run automated state preservation logic in production pipelines.

Recap

Autocompact is Claude Code's self-preservation mechanism: when the context window approaches its limit, the harness summarises older turns and continues from the boundary. It is lossy — exact values, reasoning chains, and file state from before the boundary may not survive in full detail.

The strategies that matter most: keep your  focused and move rarely-needed procedures to Skills; prefer targeted reads ( + partial ) over whole-file reads; write durable values to files rather than leaving them in the message array; and manage MCP tool registrations to avoid inflating the system block unnecessarily.

The next chapter looks at how to structure the work that happens within* the context — prompting patterns and task decomposition that make long sessions more predictable and less prone to compaction surprises.
context-window-budget:
The context window & its budget

The context window is the entire working memory Claude has for a session — everything it can see at once. This chapter maps what fills that space, shows how quickly each category grows, and gives you concrete strategies to spend the budget where it earns the most.

What lives in the context window

Every Claude session is backed by an append-only message array. Nothing is ever silently removed from it mid-session — entries only accumulate. When the model replies to you, it has read every byte in that array. When a tool runs and returns output, that output is appended. The array is the complete shared state.

Four categories of content compete for space in it:

| Category | Examples | Token range |
|---|---|---|
| System block | System prompt, , tool schemas | 500 – 50 000 |
| Conversation turns | Your messages, Claude's replies | 50 – 5 000 per turn |
| Tool outputs | File reads, Bash stdout, search results | 100 – 30 000 per call |
| Injected context | Memory files, skill content at invocation | 200 – 10 000 |

The sim below lets you see these forces in action. Switch between "Lean session" and "Bloated session", drag the turn slider, and watch the fill bar approach the compaction threshold.

A single  of a 500-line TypeScript file costs around 4 000 – 6 000 tokens. Ask Claude to read ten files in one turn and you can burn 40 000 – 60 000 tokens before a single line of work has happened. This is the most common source of unexpectedly short sessions.

Anatomy of the system block

The system block is loaded once — at the very first request — and then prompt-cached for every subsequent turn. Prompt caching means the model does not re-encode those tokens on turns 2, 3, 4 … The repeated read is cheap. The first read is not.

What lands in the system block:

Tool schemas are a hidden cost. Every MCP server you connect adds its tool definitions to the system block. A server exposing 20 tools at 300 tokens each contributes 6 000 tokens before you type a word. Claude Code mitigates this with deferred tool loading (): MCP tool schemas are not loaded upfront; they are fetched on-demand when Claude searches for them. This keeps the system block lean for servers you rarely use.

CLAUDE.md content is technically injected as a user message (not in the system prompt itself), but the harness caches it after the first request so subsequent turns pay negligible cost to re-send it. What matters for budgeting is size: a 400-line CLAUDE.md costs around 6 000 – 8 000 tokens, static for the session.

How turns accumulate

After the system block, every turn in the session is appended in chronological order. The model sees the full history every time it replies — there is no sliding window that drops older turns automatically.

Turns grow the context in three ways:

1. Conversation breadth — long replies, long user messages.
2. Tool verbosity — stdout from Bash commands, search result dumps, file contents.
3. Repetition — asking Claude to re-read the same file twice stores two copies.

The most effective lever is controlling tool verbosity. A  that dumps 300 filenames is cheaper than a  of a single large file. Prefer targeted over broad.

The compaction threshold

When the total token count approaches the model's context limit, Claude Code triggers automatic compaction. The harness summarises the older portion of the conversation, replaces those turns with a compact digest, and emits a  system message. The session continues from that boundary with breathing room.

Compaction is intentionally transparent — the loop keeps going. But it is lossy: fine details from early turns (exact values, verbatim outputs) are replaced by summaries. If a later step depends on a precise value from an early step, write it to a file on disk before context fills up.

You can also trigger compaction manually with  before it happens automatically — useful when you want to summarise a completed sub-task before starting the next one, keeping the summary accurate while full detail is still available.

After compaction the model cannot recall the verbatim text of early tool outputs. If a later step needs an exact string from an early file read or Bash result, instruct Claude to write it to a file first.

Reading the budget

Here is how the token categories sum in a realistic session:

On a 100 000-token budget, that 20-turn session uses about half the window. Add a large CLAUDE.md (15 000 tokens), several extra tool schemas, and a few code-heavy file reads, and the same session hits 80 % — near the compaction threshold.

The takeaway: the system block is fixed overhead; tool outputs are the variable you control session-to-session.

Strategies for a healthy budget

Keep the system block lean

- Trim  to what future-you actually needs. Remove resolved bugs, one-off notes, and content already captured in skills.
- Use Skills for large procedures and workflows. Skill content loads only when the skill is invoked — not on every turn. A 2 000-token procedure sitting in a skill costs nothing until you call it.
- Disable MCP servers you are not using for a session. Each one contributes tool schemas even if you never call it.

Be surgical with file reads

- Ask Claude to read specific line ranges rather than whole files when only a section matters.
- When exploring an unfamiliar codebase, ask Claude to use  and  first (cheap — returns file names and match counts) before committing to  (expensive — returns full content).
- If Claude needs to refer to a large file multiple times, have it extract the relevant sections into a temporary file that costs far fewer tokens to re-read.

Prefer writing results to disk over keeping them in context

- When a long Bash output will be needed later, pipe it to a file: . Claude can then read specific lines rather than holding the full output in the message array.
- This pattern also survives compaction: disk is not subject to the lossy summary.

Use  strategically

- Before switching from exploration to implementation, compact the research phase. The summary preserves decisions without preserving every file dump.
- Before a very large file write (which will itself consume tokens), compact earlier conversation to free space.

Watch the fill bar

In the Claude Code CLI,  shows the current token count and fill ratio. Glance at it before long autonomous runs. If you are already at 60 % after setup, consider whether the task will complete before hitting the threshold — or whether you should compact first.

 defaults to  in settings. You can disable it with  or  — but then you are responsible for noticing when the context is full and compacting manually. Most users should leave it on.

What engineers should instrument

If you are embedding the Agent SDK, the  carries token usage:

The  value tells you how much of the system block is being served from cache (good: cheap) versus re-encoded (less good: full cost). A healthy session shows high cache hits after turn one.

For production pipelines, log usage per  and alert when average input tokens per session climbs — it is an early signal that system block bloat or overly verbose tool calls are degrading cost efficiency.

Recap

The context window is an append-only bucket. The system block (static overhead: instructions, , tool schemas) is cached after the first request. Conversation turns, tool outputs, and injected memory fill the remainder turn by turn. Compaction summarises older history when the bucket approaches its limit — it is automatic and lossy.

Your levers: keep the system block intentionally small; be surgical about which files you ask Claude to read and how many times; write durable results to disk rather than holding them in the message array; use  before pivoting to a new sub-task.

The next chapter builds on this foundation to explore context engineering — how to deliberately shape what enters the window, in what order, and at what cost, to get reliable, high-quality behaviour from long autonomous sessions.
docs-as-context:
Documentation as context

Every Claude Code session starts with a fixed mental model of your codebase — one built entirely from what you have written down in advance. This chapter shows you how to write documentation that Claude can actually use: what to put in , which facts belong in memory files, and how to structure domain knowledge so that short prompts produce correct, informed work.

Why documentation beats per-prompt explanation

The first instinct, when Claude gets something wrong, is to write a longer prompt. That instinct is usually backwards. A longer prompt fixes one conversation; good documentation fixes every conversation.

The underlying reason is mechanical. Claude Code loads  into the context at the start of every session and re-injects it on every request (prompt-cached after the first, so it carries no per-turn cost). The architecture docs, conventions, and known gotchas you write there are available before you type a single word. Conversely, context that exists only in your head — or that you repeat verbally — evaporates when the session ends.

From the research behind this book: a real production codebase accumulates a  of 400+ lines covering architecture, conventions, schema highlights, known gotchas, and sharp edges. Human prompts in that project average 10–80 words. The ratio inverts the common instinct: invest in the standing document, not the per-prompt context. The documentation carries the instructional weight; the prompt carries only the goal.

When your CLAUDE.md is thorough, a prompt like "fix the round-robin assignment bug" is enough. Claude already knows the assignment algorithm, which files implement it, and what invariants it must preserve. You only need to name the goal.

What CLAUDE.md is (and is not)

 is a Markdown file that Claude Code loads automatically. Multiple can exist — one at the project root, one in each subdirectory down to the git root, and a personal one at  that applies to every project. All are loaded and composed; the personal file acts as global standing instructions.

What it is not: a substitute for code comments, a place to re-document your API, or a place to duplicate things already captured in your schema. Its job is to give Claude the context a new senior engineer would need on day one — the things that are not obvious from reading the code.

Good things to put in :

- Architecture in plain language. How the system fits together: which processes talk to which, what the data flow looks like end to end, which repos/services are active vs. archived.
- Naming and structural conventions. The module layout, file-naming patterns, which packages are canonical for which jobs.
- The "do not do this" list. Gotchas, anti-patterns, and foot-guns that look reasonable on the surface but break invariants. These are the highest-value lines you can write.
- RBAC, auth, and permission rules. Any system where getting it wrong is a security issue deserves explicit prose.
- Known sharp edges and open bugs. A bullet list of things that are broken or incomplete. When you fix one, delete the bullet. When you find a new one, add it. This list is more valuable than almost any other section.

Things to leave out:

- Step-by-step tutorials — those belong in  or onboarding docs.
- Information that is obvious from reading the code.
- Vague advice ("write clean code", "test everything").

A concrete structure that works

Below is the skeleton of a  that reflects what effective practitioners actually ship. Adapt the section names to your domain.

The "known gotchas" section earns its place over and over. If Claude hits a prod migration issue because  doesn't generate migration files, and you document that fact, the next session — or the next engineer — will not hit the same wall. The documentation is a living record of hard-won knowledge.

Memory files for durable facts across sessions

 captures structural knowledge. Memory files capture decisions — the answers to "why did we do it this way" that would otherwise be re-litigated in every session.

Claude Code's auto-memory system ( by default) lets Claude read and write structured facts that persist across sessions. But the most powerful use of memory is deliberate, not automatic: after a significant architectural decision, write a short file recording what was decided and why.

A good memory file has three elements:

1. The decision. "We chose X over Y."
2. The constraint that drove it. "Because Z prevents us from doing Y in production."
3. The operational consequence. "So whenever you see pattern P, do Q instead."

Examples of decisions worth encoding this way:

- "Auto-CD does not run . A schema column added in code but missing from prod will pass smoke tests and 500 in production on first query. Add a migration file or a hotfix SQL under  before the deploy lands."
- "CD runs in the  regional pool. The global  command shows nothing. Never conclude CD did not fire from a global list; re-check in the right region."

These are not edge cases — they are the class of knowledge that, undocumented, causes every new session (human or AI) to hit the same failure mode and spend an hour diagnosing it from scratch.

A memory file that describes a system that no longer exists is worse than no documentation. When you change the deployment topology, rotate a secret, or remove a feature, update the corresponding memory file in the same change. Stale facts injected into context cause confident wrong answers.

Structuring domain knowledge for Claude to use

Technical documentation is the easier half. Domain knowledge — the business rules, the entity relationships, the lifecycle states that only exist in the product spec and in the heads of the team — is harder to write in a form Claude can use.

Two principles help.

Make states and transitions explicit, not implicit. If your lead record has a 22-stage funnel, write out the stages and the automatic progression rules. "At four or more inbound messages on a  lead, the system promotes it to  automatically. Any code that mutates  must also write a  row." Without this, Claude will implement stage mutations and silently omit the history row, because that invariant is invisible from the schema alone.

Write the negative cases. Not just "here is what the system does" but "here is what it must never do." "Do not bypass  with a direct ; that skips the  row and the activity audit entry." Claude is very good at following explicit rules and very likely to take the straightforward path when rules are absent.

The skills pattern: lazy-load procedural knowledge

One practical problem with  is that it loads into every session, whether or not that session needs it. A 400-line file is fine. A 4,000-line file starts to consume meaningful context and slow down every response.

The answer for procedural knowledge — step-by-step workflows, runbooks, deployment sequences — is skills. A skill is a Markdown file in  that only loads when you invoke it by name. It carries no context cost when you are not using it.

The split is straightforward:

- *: architecture, invariants, conventions, gotchas — things Claude needs on every task.
- Skills: procedures, playbooks, and workflows — things Claude needs for specific, named tasks.

A deploy runbook as a skill might look like:

This is documentation that Claude can execute, not just read.

Maintaining documentation as the codebase evolves

The single most common failure mode for  is staleness. When the system changes and the documentation does not, Claude gets confidently wrong answers backed by outdated facts.

Two practices prevent this:

Update in the same change. When you write a PR that adds a route, changes a schema, introduces a new pattern, or removes a sharp edge — update  in the same commit. Treat it as a required part of every significant change, not an optional follow-up.

The sharp-edge list as a changelog. The "known gotchas" section of  is a list that should shrink over time. When a gotcha is resolved, delete the bullet. When a new one is discovered (ideally before it causes a production incident), add it. The list's current length is a rough proxy for accumulated technical debt.

A doc that says "service X reads from the Y table" when service X was decommissioned six months ago actively misleads Claude. Claude will reason from it confidently. If you cannot maintain a section, delete it rather than leaving it to rot.

Recap

Documentation is the most leveraged investment you can make in your Claude Code workflow. A well-maintained  transforms every session: you delegate goals instead of instructions, and Claude can act on deep context it would otherwise have to reconstruct from scratch on every task.

The three-layer model:

1.  — architecture, invariants, conventions, known gotchas. Loaded every session. Keep it accurate and lean.
2. Memory files — decisions: what was chosen, why, and what it means for future work. Written after significant decisions; updated when they change.
3. Skills — procedures and workflows. Loaded on demand only. Write them when you find yourself giving the same multi-step briefing more than twice.

Next up:** the chapter on hooks shows you how to run your own code around Claude's tool calls — enforcing invariants, logging decisions, and building quality gates directly into the session lifecycle.
long-running-no-bloat:
Long-running tasks without context bloat

The context window is append-only: every file read, tool output, and response accumulates until something gives. This chapter shows you the operator-level techniques for sustaining multi-hour — and multi-day — jobs without drowning the window, triggering runaway compaction, or losing continuity between sessions.

Why context bloat is an engineering problem, not a UX annoyance

Context growth is not a nuisance. It is a structural constraint that degrades output quality and drives up cost at the same time. When the window fills:

- The model starts dropping earlier reasoning — not because it forgets, but because earlier tokens are literally further from the attention peaks.
- Compaction runs and collapses detail you may need later.
- Every subsequent turn pays more in tokens whether or not those old turns are still relevant.

The good news: the shape of the problem is predictable. Tool outputs are the primary driver of fill. Each file read, each shell command, each search result appends to the message array. A single read of a large file or a verbose bash output can consume thousands of tokens in one turn. Understanding this lets you design sessions — not just react to them.

Use the simulator above to develop intuition. Switch the preset to bloated and drag the turn count upward. Watch how file reads and tool results eat the budget compared to plain messages. Then switch to lean and observe how bounded tool calls keep the window stable through the same number of turns.

The four patterns that cause bloat

Before the fixes, the sources:

1. Reading files that Claude does not need to write. Every  of a large file that only provides background context — not something Claude is editing — is often avoidable. Background can live in  or a summary instead.

2. Verbose bash output. A command that dumps hundreds of lines of logs, a full  trace, or a recursive directory listing can fill more context than a dozen normal conversation turns. The default output cap is 30,000 characters per command.

3. Redundant re-exploration. Without a persistent knowledge store, a new session re-reads the same files, runs the same searches, and reconstructs the same understanding it built last time. This is wasted context on every session.

4. Sprawling single sessions. Trying to do an entire multi-day feature campaign in one session forces every intermediate step — dead ends, diagnostic detours, discarded drafts — to stay in the window until compaction wipes them.

The operator's playbook

Pattern 1 — Scope the session to one stage

Long jobs have stages. A campaign to fix 123 security findings across 7 domains is not one session — it is 7 sessions, one per domain batch. Each session starts focused, ends focused, and the window never accumulates the earlier batches' tool noise.

The practical way to enforce this is to name the scope explicitly in the opening prompt:
