This is not just good housekeeping. It prevents Claude from chasing related issues in adjacent modules, which would pull those files into context and expand the working set.

Each stage gets its own git worktree — a separate physical directory on disk, a separate branch, and a separate Claude Code session. Context is isolated per worktree automatically. If Claude is in , it cannot accidentally read or edit files that only belong to batch 1's worktree. Isolation by directory is more reliable than isolation by instruction.

Pattern 2 — Automate session memory so you never start cold

The most expensive form of context bloat is not what happens inside a session — it is what happens at the start of the next one. Without memory, every session burns its opening turns re-reading the same files, reconstructing the same architectural understanding, and rediscovering the same sharp edges.

The fix is automated extraction, not manual summarisation. A  hook can fire a lightweight summariser after every meaningful tool call, accumulating a compressed fact log that persists across sessions. At the next , the relevant portion is injected into context automatically.

This approach was observed running across more than 1,200 production sessions on a complex two-repo CRM. The manual  command was invoked exactly once across 76 sessions in the primary project — not because sessions were short (the largest reached 14 MB / 3,575 lines), but because inter-session continuity was automated. The next session always had the previous session's outcome available without re-running any tools. (Source: packet-E, F-09)

The key design choice: store facts, not transcripts. A structured memory file for an architectural decision takes a few hundred tokens. A transcript of the session that produced that decision would take tens of thousands.

That 60-token reference entry replaces re-reading the auth module, the session model, and the relevant PR description at the start of every subsequent session.

Pattern 3 — Put knowledge in CLAUDE.md, not in the prompt

 content loads into context on every session, but it is prompt-cached after the first request. You pay the encoding cost once per session, not once per turn. (Source: packet-A, §1)

That makes  the right place for:
- Module maps and ownership
- Invariants and known sharp edges
- Naming conventions and schema highlights
- Anti-patterns to avoid

The wrong place for the same content is the per-session prompt. A 400-line  that covers architecture, conventions, and known gotchas is what allows per-session prompts to stay under 80 words. Short prompts work because long standing documents exist — the ratio inverts common intuition. (Source: packet-E, F-33)

Skills are lazier still: they load only when invoked. Procedures that are used occasionally — deploy runbooks, code review checklists, migration playbooks — belong in skill files, not in . They contribute zero tokens to sessions that never call them.

Pattern 4 — Bound your tool calls

Every tool output is a token cost you chose to pay. Before issuing a tool call, ask whether the result is strictly necessary for the current turn's decision, or whether it is background research that could be summarised elsewhere.

Practical bounds:

| Situation | Bounded alternative |
|---|---|
| Reading a large file for background | Store the relevant excerpt in  or a memory file |
| Running a noisy build command | Pipe output through  or  to limit what lands in context |
| Exploring a codebase you've visited before | Use a memory file with the module map instead of re-running searches |
| Listing all files in a directory | Use  with a specific pattern rather than a recursive listing |

Bash output is capped at 30,000 characters by default. That cap protects against runaway verbosity, but 30,000 characters is still a substantial token cost. For diagnostic commands, always pipe through a filter — the cap does not help if the first 30 K characters of a log are what you wanted to avoid.

Pattern 5 — Use compaction as a scheduled checkpoint, not an emergency brake

The  command summarises older history in place and emits a  marker. Auto-compact fires automatically when the context approaches the limit (controlled by , on by default). The  and  hook events fire around it.

The problem with relying on auto-compact is that it runs at the worst moment — when the window is nearly full — and at that point important intermediate state may already be degraded. A better pattern for sessions that will genuinely need to run long:

1. Scope the session tightly (pattern 1) so it does not reach auto-compact territory.
2. If a session must be long, invoke  proactively at a natural breakpoint — after a diagnostic phase concludes, before starting an implementation phase — not reactively when the model starts forgetting.
3. For cross-session continuity, rely on external memory (pattern 2) rather than on compaction, which collapses but does not persist.

Parallel agents as a context-isolation primitive

The deepest form of context isolation is running separate agents. When a sub-agent finishes and returns to the parent, only the final summary crosses the boundary — not the thousands of tokens of intermediate tool outputs and reasoning the sub-agent accumulated. (Source: packet-A, §7)

This is why parallel sub-agent dispatch works well for large sweeps. A typesafety campaign that eliminated 386 TypeScript errors used three parallel sub-agents in the sweep phase, each scoped to a disjoint file set. Each agent built up its own context working through its files; the parent only received a compact outcome report from each. (Source: packet-E, F-15)

The parent's context stays thin. The sub-agents' contexts can grow as large as needed — independently, in parallel — and the cost never rolls back into the parent's window.

The constraint: tasks dispatched to parallel agents must operate on disjoint files. Two agents editing the same file simultaneously will produce conflicts. Scope partitioning is the prerequisite for safe parallel dispatch.

A named agent is not a session — it is a tag. The  campaign that ran 275 recorded invocations did so across multiple sessions over roughly two weeks, each individual session staying focused on one stage. The name gives you an external handle to group related work without forcing it into a single sprawling session. (Source: packet-E, F-24)

Designing for longevity: the checklist

Before starting a job that will run long:

The last step is as important as the first. Decisions documented after a session are available at zero token cost in the next one. Decisions left only in the transcript force the next session to re-read, re-discover, or worse, re-decide.

What a lean session looks like

A well-structured session for a large job:

1. Opens with injected memory — the previous session's outcome in a few hundred tokens, not a re-exploration.
2. Reads only what it needs to write — files under active modification, not background files.
3. Uses bounded bash output — piped, filtered, or truncated before hitting context.
4. Stays scoped to one domain — touches a coherent set of files, not the whole codebase.
5. Ends by writing a memory file — the outcome, any decisions, any new sharp edges discovered.

The session may still run for many turns and many thousands of tokens. But the tokens it spends are on the work itself — not on re-learning the codebase, not on verbose noise, and not on carrying the weight of six previous sessions' tool outputs.

Recap

Context bloat is a design problem with design solutions. The window is append-only and tool outputs are the primary driver of fill. The techniques that contain it — scoped sessions, automated cross-session memory, purpose-built  content, bounded tool calls, proactive compaction, and parallel agents as isolation primitives — all share the same underlying logic: spend context tokens on decisions, not on rediscovery.

The next chapter covers dynamic workflows — the mechanism that moves orchestration logic out of Claude's context window entirely and into executable JavaScript, letting you coordinate hundreds of agents without any of their intermediate work touching the coordinator's window.
memory-claude-md:
Memory — CLAUDE.md & the remember pattern

By default, Claude Code remembers nothing between sessions. Each new session opens with a blank slate — no knowledge of your project's architecture, your team's conventions, or the decisions made last week. This chapter covers the three mechanisms that break that amnesia:  files for standing context, auto-memory for cross-session facts, and the  pattern for explicit, durable knowledge capture. By the end you will know how each works, when to reach for each one, and how to combine them into a memory system that makes every session feel like a continuation of the last.

Why session amnesia matters

The agent loop is append-only within a session. Everything Claude reads, every file it edits, every decision it makes — all of it accumulates in the context window and is available for reasoning until the session ends. The moment a session closes, none of that survives. Tomorrow's session starts with the same blank model that has never heard of your codebase.

This has a cascading effect. Without standing context, Claude has to re-explore the codebase from first principles at the start of every task. It re-discovers conventions it violated last session. It asks questions it already answered. The productive hours of deep context get spent on re-orientation.

The three memory mechanisms below exist to solve different parts of this problem.

Memory mechanisms don't expand the context window — they populate it. Each mechanism is really a way of getting the right information into the context at the start of a session, so Claude can reason about it without burning turns re-discovering it.

CLAUDE.md — the standing brief

 files are Markdown files that Claude Code loads automatically at the start of every session. Their content is injected as a user message after the system prompt, before your first prompt arrives. They are the primary way to give Claude persistent, session-spanning knowledge about your project.

Where they live and how they load

Claude Code looks for  files in a layered set of locations, loading all that match:

All matching files load together. Subagents also load CLAUDE.md, with two exceptions: the built-in  and  subagents skip it deliberately, to keep research fast.

The  settings key accepts glob patterns to skip specific files — useful when a repo contains auto-generated directories that happen to have CLAUDE.md files you don't control.

What to put in CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md is most valuable for facts that are both stable and consequential — things Claude would need to re-discover on every session start if you didn't state them upfront.

Effective CLAUDE.md content:

- Architecture summary — what the system is, which repos are active, how they connect
- Technology decisions — language version, framework choices, patterns to follow
- Invariants and constraints — "soft delete everything", "use GCS not S3", "no AI attribution in commits"
- Known sharp edges — production bugs, tricky environmental facts, gotchas that trip up fresh explorations
- Command reference — how to run tests, start the dev server, apply migrations

Content that belongs elsewhere:

- Step-by-step procedures → use Skills (lazy-loaded, not in every request)
- Per-session context like today's PR list → use a  hook (dynamic, fresh each session)
- Ephemeral state like current branch → don't persist; let Claude discover it

The token cost of standing context

Every line of CLAUDE.md is injected on every request. Longer files cost more tokens — both in spend and in context window. Claude Code caches CLAUDE.md content after the first request of a session (prompt caching), so within a session the incremental cost drops sharply. But the first injection still counts.

The practical consequence: write CLAUDE.md for density. Each line should earn its place. Architecture docs that run to thousands of words should live in separate files that CLAUDE.md links to, not inline in CLAUDE.md itself.

Monorepo layouts

In a monorepo with multiple active services, stack CLAUDE.md files by scope:

When Claude works in , it loads both the root and the service-level file. When working in , it loads the root plus the web file. Each layer adds only the context relevant to that scope, without polluting sessions in other directories.

Auto-memory — cross-session fact persistence

Auto-memory is Claude Code's built-in mechanism for persisting structured facts across sessions without manual curation. It is enabled by default ( in settings).

When auto-memory is active, Claude reads relevant files from  at session start and writes updated facts as it learns them during the session. The directory path is configurable via .

What auto-memory stores

Auto-memory is most useful for preferences and procedural facts that Claude learns through interaction — things you correct once and want remembered forever. Examples from real usage:

- Your preferred commit message format
- That you always want tests before implementation on this project
- That  is the package manager, not 
- That the staging environment was torn down and shouldn't be referenced

These are the kind of low-friction corrections that feel tedious to re-state but are trivial to learn once.

Disabling auto-memory

If you want strict control over what Claude knows between sessions — for security, compliance, or reproducibility — auto-memory can be disabled in two ways:

or via the environment variable . When disabled, no facts persist automatically; every session starts with only what CLAUDE.md and explicit memory files provide.

The /remember pattern — explicit, durable knowledge

The  slash command (provided by the  plugin) gives you explicit control over what gets persisted. Rather than trusting automatic extraction, you decide what matters and when to capture it.

What to /remember

The pattern works best for:

- Architectural decisions with rationale — not just "use GCS" but "use GCS not S3 because the SA key policy blocks new key creation"
- Prod-vs-dev divergence facts — "CD runs , not ; seed-only rows never exist in prod"
- Operational gotchas — "run  with  or you'll see the wrong build pool"
- Preference feedback — corrections to Claude's default behavior that you want applied from now on

These are the notes a senior engineer would write in a runbook after a prod incident. The /remember pattern makes those notes automatically available to every future session.

How the remember plugin works

The  plugin (available via the Claude Code plugin marketplace) maintains a directory of dated log files and structured memory files. Two hooks drive it automatically:

- A  hook fires after tool calls and periodically extracts session highlights using a lightweight model, appending them to a dated log ().
- A  hook reads the relevant memory files and injects a summary into context via .

This means the plugin can operate in fully automatic mode — you never need to type  manually if the automatic extraction captures what matters. You use the explicit command for decisions you want to make sure survive, regardless of whether the automatic pass catches them.

The memory file taxonomy

A mature remember setup typically maintains three tiers:

| File | Purpose | Lifecycle |
|---|---|---|
|  | Daily working log; appended during the session | Archived weekly |
|  | Weekly roll-ups from daily logs | Grows indefinitely; queryable |
| Structured fact files (, , ) | Named, typed, durable facts | Explicitly authored; never auto-expire |

The structured fact files are the most durable tier. Each has a name, type, and description so the injection system can select relevant ones without loading all 65 (or however many accumulate) into every session.

Composing the three layers

The three mechanisms are complementary, not competing:

A practical division of responsibility:

- CLAUDE.md carries everything that would be true on a fresh clone by any engineer — repo structure, active services, conventions, command reference. Check it in. Keep it up to date when you change architecture.
- Auto-memory carries preferences and procedural corrections that are personal or project-specific but don't need to be shared with the team. Let it run automatically.
- /remember carries decisions, gotchas, and operational facts that you explicitly want durable. Use it after incidents, after significant architectural decisions, after any correction you've had to make more than once.

Living documentation: keeping CLAUDE.md accurate

A CLAUDE.md that drifts from the codebase is worse than no CLAUDE.md. Stale facts mislead Claude in exactly the situations where correct facts matter most.

When you add a route, change the DB schema, remove a sharp edge, or introduce a new pattern that becomes load-bearing — update CLAUDE.md in the same commit. Don't leave it for a cleanup pass. The next session will read the stale version and reason from it.

Some teams treat CLAUDE.md maintenance as part of the definition of done for a feature PR. If the feature added a new module key, a new migration pattern, or a new sharp edge — the PR isn't complete until CLAUDE.md reflects it.

The sharp edges section is the most valuable part

Sharp edges — known gotchas, prod traps, non-obvious invariants — are the highest-leverage content in a CLAUDE.md. They encode institutional knowledge that took an incident to learn. A fresh Claude session reading "the shadow DB is broken; hand-author SQL and insert a  row manually" avoids a 20-minute debugging cycle that every previous session had to repeat.

When you fix a sharp edge, delete the bullet. Leaving it as "fixed in PR #123" creates noise. When you discover a new one, add it immediately — the discovery context is exactly when the wording will be clearest.

A worked example: project onboarding

To make this concrete, here is what a minimal but effective CLAUDE.md might look like for a two-service project:

bash
pnpm dev           # both services via concurrently
pnpm db:push       # sync schema (dev only)
pnpm db:migrate    # generate + apply migration (use when promoting)

This fits in under 30 lines. It tells Claude which repos are active, what the stack constraints are, how to run the project, and the two most expensive prod traps the team has hit. Every session starts from this foundation without any re-exploration.

Recap

Three mechanisms fill Claude's blank slate at session start:

1. CLAUDE.md — static, team-shared, injected on every request. Write it for architecture, constraints, and sharp edges. Keep it accurate; stale facts mislead.
2. Auto-memory — adaptive, personal, automatic. Let it capture preferences and behavioral corrections across sessions. Disable it if you need reproducibility.
3. /remember — explicit, durable, on-demand. Use it for architectural decisions, operational gotchas, and any fact you've had to re-explain more than once.

Together they let you delegate goals rather than instructions — because Claude already knows the how.

Next: the context window and compaction chapter covers what happens when sessions grow large, how auto-compaction works, and how to design tasks that stay within budget.
effective-prompting:
Effective prompting for Claude

A better prompt is not longer — it is more specific. This chapter distills the patterns that reliably produce better output: how to give Claude the right context up front, how to use examples as a precision instrument, and how to structure instructions so the model can parse them without guessing.

Why prompts matter even with a smart model

Claude is a strong reasoner, but it is working with whatever information you give it. A vague prompt does not unlock less capability — it forces the model to fill the gaps itself, which means it makes assumptions where you wanted decisions, and hedges where you wanted commitment.

The prompting patterns in this chapter are not tricks. They are ways of transferring information more completely — from your head into Claude's context window — so that Claude can spend its reasoning budget on the actual problem rather than reconstructing what you meant.

Whether you are typing into Claude.ai, running Claude Code in a terminal, or calling the API from an application, the same prompting principles apply. The chapter examples use natural language, but engineers will see how the same ideas translate directly to system prompts and API calls.

The anatomy of an effective prompt

Most prompts that produce weak results are missing one or more of three ingredients:

1. A clear task — what you want Claude to produce
2. Sufficient context — what Claude needs to know to produce it well
3. Output constraints — format, length, tone, or other properties the result must have

A prompt that contains all three is specific. Prompts that are missing one are ambiguous. Prompts that are missing two are vague.

The three-ingredient model sounds simple, but most people write prompts that have a task and skip the other two. The sections below address each in turn.

Specificity: the task itself

The single most common prompt failure is describing a category of output instead of the specific output you want.

| Vague | Specific |
|---|---|
| "Write an email to the client" | "Write a two-paragraph email to the client explaining why the deadline moved by one week. Be direct and do not over-apologise." |
| "Summarise this document" | "Summarise this document in three bullet points. Each bullet should be one sentence and suitable for a non-technical executive." |
| "Fix this bug" | "The function  crashes when the input is an empty string. Fix it without changing the function signature." |
| "Improve this code" | "Refactor this function to remove the nested  blocks. Prefer early returns. Do not change observable behaviour." |

Notice what is different in the specific versions: named output (bullet points, email), a stated audience (non-technical executive, client), explicit constraints (two paragraphs, one sentence per bullet), and named behaviour boundaries (do not change the function signature).

Name the output format explicitly

Claude can produce many formats — prose, lists, JSON, Markdown, YAML, code — but it defaults to whatever seems most natural for the task. Name the format you want rather than hoping Claude infers it.

Set a length target

Without a length signal, Claude calibrates to what feels complete for the task type. This is often longer than you need. A length target is not a hard constraint — it is a signal about desired depth.

Context: what Claude needs to know

Specificity about the task tells Claude what to produce. Context tells Claude how to produce it correctly. The most useful context is:

- Domain knowledge Claude does not have — your project conventions, your team's terminology, business rules that are not visible in the files
- The audience or reader — who will consume the output and what they already know
- Constraints on the solution space — what has already been tried, what is off-limits, which approach you prefer

Give the background, not the backstory

Context should be dense and relevant. Do not narrate how you arrived at the problem — describe the problem state directly.

The second version gives Claude the data structures, the mechanism, and the symptom — everything it needs. The first gives history.

State what you already know or have tried

One of the highest-leverage pieces of context is the approaches that did not work. Without it, Claude often suggests what you already tried.

With that context, Claude skips the obvious paths and reasons from where you actually are.

If you use Claude Code in a codebase regularly, the best context you can provide is a well-maintained . It loads at the start of every session so you do not have to re-explain conventions, schema highlights, or known gotchas each time. Think of it as a persistent context prefix. Invest effort in it once; every future prompt benefits.

Examples: the precision instrument

Examples are the most underused prompting technique. They communicate things that instructions struggle to: tone, structure, level of detail, and the exact boundary between what counts as correct and what does not.

The technical term for including examples in a prompt is few-shot prompting — you give the model one or more input–output pairs before the actual task, and the model generalises the pattern to the new input.

When to use examples

Use examples when:

- The output format is unusual or highly specific
- Tone is important and hard to describe in words
- You have had to correct Claude's interpretation multiple times on similar tasks
- The task involves classification with non-obvious category boundaries

One good example beats five paragraphs of instructions

The example does in thirty words what five bullet points cannot: it demonstrates the sentence rhythm, the level of technical detail, and the absence of preamble.

Structure your examples clearly

When your prompt includes examples, label them so Claude knows what is input and what is output.

---`) makes the transition from examples to the real task unambiguous.

Negative examples for boundary cases

If there is a common mistake you want Claude to avoid, show it explicitly.

Structure: making instructions parseable

Long prompts often fail not because they lack information, but because Claude cannot easily parse which parts are instructions versus context versus examples. Structure helps.

Use headers or numbered steps for multi-part tasks

If a task has a clear sequence, number the steps:

Numbered steps produce predictable, ordered outputs. Prose descriptions produce prose outputs — which may cover the same ground but in a different order and harder to verify.

Separate context from instructions

When a prompt mixes context and instructions, Claude can lose track of which sentences are background and which are directives. A simple separator makes both sections cleaner.

Chain of thought for complex reasoning tasks

For tasks that require multi-step reasoning — debugging a tricky bug, designing an architecture, reviewing a security posture — explicitly ask Claude to reason before answering. This is sometimes called chain-of-thought prompting.

Or, for a more structured version:

Asking Claude to externalize its reasoning tends to produce more accurate conclusions — and it lets you catch reasoning errors before they become recommendations you act on.

Prompts like "give me the answer directly, skip the explanation" are fine for simple lookups. For hard reasoning tasks, they often produce confident-sounding but less reliable answers. The reasoning is not decoration — it is part of how Claude gets to a good answer.

The PromptLab — try it now

The widget below scores your prompt across four dimensions — specificity, context, examples, and structure — and shows you where to improve. Load a curated before/after pair to see the same task written weakly and well, then try editing it.

Putting it together: a worked example

Here is the same task written as a weak prompt, then rebuilt using the patterns above.

Weak:

Rebuilt:

The rebuilt version delivers: a named file, a stated symptom, what has already been tried, a sequenced multi-step task, an output format, and a constraint. That is all three ingredients — task, context, and constraints — plus a structure that makes the sequence unambiguous.

Quick reference: the prompting checklist

Before submitting a complex prompt, run through these questions:

- Task: Have I named the specific output, not just a category of output?
- Format: Have I specified the format (prose, list, JSON, code, table)?
- Length: Have I given a length signal if brevity or depth matters?
- Context: Have I told Claude what it needs to know that is not in the attached files?
- Tried: Have I mentioned what I have already tried, if relevant?
- Audience: Does Claude know who the output is for?
- Steps: For multi-part tasks, have I numbered the steps?
- Constraints: Have I listed what Claude should not do or change?
- Examples: For unusual formats or tone, have I shown at least one example?

You do not need all nine for every prompt. A one-sentence clarification request needs none of them. A complex refactoring task benefits from most of them.

Recap

Effective prompting is precise information transfer: task, context, and constraints delivered clearly enough that Claude does not need to guess. Specificity defines the output. Context gives Claude what it cannot infer. Examples calibrate tone, format, and boundary cases more precisely than instructions can. Structure makes multi-step tasks parseable and sequenced.

The patterns here apply to any interface — chat, terminal, API — and at any complexity level from a quick question to a multi-thousand-token system prompt. The next chapter looks at how to take this further by writing specs and briefs that hand off complex work to Claude reliably, without needing to be present for every step.
output-styles:
Output styles & compression

Claude Code ships with a small but high-leverage system for changing how it communicates: output styles. This chapter covers the four built-in styles, how to write your own, and one power-user compression technique — caveman mode — that cuts response length by roughly three-quarters without sacrificing technical accuracy. You will also see when compression is worth the trade-off and when it is not.

What output styles actually are

An output style is a named modification to Claude's system prompt. When you activate a style, Claude Code replaces (or augments) its built-in engineering instructions with whatever the style file specifies. The result is a different default behaviour — more verbose, more educational, more terse — without you having to repeat preferences in every message.

Styles are not per-message instructions. They persist for the session and survive context compaction. They are the closest thing Claude Code has to a personality dial.

An output style changes what Claude Code injects before your first message. It does not change how the model reasons or which tools it can use — only how it communicates and, in some cases, how eagerly it acts.

The four built-in styles

Claude Code ships four named styles out of the box. Each corresponds to a different working mode.

| Style | Core behaviour | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Default | Built-in engineering instructions, balanced verbosity | Everyday coding tasks |
| Proactive | Immediate action, reasonable assumptions, less planning | Rapid iteration, well-scoped tasks |
| Explanatory | Adds "Insights" callouts between engineering steps | Onboarding, learning a new codebase |
| Learning | Insights +  markers for deliberate practice | Building skills, paired programming |

A note on what Proactive does and does not do: it makes Claude lean toward execution over clarifying questions, but it does not change your permission mode. You still see approval prompts for Bash and file writes. Proactive affects the stance, not the guardrails.

When each style earns its place

Default is the right choice for most sessions. It is what Claude Code was designed around.

Proactive shines when you have already scoped a task clearly and want Claude to start rather than ask. Pair it with a well-written  or a detailed prompt, and it cuts the planning overhead. Avoid it for open-ended exploration — you want questions, not assumptions, when the problem space is fuzzy.

Explanatory and Learning are teaching modes. They trade throughput for understanding. If you are pairing with a junior engineer, onboarding someone to a codebase, or deliberately building your own mental model of a new system, these styles make every action an annotated example. For high-velocity solo work, they are too slow.

You can change the active style mid-project by editing  in your settings and running  (or starting a new session). Consider Default for feature work and Explanatory for architecture explorations — the same project, different phases.

How to switch styles

The canonical path is  in the CLI, which shows a menu for Output style. The setting persists to :

Valid values: , , , , or any custom style name you have defined. The change takes effect after  or a new session — not mid-conversation, because the system prompt is only injected at session start.

The standalone  slash command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91. If you see references to it in older guides, they are stale. Use  instead.

Custom output styles

You can define styles for your own working preferences. A style is a Markdown file placed in:

-  — personal, applies to all your projects
-  — project-local, shared with teammates

The filename without the  extension becomes the style name (override with a  frontmatter field).

A minimal custom style looks like this:

The  field tells Claude Code to add your content on top of the built-in engineering instructions rather than replacing them. If you omit it (or set it to ), your style replaces the engineering baseline — suitable for non-coding use cases, risky for anything involving files and shell commands.

One more field worth knowing:  makes a style auto-activate whenever a particular plugin is enabled. This is mostly relevant to plugin authors, but it shows that styles are a first-class integration surface.

Compression: the caveman pattern

Output styles address the shape of responses. Compression addresses the volume. These are orthogonal levers — you can have a terse version of any style.

The caveman pattern is a community-developed compression technique that emerged from heavy Claude Code usage. The core idea: teach the model to drop low-information words without dropping technical precision.

What caveman mode changes:

- Drops articles ("the", "a", "an")
- Uses sentence fragments where meaning is unambiguous
- Abbreviates common technical terms (, , , , , , )
- Uses arrows () for causality instead of "which causes" / "resulting in"
- Drops affirmations ("Certainly!", "Of course", "Great question")

What it explicitly keeps:

- Code, exact CLI commands, error messages — written verbatim
- Commit messages and PR descriptions — full prose
- Security warnings — never abbreviated
- Ambiguous cases — stated clearly even if longer

The net effect, measured empirically on real sessions, is roughly 75% token reduction in explanatory prose without loss of technical accuracy. Code blocks are unchanged. The saving is in the connective tissue between code blocks.

A caveman response for "why is the permission cache not invalidating?" might look like:

Versus the default style, which would add prose framing ("Great question — let me walk you through the caching architecture…"), restate the question, and conclude with a summary. The caveman version surfaces the answer in four lines.

Implementing caveman as a custom style

Place this in , set  in settings, and  to activate.

You do not have to set caveman as your default. You can say "switch to caveman mode" at the start of any session and Claude will apply the compressed style for that conversation. Revert any time with "normal mode" or "stop caveman".

When compression pays off — and when it hurts

Compression is not universally beneficial. The right call depends on what you are using Claude for.

The cost of compression is reduced legibility for anyone other than the person who set the style. If you share session transcripts with teammates, a caveman session reads like notes, not documentation. If your organization uses Claude Code for onboarding, the Learning style is the opposite of caveman for good reason.

The benefit is speed and focus. When you trust the model, know the codebase, and want answers — not explanations — compression removes friction from every response.

Styles in multi-session projects

Output styles interact with the memory system in a subtle way. The style modifies the system prompt injected at session start. If your project uses the remember plugin or structured memory files, those facts are injected on top of whatever system prompt the style produces. The style sets the register; memory fills in the substance.

This means: if you want consistent terse behaviour across sessions without re-activating caveman each time, set  in your project-level . Every session on that project picks it up without any per-session prompt.

For an organization that wants consistent style across all developers on a project, this is the right place to set it — the file is committed to the repository and shared.

Recap

Output styles are named system-prompt modifications that persist for the session. The four built-ins cover the main modes: balanced (Default), action-first (Proactive), educational (Explanatory), and learn-by-doing (Learning). Custom styles live in  or  and become available by name via .

Compression — the caveman pattern — is a separate but complementary lever that cuts explanatory verbosity by roughly 75% while leaving code and commit prose intact. It suits high-trust implementation sessions and scales well across multi-session projects when set in .

The next chapter turns from how Claude communicates to how you can spec and structure the work itself — writing prompts and task descriptions that get reliable results on complex, multi-step problems.
plan-an-idea:
Planning an idea — brainstorm to spec to plan

Before Claude writes a line of code (or a line of anything), you and it need to agree on what "done" looks like. This chapter walks you through the three-stage funnel — brainstorm, spec, plan — that turns a vague idea into a sequence of steps Claude can execute autonomously with minimal back-and-forth.

Why the funnel matters

Most failed Claude sessions do not fail because the model is incapable. They fail because the prompt was a brainstorm handed to an executor. Vague input produces exploratory output when what you wanted was decisive action.

The three stages create a clean handoff:

| Stage | Input | Output | Who drives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brainstorm | A rough idea | A clarified problem statement + options | Collaborative — you and Claude |
| Spec | The chosen option | Constraints, scope, acceptance criteria | Mostly you, Claude as interrogator |
| Plan | The spec | Ordered, dependency-aware task list | Claude, ratified by you |

Each stage consumes the output of the previous one. Skipping a stage is what causes "Claude went in the wrong direction for twenty turns."

Stage 1 — Brainstorm

What a brainstorm session is for

Brainstorming with Claude is not about getting answers. It is about expanding and then collapsing the option space. You arrive with a rough signal; you leave with a single chosen path.

A good brainstorm prompt names the domain, the rough goal, and any hard constraints you already know. Then it explicitly invites Claude to generate alternatives and surface assumptions:

Claude will enumerate approaches, trade-offs, and hidden considerations. Your job during this phase is to eliminate options and surface non-negotiables. "PDF is too complex for now" and "CSV is fine, but we need to handle 50 000-row exports without timing out" are the outputs you want.

The clarification turn

After Claude's first response, ask the narrowing question:

This forces a concrete recommendation under constraints. You are not asking Claude to decide for you — you are using it to pressure-test each option before you commit.

At the end of a brainstorm, try: "What questions should I be able to answer before I write a spec for this?" Claude will surface the unknowns you have not consciously named yet — dependencies on other systems, edge cases, who the actual user is, whether a simpler version already exists.

When to stop brainstorming

Brainstorming is over when:

1. You can name the approach you are going with.
2. You can state two or three things it will deliberately not do.
3. You have identified the riskiest unknown (the one thing that could make the whole plan wrong).

If you cannot answer those three questions, keep going. If you can, move to spec.

Stage 2 — Spec

A spec is a written contract between you and Claude about what will be built. It does not describe implementation — it describes the result. The implementation is Claude's job; the spec is yours.

The minimum viable spec

A spec does not need to be long. It needs to be complete on five questions:

1. What is the user doing? (one sentence, present tense)
2. What does success look like? (observable, testable)
3. What is explicitly out of scope?
4. What are the hard constraints? (performance, security, compatibility)
5. What does the edge-case handling look like? (what happens when it fails or gets bad input)

For the CSV export example, a spec might look like this:

Using Claude to stress-test the spec

Before treating the spec as final, ask Claude to attack it:

This is the most valuable prompt in the entire funnel. It surfaces the gaps that would otherwise appear as surprised behaviour mid-execution. Every ambiguity Claude names is a decision you get to make now, when it is cheap, rather than during implementation, when it is expensive.

An unspecified edge case discovered at implementation time costs multiple turns of context, potential backtracking, and a partially-written codebase that is now in an unknown state. An unspecified edge case discovered during spec review costs one sentence.

Locking the spec

Once Claude's stress-test returns no material ambiguities, the spec is locked. Write it down somewhere durable — a file in the project, a memory entry, or a comment in a ticket. The spec is the reference document for the entire plan phase and for any future session that picks up this work.

A spec written to a file survives session compaction and can be referenced in future sessions with a simple . A spec that exists only in the chat is lost when the context is compacted or the session ends. The research behind this book found that 65 structured memory files were maintained for a single production project, each encoding a decision or spec so future sessions did not have to re-derive them (packet E, F-08, F-34).

Stage 3 — Plan

With a locked spec, Claude can now write an execution plan. The plan is an ordered, dependency-aware list of tasks. Unlike the spec (which is outcome-oriented), the plan is action-oriented: each step is something Claude can do in a single, bounded session.

Asking for the plan

A good plan response for the export feature might look like this:

Reviewing the plan

Before executing, read the plan as if you were a different engineer looking at it cold. Ask:

- Are the "done" definitions actually observable? ("The button works" is not observable; "clicking Export downloads a file named leads-YYYY-MM-DD.csv" is.)
- Are the dependencies correct? Would any task fail if run before its predecessor?
- Is any task too large — does it touch too many systems to be a single focused session?

If you spot a task that is really two tasks, split it before Claude starts. Splitting during execution means context mid-flight.

The decision-guide

Not sure which Claude mechanism to use to execute the plan once you have it? The widget below routes you to the right tool:

Putting it together — the complete flow

Common failure modes (and what they signal)

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Claude keeps asking clarifying questions mid-task | Spec had unresolved ambiguities | Go back and answer them in the spec |
| Output is correct but not what you wanted | Brainstorm skipped; wrong option selected | Re-run brainstorm, choose differently |
| Tasks bleed into each other | Plan dependencies wrong | Re-order plan before next session |
| Session ends mid-task, progress lost | Task too large for one session | Split into smaller tasks; write progress to disk |
| New session ignores previous decisions | Spec not persisted | Save spec to a file; reference it in the new session |

For engineers: plan-mode as a structural tool

Claude Code has a built-in plan mode (toggle with  or ). In plan mode, file edits are never auto-approved — Claude can read and explore but cannot change anything without your explicit sign-off. This makes plan mode the natural environment for stages 1 and 2: Claude can read your codebase, understand the current state, and help you write the spec without accidentally modifying anything.

The  and  tools give SDK users the same capability programmatically:

From the research behind this book: the author ran 100% of production sessions in  mode, but that was paired with a  hook that blocked git commits with wrong authorship (packet E, F-03, F-05). Full autonomy plus a targeted guardrail at the irreversible side-effect. For most engineers starting out,  mode during the spec phase and  during execution is a more conservative — and equally effective — approach.

For automators: persisting plans across workflow steps

If you run Claude Code via the Agent SDK as part of a larger automation, the plan is a natural checkpoint artifact. Write it to a file after stage 3, then pass the file path as context to the execution step:

This pattern ensures that a failed execution step does not require re-running the expensive brainstorm and spec phases. The plan file is the durable handoff between stages, and each stage can be retried independently.

The audit-remediation case study in the research behind this book used a tiered model approach: a capable model for planning and implementation, a cheaper model for mechanical gate-checking (packet E, F-14). The same principle applies to the brainstorm-spec-plan funnel: once the spec is locked and the plan is mechanical, verification sub-tasks can be delegated to lower-effort model calls without sacrificing quality.

Recap

The brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan funnel is a forcing function: it makes you do the hard thinking before Claude does the expensive doing. Brainstorm to collapse the option space. Spec to freeze the scope and remove ambiguity. Plan to sequence the work into sessions Claude can execute autonomously.

The key habits: ask Claude to stress-test the spec before you lock it; write the spec and plan to disk so they survive session boundaries; split any task that touches more than one logical system.

The next chapter covers how to brief a Claude session — how to hand it the plan and context it needs at the start of an execution session, so the first turn is work, not orientation.
tdd-with-cheap-agents:
TDD with low-cost agents

You will learn how to run genuine test-driven development with AI agents — specifically how to pair the Red → Green → Refactor cycle with cheap, fast models so each loop stays short and the feedback stays honest. By the end you will have a concrete mental model for when to use a powerful model, when to use a cheaper one, and how to build the local environment that makes the whole thing work at speed.

Why TDD and agents are a natural pair

Test-driven development has always been about tight feedback loops. Write a failing test, make it pass, clean it up — then repeat. The discipline lives or dies on how long each loop takes. When a loop takes seconds you stay in flow. When it takes minutes you drift.

Agents accelerate every phase of the loop without changing its shape. A cheap agent can draft edge-case tests from a prose description. A cheap agent can generate a minimal implementation that passes exactly those tests. A more capable model handles the refactor phase where structural judgement matters. The discipline stays yours; the typing and first-draft thinking shifts to the model.

The key word above is cheap. The Red and Green phases are largely mechanical: translate a specification into test assertions, then translate failing assertions into passing code. These tasks do not require the deepest reasoning model available. They require speed and iteration. Over-spending on model capability here is a common mistake — it slows the loop and inflates cost without improving correctness, because the test suite is the correctness oracle, not the model.

Explore the three phases above. Notice the Agent contribution bar: Red and Green are high-automation phases where a cheap model carries most of the cognitive load. Refactor is lower — the agent can apply targeted cleanups, but the human still identifies what needs improving. The cycle runs fastest when you match model capability to phase needs.

Building the environment for fast loops

The agent loop is only as fast as its environment. Three investments pay off across every TDD cycle you run:

1. A test runner that exits immediately

The agent should be able to run a single test file — or a single test — in under five seconds. A full suite run at the wrong moment is a context-window tax and a time cost rolled into one. Configure your test runner to support focused mode:

In the agent's task instruction, tell it to use the focused invocation at every step — not the full suite. The full suite runs once at the end, as a final gate.

2. Automatic permission pre-approval for the test command

Nothing breaks the loop more reliably than a permission prompt interrupting a  call. Pre-approve the exact command pattern in :

With  mode enabled globally, this is unnecessary — but in team settings where bypass is inappropriate, the targeted allow list keeps the agent autonomous on test commands while leaving file writes and deploys gated. (Source: packet-A, §3)

3. A test file scaffold that the agent fills in

Instead of asking the agent to create both the file and the tests from scratch, give it a scaffold that enforces your project's conventions:

This scaffold approach gives the agent a bounded task: translate the SPEC comment into  blocks. The output is predictable, the import path is set, and the conventions are already applied. Contrast this with the open-ended "write tests for my token estimator" prompt — that version requires the agent to discover your conventions, infer your file layout, and make architecture choices. The scaffold removes all of that from the agent's context budget and from your review burden.

If your project has many test files with consistent structure, a cheap model can generate the scaffold from a template before the capable model fills in the test cases. Two cheap invocations and one moderate one replaces one expensive one — the loop stays fast throughout.

The audit pipeline: cheap → verify → capable

One of the most reliable patterns observed in practice is a multi-stage pipeline where model tier matches task difficulty. From a large security audit remediation spanning 123 findings across 7 domain batches (Source: packet-E, F-14):

> (1) Sonnet planner re-verified findings against the live branch; (2) Sonnet TDD implementer wrote tests first, then implementation; (3) Haiku verifier checked gates — test count, diff coverage, regression detection — the cheap model was used here specifically because the task is mechanical; (4) an adversarial reviewer looked for regressions and false fixes; (5) Sonnet fixer addressed review findings.

The cheap model (Haiku) at step 3 is the key insight. Verification is a gating task: does the count of new tests meet the minimum? Does the diff touch only the intended files? Does re-running the suite produce zero failures? These are yes/no questions that a fast, cheap model answers correctly and quickly. Escalating to a capable model for mechanical verification wastes both money and wall-clock time.

The gate between Green and Refactor is inexpensive to run on every cycle. It catches the most common failure modes — tests that were accidentally removed, diffs that drifted outside their intended scope, or implementations that silently pass by making tests trivially true — before the capable model ever sees the code.

Keeping the gate honest

The verification gate only works if it cannot be passed by a technically-correct-but-wrong implementation. Two common honesty problems:

The trivial-pass problem. An agent under pressure to make tests pass can sometimes write an implementation that hard-codes the test inputs and returns their expected outputs. The test suite turns green; the implementation is useless. The fix is to include at least one test that uses an input not mentioned in the spec:

This forces generalization without requiring a full property-based test suite.

The deleted-test problem. If the agent's task is to make the suite pass, deleting failing tests is technically a valid strategy. The verification gate should check that the test count in the target file has not decreased:

A three-line bash snippet and an exit code is all the gate needs. (Source: packet-A, §5 — exit 2 from a hook blocks the next tool call; the same exit-code semantics apply to inline checks.)

The test suite is your specification, not a proof of correctness. An agent that passes your tests has met your specification — no more. Write your specifications carefully. Test the boundary conditions. Include at least one test that the agent could not have seen during implementation.

Practical prompt shapes for each phase

The agent's prompt in each phase should be narrow enough to complete in a small number of turns. Open-ended prompts produce open-ended context growth.

Red phase prompt:

Green phase prompt:

Refactor phase prompt:

Notice that each prompt names the exact file, names the exact test command, and ends with a constraint. The narrow scope keeps the agent's context budget focused and makes the output easy to verify.

Worktrees make TDD isolation safe

Each TDD feature should live in its own git worktree. This is not optional ergonomics — it is what prevents a failing Red phase from contaminating a passing Green phase that is already in progress on another feature.

When the Red phase produces a legitimately failing test and commits it, that commit lives in the feature worktree's branch. The main checkout and every other feature worktree remain untouched. The loop's intermediate state is isolated by default. (Source: packet-E, F-10)

Claude Code stores session history under a directory derived from the working directory. A worktree at  gets its own session entry — separate from the main project. When you resume TDD on that feature after a break, the session history is where you left it, not mixed with other features' histories.

What the full loop looks like end to end

Steps 2–5 are agent-driven. Steps 1, 6, and 7 are human-driven. The human's time is spent on specification (what the code should do) and verification (does the diff reflect that?), not on the mechanical work in between.

The loop is fast when the environment is built for it: a focused test runner, pre-approved test commands, a bounded scaffold, a cheap verification gate, and a worktree that isolates each feature's intermediate state.

Recap

TDD with low-cost agents works because the Red → Green → Refactor cycle has predictable phases with predictable difficulty. The Red and Green phases are specification-to-code translation problems — fast, mechanical, and well-suited to cheap models. The Refactor phase requires structural judgement and benefits from a more capable model. A verification gate between Green and Refactor catches honesty failures — trivial passes and deleted tests — before they reach review.

The environment matters as much as the prompts: focused test commands, pre-approved permissions, file scaffolds that encode conventions, and per-feature worktrees that isolate intermediate state.

The next chapter covers parallel agent orchestration — how to run multiple TDD loops simultaneously on disjoint parts of a codebase, dispatch the right model tier to each, and collect the results without conflicts.
what-claude-expects-trust:
What Claude expects from you & building trust

Delegation is a two-way contract. Claude brings capability; you bring context, constraints, and calibrated autonomy. This chapter lays out exactly what your side of the contract looks like — what you owe Claude before the first prompt, how to grant autonomy without losing control, and how trust is earned in both directions over time.

The delegation contract

When you hand a task to a capable colleague, you don't re-explain the entire codebase. You trust that they've read the docs, understand the domain, and know the guardrails. You say "fix the round-robin bug" — not "open , find the function that counts assignments, check the sort logic, then…"

Claude works the same way. Prompts in the 10–80 word range consistently produce the best results — not because brevity is a virtue, but because the context that makes short prompts work belongs in standing documentation, not in every message. When that documentation is thorough, the prompt only needs to carry the goal. The architecture docs, conventions, and known gotchas carry the rest. (Source: packet-E, F-33)

A 400-plus-line CLAUDE.md means a 20-word prompt can be enough. The ratio inverts what most people expect: the document does the heavy lifting; the prompt names the target.

This is not just convenience. It is what makes autonomous sessions safe. An agent that knows your schema, your RBAC rules, your known gotchas, and your sharp edges is far less likely to produce a change that looks right but breaks an invariant. Context you write once benefits every session. Context you repeat in prompts evaporates when the session ends.

What Claude needs from you

1. A truthful picture of the codebase

Claude cannot discover what you haven't described. If a module is deprecated but still on disk, say so — or Claude will touch it. If a migration pattern changed six months ago, update CLAUDE.md — or Claude will use the old pattern. If there are two ways to do something and one of them is wrong for your project, write down which is which.

The highest-value lines in any  are the "do not do this" entries: the anti-patterns that look plausible from the code but break invariants at runtime. When you find a new one, add it immediately. When you fix one, delete the bullet — stale gotchas are actively harmful because Claude will flag fixed problems as warnings.

2. Clear scope and constraints

Claude follows scope boundaries when they are explicit. "Fix the session expiry bug in the auth module" is a well-scoped task. "Clean up the auth code" is an invitation to touch files you didn't intend, discover adjacent issues, and expand the working set in ways that surprise you.

For larger campaigns, the most reliable enforcement is physical rather than instructional. A git worktree per stage — a separate directory, a separate branch — means Claude literally cannot edit files that belong to a different batch. The scope is enforced at the filesystem level, not by an instruction that might get overridden when Claude finds a "related" issue two modules away. (Source: packet-E, F-10)

3. A decision about autonomy level

Every session involves an implicit choice: how much approval overhead do you want? The answer should be deliberate, not accidental.

Claude Code offers six permission modes — from  (prompt for every potentially dangerous operation) to  (skip all checks, for isolated containers). In between:  (auto-approve file writes and common filesystem ops),  (read-only exploration, never auto-approve edits), and  (pre-approved tools only, everything else denied — useful for CI). (Source: packet-A, §3)

The pattern that works for sustained autonomous sessions:  for the session, combined with a targeted  hook that blocks the one irreversible side-effect you care about most. In practice, that is a hook that verifies git commit author identity and rejects AI attribution strings before any  Bash call goes through. Full autonomy for file writes and shell commands; a single hard gate at the boundary that matters. (Source: packet-E, F-05, F-27)

This mode skips all permission checks. It is appropriate when Claude is working in an isolated worktree on your own machine, or in a sandboxed container. On a shared machine, or in a session where the scope is unclear, start with  and add allow-rules as you go.

For engineers wiring Claude into automation pipelines, the relevant mode is : tools not covered by explicit allow-rules in  are denied rather than prompted. This gives you a deterministic, non-interactive agent suitable for CI/CD.

4. Goals, not procedures

The clearest signal that a delegation is well-formed: you have described what you want, not how to get it. Claude navigates the "how" better than a step-by-step instruction set can predict, especially when the task involves discovering the shape of the problem as it goes.

Compare:

| Instruction-oriented | Goal-oriented |
|---|---|
| "Open . Find the assignment count query. Check whether it filters by UTC midnight. If not, add the filter." | "The round-robin is not resetting daily. Fix it." |
| "Add a  column to the Lead model, run , then update the form component." | "Add best-time-to-call to the lead creation flow, including schema and UI." |

The goal-oriented form gives Claude room to discover that the real problem is upstream of where you pointed, or that the "obvious" fix has a migration implication, or that the UI already has a similar pattern in a different component it should reuse. Procedure-oriented instructions short-circuit that discovery — they make Claude an executor rather than a collaborator.

What Claude owes you in return

The contract runs both ways. Claude brings three things to its side:

Honesty about uncertainty. When Claude doesn't know something, it should say so rather than confabulate a plausible-sounding answer. When it can't determine from context whether a pattern is intentional or a mistake, it should ask — not decide silently.

Conservative interpretation of scope. A well-calibrated agent does not expand the working set on its own initiative. If the prompt says "fix the bug in auth", changes to the directory module need an explicit go-ahead, not a unilateral decision that "it was related."

Visible reasoning when stakes are high. For irreversible operations — migrations, deletes, publishes — Claude should make its plan legible before executing, not after. The  mode and plan-first prompting patterns both serve this function.

How trust is earned — and maintained

Trust between you and Claude is not a fixed property. It is a function of context richness, track record, and system design.

The reinforcing loop in the lower half is where effective Claude users operate. It takes a few hours of upfront investment — writing the architecture doc, documenting sharp edges, setting up memory automation — and then every subsequent session costs less friction.

Concretely:

- Start with lighter autonomy on a codebase Claude hasn't seen before. Run a session or two in  mode. Observe what surprises you. Document the surprises as gotchas or scope constraints.
- Expand autonomy as the context matures. Once CLAUDE.md covers the invariants and the worktree discipline is in place,  with a commit hook is a reasonable operating point for a trusted, well-documented codebase.
- Treat surprises as documentation debt, not model failures. When Claude does something unexpected, the first question is: "Was this in the docs?" Usually the answer is no. Add it. The same surprise will not recur.

The context that makes Claude accurate — the architecture knowledge, the sharp edges, the conventions — is not re-discoverable from the code on every session. Automated session memory (a PostToolUse hook that extracts key facts into structured files) means each session inherits what previous sessions learned. Without it, trust resets on every fresh context. (Source: packet-E, F-06, F-08)

The automator's checklist

For readers building systems where Claude runs without a human in the loop:

The last item deserves emphasis. The instinct after an unexpected result is to write a more specific prompt for next time. The better response is to write a new gotcha bullet in CLAUDE.md. Constraints in documents outlast constraints in prompts by an order of magnitude.

Recap

The delegation contract asks you to provide: an accurate picture of the codebase (in documentation, not in prompts), explicit scope, a deliberate autonomy level, and goals rather than procedures. In return, Claude provides honest uncertainty signals, conservative scope interpretation, and legible reasoning before high-stakes operations.

Trust is not a given — it is a feedback loop. Rich context produces accurate output; accurate output justifies higher autonomy; higher autonomy justifies the investment in richer context. The loop starts with the first draft of your  and compounds from there.

Next: Part 5 looks at the agent loop itself — what Claude does between receiving your goal and producing a result, how tool calls compose, and where the loop can go wrong.
cost-tiering:
Cost-tiering — cheap for grunt, expensive for judgment

Every agent pipeline has two kinds of work: mechanical work that needs to be done correctly, and judgment work that needs to be done wisely. Routing each kind to the right model tier is the single highest-leverage cost decision in agent design. This chapter gives you the framework for that decision — how to identify which tier a task belongs in, how to wire the model field in subagent definitions, and how real multi-stage pipelines have applied it.

Why the tier decision matters more than it looks

Model invocations are the dominant cost in an agent pipeline. Unlike cloud compute, where you pay for uptime, you pay for model tokens whether the task needed deep reasoning or not. A mechanical verification step run on an expensive model is not just wasteful — it makes your pipeline slower because capable models take longer to respond, which extends wall-clock time for tasks that do not benefit from the extra capability.

The converse failure is also real: routing a task that requires genuine judgment to a cheap model, then treating its output as authoritative, produces errors that are expensive to recover from downstream. Wrong architecture decisions, missed edge cases, subtly incorrect security fixes — the cost of these dwarfs the few tokens you saved.

The framework is simple: match model cost to the value that model capability delivers on that specific subtask.

Specific model names and pricing shift over release cycles. The principle — cheap model for mechanical tasks, capable model for judgment tasks — is stable. "Cheap" and "capable" here are relative terms within whatever model family you have access to: a fast, smaller model vs. a slower, larger one. Apply the framework to whatever tiers exist when you read this.

The two task classes

Nearly every subtask in an agent pipeline falls into one of two classes.

Mechanical tasks have objectively correct outputs you could verify with a script. Examples:

- Count the number of test cases in a file and compare to a threshold.
- Extract a list of failing TypeScript error codes from  output.
- Check whether a diff touches only files in a declared scope.
- Summarize a session transcript into a compact bullet list (the shape is deterministic even if the prose varies).
- Confirm a suite is green by reading test runner output.

These tasks do not require the model to reason about the problem domain. They require it to parse structured input and produce structured output. A capable model does them correctly. A cheap model does them correctly and returns faster and cheaper. There is no quality advantage to over-spending here.

Judgment tasks have outputs where capability differences produce meaningfully different quality. Examples:

- Design the API surface for a new module.
- Identify which of twelve open issues shares a root cause.
- Review a 400-line diff for security vulnerabilities.
- Write a system prompt that handles edge cases a simple version would miss.
- Decide how to partition a migration across phases to minimize risk.

These tasks reward deeper reasoning. A capable model with higher effort will catch things a cheap model misses — and those misses are not random; they tend to cluster on exactly the cases that matter most.

Where this appears in Claude Code

Claude Code surfaces the tier decision in three places.

The  field in subagent definitions

Every subagent definition file can specify which model it uses:

The parent orchestrator dispatches this agent at the verification step without caring which model it uses internally. The model selection is an implementation detail of the agent definition, not the orchestrator prompt.

The  field in the SDK's  options

When embedding agents in your own application via the Agent SDK, pass  as an option alongside , , and :

The two calls represent two different tiers for two different purposes. The effort level moves independently of the model — setting  on the capable model trims its thinking budget even if you want that model for domain reasons.

The  setting and  command

Effort level is a second axis on top of model selection.  control the reasoning depth per turn — more effort means more thinking tokens, higher cost, and slower response, but better results on complex problems. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Effort level applies within a model tier, not across tiers. A cheap model at  effort is not equivalent to a capable model at  effort. Use effort to tune within a tier, not as a substitute for picking the right tier.

A real pipeline: the five-stage audit

The audit remediation case study — 123 security findings fixed across 7 domain batches in two days — ran a five-stage pipeline per batch that explicitly assigned each stage to an appropriate tier. (Source: packet-E, F-14)

Stage 3 is the critical tier decision. The verification gate asks: did the test count hold? Does the diff stay in scope? Is the suite green? These are yes/no questions with objectively correct answers. A cheap model answers them correctly. The stage was fast, low-cost, and ran on every batch without accumulating meaningful spend — which is exactly what made it practical to include at all.

The visualizer above shows how pipeline stages with different model tiers map to different lane heights and colors. Switch to the audit pipeline preset to see the tier assignments laid out across the five stages. Notice how the cheap verification lane is narrow (few turns, short wall-clock time) while the capable implementation lanes are taller and slower.

Practical decision guide

For any new subtask in a pipeline you are designing, answer three questions in order:

1. Can the output be verified programmatically?
If yes, the task is mechanical. Use the cheap tier.

2. Does the task require understanding the problem domain?
If no (it is parsing, counting, formatting, extracting), use the cheap tier. If yes, continue.

3. What is the cost of a wrong output?
If wrong output is caught by the next stage (a verification gate, a test run, a human review), a moderate capability level may be fine. If wrong output propagates unchecked into production or into another agent's context as ground truth, use the capable tier with higher effort.

The gate is cheap. A bad output from the stage before it that reaches production is expensive. The temptation to remove the gate when budgets are tight is exactly backwards — the gate is what makes cheap models safe to use at scale.

Wiring it in practice

A minimal two-tier subagent roster for a code-change pipeline:

The orchestrator never hard-codes model names in its prompt. It dispatches  for the planning step and  for the verification step. If you want to upgrade the planner to a more capable model next quarter, change one line in one file.

Budget caps as a safety net

The  option in the SDK's  call sets a hard spend ceiling per agent invocation. (Source: packet-A, §1)

 does not replace tier decisions — it is a guard against runaway loops on capable models, not a reason to run judgment tasks on cheap ones. Set it on every capable-tier invocation in automated pipelines. If it fires unexpectedly, the  subtype  tells you to investigate why the task needed more turns than budgeted.

The effort-vs-tier distinction

A common point of confusion: effort level () and model tier are independent controls that compose.

- Model tier determines the model's capacity for reasoning — how much capability it has.
- Effort level determines how much of that capacity it uses per turn — thinking tokens, reasoning depth.

Running a capable model at  effort gives you fast, cheap responses from a high-ceiling model — useful when you need the model's domain knowledge but the specific task is not complex. Running a cheap model at  effort gives you the model's best attempt at a hard problem — but the ceiling is lower, so the ceiling matters more than the effort for truly difficult reasoning tasks.

The useful combinations:

| Model tier | Effort | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| Cheap |  | Pure mechanical — parse, count, format |
| Cheap |  | Slightly structured judgment — summarization, extraction with judgment |
| Capable |  | Standard engineering tasks, code review |
| Capable |  /  /  | Architecture decisions, complex debugging, adversarial review |

The built-in agents already do this

Claude Code's built-in subagents demonstrate the pattern. The  agent runs on Haiku — a cheaper, faster model — for read-only codebase search. The  agent also runs on Haiku for answering feature questions. (Source: packet-A, §7)

These are mechanical tasks: search files matching a pattern, retrieve documentation about a feature. They do not require the depth of a capable model. By routing them to Haiku, Claude Code keeps the cost of ambient, exploratory operations low without degrading the quality of those specific operations.

The session memory extraction in the  plugin follows the same logic: a cheap model is used to summarize session transcripts into compact bullet points, running after every tool call on a cooldown timer. (Source: packet-E, F-06) The task is deterministic in shape even if not in content — summarize N exchanges into M bullets — and the cheap model handles it correctly while keeping extraction cost negligible across hundreds of sessions.

Recap

Model tier is a per-subtask decision, not a per-session one. Mechanical tasks — those with objectively verifiable outputs, no domain reasoning required — belong on the cheap tier. Judgment tasks — those requiring domain knowledge, careful reasoning, or where errors propagate unchecked — belong on the capable tier. The two tiers compose: a five-stage pipeline can use capable→capable→cheap→capable→capable and pay cheap rates only for the gate in the middle.

Wire the tier into the subagent  field, not into the orchestrator's prompt. Keep budget caps on every capable-tier invocation in automated pipelines. Never remove verification gates to save money; the gate is what makes cheap models safe to use at scale.

The next chapter covers budget governance at the pipeline level — how to track cumulative spend across parallel agent branches, set policies that prevent runaway costs in production, and instrument pipelines so spend anomalies surface before they become incidents.
parallel-agent-teams:
Parallel agent teams

Fan-out orchestration — running multiple agents simultaneously on different slices of a problem — is one of the highest-leverage techniques available in Claude Code. This chapter gives you a precise mental model for when parallelism wins, when it backfires, and how to design the coordination layer that makes it reliable.

The core intuition: wall-clock time vs. serial time

Every task has two costs: the time to complete it serially, and the wall-clock time when work runs in parallel. For purely sequential work, these are equal. For independent work, wall-clock time collapses to the duration of the longest single task.

The gain only materialises when tasks are genuinely independent. Independence means: no shared files, no ordering constraints, no shared mutable state. Break that and you do not get concurrency — you get a race condition that silently corrupts output.

The visualizer above shows three presets. The speedup column illustrates the point: a typesafety sweep over disjoint file groups runs several times faster in parallel than in series; a tightly coupled pipeline that requires each stage's output gains almost nothing.

When fan-out wins

Parallelism pays off reliably in a small set of patterns.

Disjoint file scopes

The most common and safest use. Divide the codebase into non-overlapping groups — for example,  in one agent,  in a second,  in a third — and dispatch all three simultaneously. Each agent reads and writes only its own files. No merge conflict is possible because the scopes never touch. The typesafety campaign described in packet E (F-15) used exactly this shape: a sequential foundation phase reduced 386 TypeScript errors to 238, then three parallel agents on disjoint module groups eliminated the remaining 238 in a fraction of the serial time.

Audit and review passes

Code review is embarrassingly parallel: each reviewer reads the same static diff and produces an independent judgment. An 8-agent review pass over a large RBAC implementation (packet E, F-16) caught 7 critical and 11 high-severity issues before merge, including a synchronous JWT verification call inside an async handler that was crashing the production process on a predictable interval. No single reviewer saw all of them; the ensemble did.

Multi-domain batch processing

When you have a list of fixed, independent units — 123 security findings, 42 API endpoints, 7 PDF template families — you can partition the list and process each partition in a dedicated agent lane. The audit remediation case study (packet E, F-14) used a 5-stage pipeline across 7 domain batches: planner, TDD implementer, verifier, adversarial reviewer, fixer. The batches ran in sequence (because each shared the same database), but within each batch the 5-stage pipeline was structured so that the cheapest-appropriate model handled each stage — Haiku for mechanical verification, Sonnet for implementation and planning.

Research fan-out

When a question has multiple independent sub-questions — "what does the payment library do?", "what does the auth module do?", "what do the webhook routes do?" — dispatch one agent per question. Each explores freely without interfering with the others. The  bundled workflow uses this structure internally: it fans out web searches, fetches sources, adversarially cross-checks claims, and synthesises a cited report (packet A, section 6).

When fan-out hurts

Parallelism has failure modes that are worse than slowness — they are silent.

Shared file writes

If two agents edit the same file, the second write wins and the first is lost, or the changes interleave in incoherent ways. This is not a theoretical risk; it is the most common mistake in parallel agent work. The fix is simple — scope agents to disjoint files — but it requires discipline at dispatch time.

Two agents writing to the same file do not raise an error. The second write silently overwrites the first. Always define non-overlapping file scopes before dispatching parallel agents, and verify at design time, not after the fact.

Ordering dependencies

Some work is inherently sequential. A schema migration must complete before the application code that uses the new columns can be tested. An authentication fix must land before a dependent feature that relies on the corrected token structure. Forcing these into parallel lanes produces builds that fail at integration, often in ways that are time-consuming to untangle.
