The heuristic: if task B requires the output of task A as input, they are sequential. If both tasks only require the original codebase as input and produce independent outputs, they are parallel candidates.

Resource contention on the host

Running many agents simultaneously places real demands on the host machine: CPU for model inference (if using local infrastructure), disk I/O for file reads and writes, and memory for each agent's context. The Claude Code workflow runtime caps concurrent agents at 16 on capable hardware and fewer on constrained machines (packet A, section 10). In practice, the SOP documented in the primary project limits parallel dispatches to approximately 5 agents to avoid host resource pressure (packet E, F-18). Beyond that number, queue depth grows and agents begin waiting rather than running.

Context cost of coordination

Each agent carries its own context window: its system prompt, its task description, the CLAUDE.md content it loads, and every tool call it makes. Spawning 10 agents where 3 would do wastes tokens, extends wall-clock time (more agents means more total work), and makes the orchestrating session harder to reason about. Fan-out is a precision instrument, not a reflex.

Designing the coordination layer

The hard part of parallel teams is not running them — the  tool handles that. The hard part is designing the boundaries cleanly enough that independent execution is actually safe.

Partitioning strategies

For file-scope partitioning specifically: list all files in scope, group them, and confirm that no file appears in more than one group. This is worth doing explicitly, not by feel. A module that imports from another module does not prevent parallelism — what matters is which files get written, not which files get read.

Worktrees as isolation units

Each parallel agent should operate in its own git worktree. A worktree is a separate physical directory rooted on the same repository, checked out to its own branch. Agents editing different worktrees cannot interfere even if their file-scope analysis was imperfect, because the files are physically separate.

In the primary project described in packet E (F-10), every feature branch lives in its own worktree directory, created via a script that always bases on . This is not just an organisation preference — it is the structural guarantee that makes parallel session isolation reliable. The stale-base incident (F-12) illustrates the failure mode: a worktree created from a branch 329 commits behind the target effectively clobbered months of shipped work. The script enforces the correct base on every creation.

Worktrees prevent file conflicts even when scope analysis misses an overlap. The cost is disk space and setup time; the benefit is a hard isolation guarantee. The  tool's  frontmatter field automates this for named subagents (packet A, section 7).

The merge sequence

Parallel agents produce parallel branches. Merging them is a sequential operation, and the order matters:

1. Each agent's branch should be reviewed independently — the output of one agent is not a precondition for reviewing another.
2. Merge to the integration branch in an order that respects any soft dependencies (e.g., if agent A adds a utility function that agent B uses, merge A first).
3. Run the full test and typecheck suite after each merge, not only after all merges. Catching an integration issue at merge 2 is cheaper than untangling it at merge 5.

Model tier selection per stage

Not every agent in a pipeline needs the same model. The audit pipeline case study (F-14) was explicit about this: the cheapest model appropriate to the task handled each stage. Mechanical verification — "does the test count match? does the diff cover the finding?" — is a pattern-matching problem that a smaller, faster model handles well. Planning and implementation require more reasoning. Assigning a slower, more capable model to a mechanical gate slows the pipeline without improving its output; assigning a weaker model to a nuanced implementation task produces subtle errors that are expensive to find later.

A practical tier assignment for a typical quality pipeline:

This tiering is not a rule — it is a starting point. Adjust based on how much reasoning each stage actually needs.

The orchestrator's responsibilities

The session that dispatches parallel agents is the orchestrator. Its job is not to do the work — it is to design the partition, dispatch the agents, collect their results, and handle failures.

The orchestrator should:

- Define scope boundaries explicitly before any agent starts
- Ensure each agent prompt includes the project CLAUDE.md reference and the specific scope it owns
- Monitor for agent failure and decide whether to retry, skip, or escalate
- Merge results in the correct order
- Run integration gates after each merge

The orchestrator should not:

- Re-do work that agents are doing
- Dispatch more agents than the host can run concurrently without queuing
- Leave scope boundaries ambiguous and hope agents will work it out

The  tool handles the orchestrator role mechanically when the task is well-defined enough to script: it moves the orchestration logic into code, keeps intermediate results in script variables rather than the context window, and runs up to 16 concurrent agents without occupying the main session (packet A, section 10). For complex multi-repo work where the partition logic itself requires judgment, the orchestrator is Claude in the main session working interactively.

A practical example: the typesafety sweep

The typesafety campaign (packet E, F-15) is worth walking through as a concrete template.

Sequential foundation phase (P1, P2): Before any parallelism, a single agent established the tsconfig flags, introduced type-guard utilities and branded ID types, and ran a first mechanical pass that reduced the error count from 386 to 238. This was sequential because the foundation phase produced types and utilities that the parallel agents would depend on.

Parallel sweep phase (P3): With the foundation stable, three agents ran simultaneously on disjoint module groups:
- Agent A: , , 
- Agent B: , , , , 
- Agent C: the remaining modules

No agent could write a file owned by another agent. All three ran to completion and produced branches that merged cleanly. The error count went from 238 to 0.

Sequential gate phases (P4, P5): ESLint with type-checking, then smoke-gate hardening and a git hook that prevents future regressions — both sequential because each built on the previous result.

The total wall-clock time was a fraction of what a purely sequential pass would have required. The P3 phase, which represented most of the mechanical work, ran in parallel without any integration issues because the partition was designed correctly.

What breaks and how to catch it

Even well-designed parallel runs produce integration problems. The most common:

False independence: Two agents both needed to update a shared constants file. One wins; the other's change is silently dropped. Detection: diff each agent's output against the baseline before merging; look for changes to shared files.

Stale base: An agent based its worktree on a branch that was already stale when it started, missing changes that affect its scope. Detection: always base worktrees on the same integration branch and verify the base SHA at dispatch time.

Cascading type errors: Agent A changes a type in a shared interface; Agent B, running concurrently, uses the old type and generates code that will fail to compile after A's changes are merged. Detection: run the full typecheck suite after each merge, not just after the last one.

Assumption drift: Each agent receives the task description as it was at dispatch time. If one agent's work changes the assumptions that another agent's plan depends on, the second agent produces output that is correct for the world as it was at dispatch, not the world as it is at merge time. Detection: in the review pass, check whether the post-merge codebase still matches what each agent assumed.

Parallel agents produce correct output for their own scope. They do not guarantee that their outputs compose correctly. The full test and typecheck suite run after each merge is the actual correctness gate — skipping it trades short-term speed for delayed, harder-to-diagnose failures.

Recap

Fan-out across parallel agents wins decisively when tasks are independent — disjoint file scopes, independent audit passes, or partitioned batch inputs. It fails silently when tasks share mutable state, have hidden ordering dependencies, or when the host lacks the resources to run the requested concurrency.

The coordination layer matters as much as the parallelism itself: clear scope partitions, worktree isolation per agent, the right model tier for each stage, and a sequential merge sequence with integration gates after each step. The typesafety and audit case studies in this book's research packets both demonstrate the pattern at scale — hundreds of errors and findings addressed in days rather than weeks, with quality that exceeded what any single-agent pass would have produced.

The next chapter looks at how to design the prompts and task descriptions that give individual agents — parallel or serial — enough context to work reliably without constant supervision.
subagents:
Subagents & the Agent tool

Subagents let one Claude instance delegate bounded, focused tasks to other Claude instances — each running its own agent loop, in its own context, with its own tool permissions. This chapter explains precisely what a subagent is, how the  tool spawns one, why context isolation is the central benefit, and how to judge when delegation is worth the overhead.

What a subagent is

A subagent is a complete agent loop running inside a parent agent loop. It has its own message array, its own tool set, its own turn counter, and its own context window. When it finishes, only the final  — the summary text, token count, cost, and session ID — returns to the parent. None of the intermediate tool outputs, file reads, or reasoning steps cross the boundary.

That last point is the entire point. The parent's context stays thin. The subagent's context can grow as deep as the task requires, then disappear. (Source: packet-A, §7)

A subagent is not a lightweight background thread. It is a full Claude model invocation — it consumes tokens, incurs cost, and runs at whatever effort level you configure. Spawning a subagent for a two-line edit is overhead, not leverage.

The Agent tool

The  tool is the built-in mechanism for spawning a subagent from within a running agent loop. It appears in the tool surface as a first-class peer of , , and . (Source: packet-A, §2)

When Claude calls , the SDK:

1. Creates a new message array for the child.
2. Injects the subagent's system prompt (its own, not the parent's).
3. Runs the child loop — tool calls, results, turns — until no tool call is issued.
4. Emits the child's .
5. Returns the result text as the tool output the parent sees.

From the parent's perspective, calling  looks identical to calling : it blocks until the result is ready (for foreground agents), then the result text appears in the message array as a tool output — compact, no matter how much the child did.

Named vs forked subagents

The  tool supports two modes:

Named subagents start with a fresh context. They load their own system prompt from a subagent definition file ( or ). They know nothing of the parent's conversation unless the parent explicitly includes it in the task prompt. This is the right choice for well-defined, repeatable roles.

Forked subagents inherit the parent's full conversation. They always run in the background, surfacing permission prompts in the parent terminal. Use forks when the task genuinely needs the accumulated context — code review against a long implementation session, for example — but be aware the child starts with a heavy context from the start. (Source: packet-A, §7)

For most orchestration work, named subagents are correct. A named agent is given a specific task prompt; it does not need to know how the parent got there.

Defining a custom subagent

A subagent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter. Place it in  (project-shared) or  (personal). The filename without the extension is the subagent's name.

Key frontmatter fields (source: packet-A, §7):

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
|  | Which model to use; defaults to parent model |
|  | Explicit allowlist; omit to inherit all parent tools |
|  | Deny list; takes precedence over  if both set |
|  | Cap on tool-use round trips before the loop stops |
|  |  (fresh git worktree) or  (default) |
|  |  to let the agent read/write user memory files |

Permission behavior: foreground subagents surface permission prompts to the user. Background subagents auto-deny unapproved tool calls and continue running. If you are orchestrating unattended, pre-approve the tools the subagent needs in your allow rules — otherwise a permission prompt will block the entire pipeline.

Context isolation in practice

The reason to delegate to subagents is not just parallelism — it is context hygiene. Consider a codebase sweep to fix 386 TypeScript errors across dozens of files.

Without subagents, the parent agent reads file after file, accumulates tool outputs, and eventually either hits context limits or starts degrading because the early reads are too far from attention peaks. The entire sweep lives in one growing window.

With subagents, the parent partitions the files into disjoint scopes, dispatches one agent per scope, and waits. Each agent runs deep in its own window — reading, editing, verifying — then returns a one-paragraph summary. The parent's window gains one tool output per subagent, regardless of how many turns the subagent took.

This structure was used in a real typesafety campaign: three parallel subagents dispatched over disjoint file scopes (leads/auth/jobs, settings/ops/directory, and remaining modules), each building deep context in its own window, reducing 238 errors to zero. The parent context accumulated three result summaries. (Source: packet-E, F-15)

The visualizer above shows how parallel subagent lanes compress wall-clock time while keeping the orchestrator's cost and context minimal. Switch presets to see different pipeline shapes — a sequential audit pipeline, a parallel sweep, a verifier stage that runs after all workers complete.

When to delegate — and when not to

The  tool has real overhead: a fresh model invocation, token cost for the child's turns, and the serialization latency of waiting for a result. Delegation pays off when the savings outweigh those costs.

Delegate when:

- The task is self-contained and the result can be expressed as a summary.
- The task involves many reads and writes that would bloat the parent context.
- Multiple such tasks are independent and can run in parallel.
- You want a specialized system prompt for a role (reviewer, verifier, planner) without polluting the parent's prompt.

Keep in the parent loop when:

- The task needs tight, turn-by-turn integration with the parent's reasoning.
- The task is small (a single file edit, a two-command diagnostic).
- The output of the task drives the parent's next decision in a way that requires the intermediate steps, not just a summary.

A useful heuristic: if you can describe the task in one sentence and the result in one paragraph, it is a candidate for delegation. If you cannot describe it without referencing intermediate state the parent holds, keep it in-process.

Built-in subagents

Claude Code ships five built-in subagents that the runtime uses automatically. You do not need to define them; they are available by name in every session. (Source: packet-A, §7)

| Name | Model | Purpose | Skips CLAUDE.md? |
|---|---|---|---|
|  | Haiku | Read-only fast codebase search | Yes |
|  | Inherits parent | Research phase for plan mode | Yes |
|  | Inherits parent | All tools, no special role | No |
|  | Sonnet | Configures the  command | No |
|  | Haiku | Answers Claude Code feature questions | No |

 and  skip  and git status by design — they are optimized for speed, and the extra context would slow them down without benefiting the read-only research they do.

In the SDK, you can suppress all built-ins by setting . This is useful when embedding Claude Code in an application where you want full control over the available subagent roster.

Orchestration patterns

The three most common patterns in practice:

Fan-out / fan-in

The parent breaks a large task into N independent chunks, dispatches one subagent per chunk in parallel, then aggregates the results. Works well for sweeps, audits, and generation tasks where the chunks do not share files.

Pipeline

The output of one subagent becomes the input to the next. Each stage receives only a summary of the previous stage's work, keeping each agent's input compact.

This pattern was used for a 123-finding audit remediation: a Sonnet planner re-verified findings on the live branch, a Sonnet implementer ran TDD per batch, a Haiku verifier checked gates mechanically (cheap model for a mechanical task), and an adversarial reviewer fed issues to a Sonnet fixer. Seven domain batches, ten PRs, two days. (Source: packet-E, F-14)

Parallel with dependency ordering

Some tasks have partial ordering. Group A must finish before Group B reads the output. Within each group, tasks are independent. The parent can dispatch Group A in parallel, await all results, then dispatch Group B in parallel — without the subagents needing to coordinate with each other at all.

Two subagents editing the same file simultaneously will produce conflicts. The disjoint-file constraint is not advisory — it is the prerequisite for safe parallel dispatch. Before dispatching N agents in parallel, verify their file scopes do not overlap. A pre-dispatch scope check is worth including in the orchestrator prompt.

Worktrees and subagent isolation

For tasks that mutate the filesystem — editing source files, running builds, applying migrations — the  frontmatter field instructs the runtime to create a fresh git worktree for the subagent. The subagent makes its changes in that worktree; the parent decides whether to merge them.

Worktree isolation is the correct choice when:
- Subagents in a parallel group might otherwise have write conflicts even on different files (e.g., generated files, lock files, build artifacts).
- You want the parent to review and approve diffs before they land on the working branch.
- A subagent's task might need to be abandoned without polluting the parent's working tree.

Without worktree isolation, parallel agents that happen to touch shared files (lock files, generated types, index files) can produce conflicts that are harder to resolve than just running them serially.

Hooks for subagent lifecycle

Two hook events fire around subagent execution. (Source: packet-A, §5)

-  — fires when a subagent is being spawned. Not blockable. Useful for logging, metrics, or setting up monitoring.
-  — fires when a subagent completes. Blockable (exit 2). Useful for validation gates: inspect the result, block if the output fails a quality check, forcing the parent to retry or escalate.

A  hook that validates the result before it returns to the parent is a lightweight way to build a quality gate into the orchestration structure without requiring the parent to parse and evaluate every subagent output manually.

Putting it together: a minimal orchestration

Below is the shape of a parent prompt that uses subagents responsibly. The specifics depend on your task; the structure is the pattern.

The parent reads one file, dispatches three agents, verifies, dispatches at most one follow-up, and reports. Its context accumulates one file read plus four tool outputs maximum. The agents do the heavy lifting in their own windows.

Recap

Subagents are complete agent loops that run inside a parent loop. The  tool spawns them; the SDK takes care of the child loop's lifecycle and returns only the final summary to the parent. Context isolation — not just parallelism — is the core value: subagents can read and write deeply without filling the parent's window.

Named subagents are defined in Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, giving each agent a role, a model, a tool set, and turn limits. The built-in agents (, , and others) handle common patterns automatically. Custom agents handle your domain-specific roles.

Delegate when a task is self-contained, potentially long, and operates on a disjoint file set. Keep in the parent loop when a task is small, tightly coupled to intermediate state, or shares files with other concurrent tasks. The decision tree above is the practical guide.

The next chapter covers dynamic workflows — JavaScript scripts that move orchestration logic entirely out of Claude's context window, enabling coordination of hundreds of agents at a scale where even a thin parent context would become unwieldy.
workflows:
Workflows — deterministic orchestration

Dynamic workflows move orchestration logic out of Claude's context window and into executable JavaScript. This chapter shows you the three structural patterns — pipeline, parallel fan-out, and loop — so you can model any repeatable multi-step job and understand exactly what the runtime guarantees at each stage.

Why orchestration needs its own layer

An agent loop is powerful but inherently linear: one message array, one thread of reasoning. When a job has ten independently solvable sub-tasks, running them one at a time means a ten-fold wait and a context window that fills with intermediate results the later steps do not need.

Workflows solve this by pushing orchestration into code. A workflow script describes what work to do and in what order; Claude Code's runtime executes it in the background. Intermediate results live in JavaScript variables — not in the model's context — so the context window stays clean regardless of how many sub-tasks run.

The orchestration structure is deterministic — the sequence, branching conditions, and concurrency limits you write in the script are executed exactly as written, every time. The output of each agent turn is still non-deterministic (it is a language model). The value of deterministic orchestration is that you can reason about flow control, retries, and sequencing without thinking about model variance.

The runtime model

Before looking at patterns, it helps to have a clear picture of the boundaries.

Key facts from the official docs:[^workflow-docs]

- Up to 16 agents run concurrently (fewer on low-CPU machines); up to 1,000 agents total per workflow run.
- The script itself has no direct filesystem or shell access — agents do that work, then return results as strings.
- No mid-run user input is possible once a workflow starts, except for permission prompts on individual tool calls.
- Spawned agents always run in  mode, so file edits inside the workflow do not pause for approval.

[^workflow-docs]: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md — last verified 2026-06-21.

Triggering a workflow

There are three ways to launch a workflow:

1. Natural language — describe the job and Claude decides to use a workflow (from v2.1.160+).
2.  keyword — include the word  in your prompt, or run . This sets  reasoning effort and tells Claude to plan a workflow for every substantive task.[^ultracode]
3. Saved slash command — save a workflow to  and invoke it as .

[^ultracode]: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md — last verified 2026-06-21.  (Win/Linux) or  (macOS) suppresses the trigger for a single prompt.

Once running, use  to inspect active and completed runs. Press  to pause/resume,  to stop,  to save.

The three structural patterns

Pattern 1: Pipeline

A pipeline is a linear chain of agents where each stage transforms the output of the previous one. Use it when steps must happen in order and each step depends on the result of the last.

What makes this a pipeline: each  call blocks until the previous agent finishes. The outputs flow forward as strings. No stage runs until its input is ready.

When to use it: when stage N genuinely cannot start without stage N-1's output — planning before execution, verification after generation, summarization after collection.

Pattern 2: Parallel fan-out

Fan-out dispatches multiple agents simultaneously on independent sub-tasks and collects results with . Use it when tasks do not share files and their outputs only need to be combined at the end.

The critical constraint: tasks dispatched in parallel must not edit overlapping files. If two agents write to the same file simultaneously, the second write clobbers the first. Disjoint file scopes are required for correctness, not just performance.

There is no merge or conflict detection between parallel agents. If agents A and B both edit , whichever finishes last wins and the other's changes are gone. Partition your file scopes before dispatching parallel agents.

When to use it: code sweeps across independent modules, batch processing of many independent inputs, running tests in separate domains after a change.

Pattern 3: Loop

A loop runs an agent repeatedly — either a fixed number of times, or until a condition in the result string is satisfied. Use it when you do not know up front how many iterations a job needs.

Always bound your loops. The  counter is not defensive pessimism — it is a correctness requirement. An unbounded loop against a budget cap will drain the cap silently; an explicit guard produces a legible failure.

When to use it: iterative refinement (generate → critique → revise), retrying flaky operations with backoff, processing a queue of items one at a time.

Combining patterns

Real workflows compose these three primitives. A common shape is pipeline-with-internal-fan-out: a planning stage runs first (pipeline step 1), then the plan is decomposed into parallel subtasks (fan-out in step 2), then results are synthesized (pipeline step 3).

Notice the dynamic fan-out: the number of parallel agents is determined at runtime from stage 1's output, not hardcoded. This is a common and powerful pattern — discover, then parallelize across the discovered set.

Choosing the right pattern

Beyond the widget, a rough rule of thumb:

| Situation | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Each step needs the previous step's output | Pipeline |
| Tasks are independent and touch different files | Parallel fan-out |
| You do not know how many iterations you need | Loop |
| Planning before execution, synthesis after | Pipeline wrapping fan-out |

Saving and sharing workflows

A workflow saved to  (project-shared) or  (personal) becomes a slash command .[^save-docs] Invoke it with arguments Claude passes as a structured  global — no argument parsing needed in your script.

[^save-docs]: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md — last verified 2026-06-21. In monorepos (v2.1.178+), saving writes to the closest  directory between cwd and repo root.

The bundled  is itself a saved workflow — fan-out web searches across independent query angles, then a pipeline synthesis step.

Permission management for long-running workflows

Workflows that encounter an unapproved tool call (a shell command not in the allowlist, a domain not pre-approved for ) will pause and wait. In a long unattended run this means the entire workflow blocks until you approve.

The fix: before starting a workflow you intend to run unattended, add the needed tool patterns to your allowlist.

In  mode or when running via the SDK, unapproved calls are auto-denied rather than pausing. Pre-approve everything you need or the workflow fails silently on the denied calls.

What the runtime does not guarantee

Workflows are not transactions. If an agent in stage 2 edits three files and the workflow is stopped mid-run ( in ), those edits remain on disk. The workflow does not roll back. Build your stages so each produces a committable checkpoint, and commit between stages when the job is long enough that partial completion is a risk.

The runtime also does not deduplicate agent runs. If you restart a stopped workflow, agents from aborted stages will re-run from scratch. Idempotent agents (those that check their own output before doing work) are more resilient to restarts than agents that blindly overwrite.

Claude Code's file checkpointing (, on by default) snapshots files before each edit.  can restore pre-edit state. In long workflows, committing after each major stage gives you an explicit restart boundary without relying on checkpoints.

Recap

Workflows give you deterministic control over how agents are sequenced and how many run at once, without filling the context window with intermediate results. The three primitives — pipeline (sequential, output-dependent), parallel fan-out (concurrent, disjoint scopes), and loop (iterative, bound with a guard) — compose into any repeatable multi-step job. Save the workflow as a slash command when the pattern is worth reusing.

The next chapter covers subagents in depth — how to define them with YAML frontmatter, control their tool access and isolation, and coordinate multi-agent teams beyond what a single workflow script handles.
worktrees:
Worktrees for isolation

Git worktrees give every feature its own physical directory, its own branch, and its own session memory. By the end of this chapter you will understand why this matters for parallel AI-driven development, how to structure the discipline so it stays automatic rather than ceremonial, and what the concrete failure mode looks like when the discipline breaks down.

The problem worktrees solve

When you work on a single checkout, all in-progress changes share the same index. A failing test from feature A is visible to an agent working on feature B. Stashing helps, but stashes are easy to forget, hard to name, and invisible to a new session that opens in the same directory.

The deeper problem with a shared checkout is session contamination. Claude Code stores session history under a directory derived from the working directory. When you open a session in the main checkout to work on feature B, you are opening it in the same project entry that holds feature A's history, notes, and context. The agent is not confused about which task it is on — but it does have access to the wrong context, and any memory or file-state assumptions from the previous session can leak.

Git worktrees solve both problems at the same level: the filesystem. Each worktree is a separate directory with its own working tree and its own . Claude Code treats each worktree path as a distinct project. Session history, memory files, and tool calls are scoped to the worktree, not to the repository root. Parallel features become parallel directories, and isolation is structural rather than procedural.

 has been available since Git 2.5. What Claude Code adds is that each worktree gets its own  entry, so session memory is isolated per worktree automatically. No configuration required.

The feature-per-worktree workflow

The workflow below is not an ideal to aspire to — it is drawn from actual usage across two active repositories with 37 concurrent worktrees. (Source: packet-E, F-10) Step through it to see each phase, the command it involves, and the pitfall to avoid.

The seven steps above collapse into a simple rule: the main checkout is a reference point, not a workspace. You never edit files there. You never check out a branch there. You create a worktree, work in it, commit, open a PR, and remove the worktree after merge. The cycle repeats.

The stale-base incident

The single most expensive failure mode in this workflow is creating a worktree from the wrong base. This is not hypothetical. From a concrete incident documented during active development (Source: packet-E, F-12):

> An estimate-PDF redesign was built on top of a checked-out  HEAD because its files "differed from dev" — it appeared to be newer. It was 314 commits stale. The work clobbered shipped dev estimate features and duplicated an already-shipped filename-rename. The entire effort had to be re-implemented from scratch on the correct base.

The incident produced two structural fixes. First, the  script was written to encapsulate worktree creation — it always fetches  and bases new worktrees on that commit, never on the current checkout HEAD. Second, a  hook was added to audit drift at session open time: (Source: packet-E, F-11)

The  subcommand runs silently when everything is healthy. If the main checkout has drifted onto a branch, gone dirty, or is no longer at , it prints a warning before any work begins.

Running  directly bypasses the base-on-origin/dev guarantee. If your working directory happens to have a branch checked out that is dozens of commits behind the integration branch, you will create a worktree from that stale point without any warning. Wrap worktree creation in a script that always bases on  (or your equivalent integration branch) explicitly.

Session memory is per worktree — by design

When you open Claude Code in , the session is stored under a  path derived from that absolute directory. When you open Claude Code in , it gets a separate entry. The two sessions never see each other's history.

This has a practical implication: when you resume work on a feature after a break, the session history from your last session on that feature is exactly where you left it. You can start with "continue from where you left off" and Claude picks up from the right context, not from whatever the last session in the main checkout was doing. (Source: packet-E, F-21)

It also means that removing a worktree after merge does not lose session context. If your workflow includes an automated memory extraction step — a hook that summarizes the session into durable facts before the worktree is cleaned up — the facts survive even though the session file does not.

Structural isolation for parallel agents

The isolation guarantee is what makes parallel agent dispatch safe. When you run three agents simultaneously on disjoint file scopes, each in its own worktree, the failure modes narrow dramatically. (Source: packet-E, F-15)

The constraint is file-level disjointness: two agents editing the same file concurrently inside the same worktree produce conflicts. Two agents each in their own worktree, each editing entirely different files, produce no conflicts at all. The worktree boundary is what gives you this guarantee.

Each worktree branches from the same  base. Each runs independently. Each merges back through a PR. The main checkout is not involved at any point.

Minimum viable setup

You do not need a custom script to get started. The discipline has two mandatory rules and one strong recommendation:

Rule 1 — Never edit files in the main checkout. Keep it clean. Keep it detached at your integration branch. Use it only as a reference.

Rule 2 — Always base new worktrees on the fetched integration branch. Not on the local HEAD. Fetch first, then base.

Strong recommendation — wrap this in a script. The two rules above are easy to state and easy to violate under time pressure. A ten-line script that does the fetch and the worktree creation eliminates the violation surface entirely. When the script is the only path people use, the rules become structural rather than remembered.

Matching worktrees to agent scope

Not every worktree needs its own agent session. A single agent can do substantial sequential work inside one worktree. The decision to dispatch parallel agents is separate from the decision to use worktrees.

What worktrees give parallel agents is a conflict-free working surface. When you dispatch three agents in parallel, the correct question is: do their file scopes overlap? If yes, serialize them or combine them into one agent. If no, each can work in its own worktree simultaneously with no coordination overhead beyond the final merge. (Source: packet-E, F-18)

A practical heuristic: scope each worktree to one module, one route group, or one coherent subsystem. Scopes that share a utility file or a shared type should be in the same worktree, not separate ones.

When a worktree is created by a script, the script can also run environment setup — , , copy a  file — so the first session inside the worktree can run the dev server immediately without a setup phase. This is especially valuable when the agent's first action would otherwise be to install dependencies.

Cleanup and the cycle

After a PR merges, the worktree should be removed. Leaving stale worktrees accumulates confusion: old branches, session histories from completed work, and outdated  that diverge from the current lockfile.

If you use a wrapper script for creation, add a paired  subcommand that prunes merged worktrees. One command to create, one command to remove — the cycle stays mechanical.

Recap

Worktrees give AI-driven development the isolation that the filesystem does not provide by default. Each feature gets a directory, a branch, and a session. The main checkout stays clean and pinned to the integration branch. Parallel agents work on disjoint file scopes in separate worktrees with no coordination overhead. The failure mode — creating a worktree from a stale base — is eliminated structurally by wrapping creation in a script that always fetches before branching.

The discipline costs almost nothing once the script exists. The alternative is sharing state across features, contaminating session memory, and occasionally discovering that weeks of work were built on the wrong foundation.

The next chapter covers parallel agent orchestration — how to dispatch multiple agents across worktrees simultaneously, assign file scopes to prevent conflicts, and collect results without merge collisions.
case-study-feature-ship:
Case study — how a feature actually ships

This chapter walks through the full lifecycle of a real feature: from the moment an idea appears to the moment it lands in production. The source is a large, anonymized set of real Claude Code sessions mined from a multi-repo CRM project. What follows is concrete — no invented steps, no idealized flow — just what actually happened, why it happened that way, and what the patterns generalize to.[^packet-e]

[^packet-e]: All findings are sourced from Research Packet E (Team E, 2026-06-21), which analyzed 1,271 sessions across 141 project directories plus 45 days of structured memory logs and 65 named memory files.

The setup: context that persists across sessions

Before any feature starts, there is infrastructure that makes everything else possible. The project maintains a 400-line  covering architecture, conventions, schema highlights, known gotchas, and the RBAC model. A  plugin (v0.7.3) runs a  hook that extracts session summaries into dated daily logs after each tool call. At session start, a  hook re-injects the relevant portions — the author never manually writes context prompts.[^f06]

[^f06]: Research Packet E, F-06: the remember plugin fires  after every tool call; a Python pipeline calls a small model to summarize exchanges into compact bullets. F-07 documents the 45 daily logs and 65 named memory files.

The result: prompts are 10–80 words. The CLAUDE.md carries the instructional weight that most developers try to stuff into their prompts. The author delegates outcomes ("implement the feature in the image") not procedures — because the procedures live in the standing document.[^f33]

[^f33]: Research Packet E, F-33: the most common prompt structure is a noun phrase for what to do, plus optional execution flags. The CLAUDE.md is the persistent instructional context that makes goal-oriented delegation safe.

This matters for what follows because every step in the feature lifecycle is shorter than it looks in a tutorial. The boilerplate is already done.

Step 1: Spawn a worktree, not a branch

The first concrete action on any feature is creating a git worktree. Not checking out a branch — creating a new worktree via a dedicated script that enforces a single invariant: the base is always , never the current checkout HEAD.[^f10]

[^f10]: Research Packet E, F-10: 17 backend and 20 frontend worktrees active as of 2026-06-21, all created via , all based on . The main checkouts stay detached and are never a workspace.

The script () does several things in sequence: creates the worktree, runs  and  inside it, copies the  file so the server starts immediately, and creates an isolated  entry for the branch. That last point matters: session memory is isolated per worktree. A session in  does not bleed into .

The step-through above shows why the main checkout stays detached. The failure mode of skipping this discipline is documented as a concrete incident: a worktree was once created from a feature branch that turned out to be 314 commits stale. The work built on it clobbered shipped features — a shipped PDF filename-rename, a shipped doctor combobox, a shipped discount model — and had to be re-implemented from scratch.[^f12]

[^f12]: Research Packet E, F-12: "I once built an estimate-PDF redesign on top of the checked-out  HEAD because its files 'differed from dev' — I assumed it was newer. It was 314 commits stale." The  script was the post-incident structural fix.

A  hook runs  every time any session opens in the project. If the main checkout has drifted onto a branch or gone dirty, it warns immediately. This is a structural check, not a reminder.[^f11]

[^f11]: Research Packet E, F-11: the hook command runs ; it warns on drift, stays silent if everything is clean.

Step 2: Implement — with bypass permissions and a commit guardrail

Once the worktree is up, the author opens a Claude Code session in that directory. Every session in this project uses  mode — 100% of 1,271 sessions.[^f03] Combined with  and  set globally, this means Claude can write files, run shell commands, call , and execute migrations without any approval prompt interrupting the flow.[^f04]

[^f03]: Research Packet E, F-03: 3,301  records across the primary project; 100% read . Global  also sets .
[^f04]: Research Packet E, F-04:  and  in , no per-project override observed.

The single guardrail is a  hook on every  call containing . It intercepts the command, checks that  and  match the expected identity, and scans the commit message for AI-attribution patterns (, , emoji indicators). Any match blocks the commit.[^f05]

[^f05]: Research Packet E, F-05:  reads , checks identity, then  for attribution strings. It is global — applies to every project on the machine.

The trust model here is deliberate: unlimited file writes and shell calls, but the one irreversible shared side-effect — the git history — has a hook that enforces correctness. The hook does not slow down ordinary work; it only fires on commits, and only blocks when something is actually wrong.

For a feature of moderate size, the implementation session looks like: a short prompt describing the outcome (often accompanied by a screenshot if it is a UI change[^f19]), Claude reads the relevant architecture sections, writes the code, runs typecheck, writes migrations if the schema changed, and opens a draft PR. The author is not typing out instructions for each file — the CLAUDE.md already contains the conventions.

[^f19]: Research Packet E, F-19: 25.3% of user turns across 265 examined turns included screenshots or image attachments. Visual context replaces lengthy descriptions of layout issues.

Step 3: The PR review pass

Before a PR is merged, the  skill runs a multi-agent code review. The prompt is typically under ten words: "open pr to dev, do e2e pr review using toolkit."

The toolkit dispatches multiple review agents in parallel, each focused on a different quality dimension — security, correctness, test coverage, API contracts, migration safety. Results from the dynamic roles feature review (8 agents) caught 7 critical and 11 high-severity issues before merge.[^f16] The most consequential finding: a synchronous  call inside an async socket handler. A synchronous throw inside a  chain produces an uncaught exception; in production, this was crashing the process on a predictable interval — roughly every 12 minutes. No automated test had caught it because the test environment did not exercise the crash path.

[^f16]: Research Packet E, F-16: 7 critical + 11 high issues found. Also caught: a hardcoded  array that silently dropped 4 new RBAC actions, and a Prisma migration blocked by a view dependency not handled by the migration script.

A second finding from the same review: a hardcoded  array that was correct when written but went stale when 4 new RBAC actions were added. The "Add role" button was silently hidden for all users including super-admins. The fix was a one-line change to derive the array from the live schema instead of hardcoding it. The review found it; linear reading of the diff would not have.

Model tier selection is deliberate: the audit pipeline (F-14) used Haiku explicitly for the mechanical verification stage — "does the test count match? does the diff cover the finding?" — because it is a pattern-matching problem, not a reasoning problem.[^f14]

[^f14]: Research Packet E, F-14: 123-finding audit remediated in 10 PRs across 7 domain batches; the 5-stage pipeline assigned Haiku to the mechanical verifier stage by design.

Step 4: Merge and promote

Merging the PR has one concrete gotcha, documented in memory: running  from inside the worktree being deleted causes the  step to abort. The merge must happen from the main checkout, not the worktree.[^merge-gotcha]

[^merge-gotcha]: Research Packet E (memory files, ): "run gh pr merge from main checkout, not the worktree being merged; otherwise --delete-branch aborts."

After merge to , the deploy path is: . A  worktree handles this — . Auto-CD (Cloud Build in the  regional pool) fires on that push automatically. There is a hard rule against triggering CD manually: the push already fired it, and a duplicate manual trigger fails on Artifact Registry tag-immutability.[^f26]

[^f26]: Research Packet E, F-26: the full deploy pipeline is triggered by short prompts; the rule against manual CD triggers is stored in memory and enforced by collective habit across sessions.

Verification is done by inspecting the live cluster (), the  , and the deploy marker commit — not by  without , which shows only the wrong pool and produces false negatives.[^cd-verify]

[^cd-verify]: Research Packet E (memory files, ): "never  without  — the default region shows PR smoke builds, never CD."

Step 5: What happens when something goes wrong in production

The typical prod failure pattern in the sessions studied: a column exists in code and in CI (which spins a fresh DB via ), but is missing from the production database because auto-CD runs  not , and no migration file was committed.[^f35]

[^f35]: Research Packet E, F-35: multiple memory files dedicated to prod-vs-dev divergence. F-23 documents the prod recovery pattern via .

The concrete incident: a  column was added to the schema and deployed. Production started returning 500 on every  request. Recovery:  with a one-off script piped from the local machine. The production container image does not include  or , so the pattern is streaming pure Node.js via stdin.[^f23]

[^f23]: Research Packet E, F-23: this pattern —  — was used for a Zoho tags backfill (317 → 2,957 rows), a schema hotfix, and an auth state reset.

CI spins a fresh database and applies . Production runs  against the live schema. A column that CI has always known about can be invisible to production if no migration file exists. The two gates are not equivalent. Adding a column now means: author a Prisma migration, commit it, and verify it applies cleanly against a prod-schema dump before the deploy lands.

This failure mode was documented as a named memory file () so that every subsequent session — regardless of topic — carries awareness of it.

What the cadence looks like at scale

The week-level output across 8 weeks of recorded sessions: 8–17 merged PRs per week, across two repos, covering infrastructure migrations, security remediations, feature development, and observability. Not in one giant context window — in individual sessions, each bounded, each starting with the relevant summary injected by the remember plugin.[^f32]

[^f32]: Research Packet E, F-32: weekly summaries from archive.md. Week of 2026-06-09 alone: 123-finding audit remediated in 10 PRs + 150 tests.

The  slash command was invoked exactly once across all 76 primary sessions. Sessions do not need manual compaction because the remember plugin handles continuity: a session ends, the summary is extracted and stored, the next session injects it.[^f09]

[^f09]: Research Packet E, F-09: 1  invocation found across 76 sessions totaling 64,568 lines and 169 MB.

The high output is not from working faster inside sessions — it is from not losing work between sessions, not losing work to stale worktree bases, and not losing time to review failures that could have been caught by automated passes.

The generalizable principles

Six things from this case study transfer to any project:

Invest in the standing document, not the per-prompt context. A 400-line CLAUDE.md means prompts stay under 80 words. The ratio inverts common intuition.

Structural enforcement beats reminders. The SessionStart hook that warns on worktree drift, the PreToolUse hook that blocks wrong-author commits, the  script that enforces the base — none of these depend on remembering to do the right thing. They make the wrong thing harder than the right thing.

Memory is automated, not curated. The author does not write session summaries. The remember plugin extracts them. The author curates only the named memory files — decisions with "why" and "how to apply" that need to survive across months, not just days.

Cheap models for mechanical gates. Haiku for "does this test count match?" Sonnet for "what is the right abstraction?" Using the wrong tier in either direction costs something real: speed if you over-provision, quality if you under-provision.

Multi-agent review catches what a single pass misses. The ensemble saw the JWT synchronous-throw crash. The ensemble saw the stale  array. No single reviewer had the combination of breadth and focus to catch both in one pass.

Prod-vs-dev divergence is a named failure class, not a surprise. Each incident became a named memory file. Future sessions carry awareness of it. The pattern of  for prod one-offs exists as a reference, not as improvised recovery.

Recap

A real feature ships through six concrete stages: worktree creation (always from , always via script), isolated implementation in bypass-permissions mode with a commit hook as the only guardrail, a multi-agent review pass before merge, merge from the main checkout (not the worktree), auto-CD triggered by a push to the deploy branch, and prod verification from the cluster — not from build logs in the wrong region.

The infrastructure that makes this fast — automated memory, structural enforcement, standing architecture docs — is not set up during feature work. It is set up once and then silently maintained. That is the actual leverage point.

The next chapter examines how to build and maintain the CLAUDE.md that makes goal-oriented delegation reliable at this scale.
code-review-panels:
Code review — adversarial subagent panels

An adversarial review panel dispatches multiple independent subagents over the same diff, each probing a different failure mode, then synthesises the findings before a single line of code merges. This chapter explains how panels work, why independence matters, when to use a cheap verifier versus a deep reviewer, and how the verify-before-claim discipline prevents the most common quality failure in autonomous coding: confident changes that are subtly wrong.

The problem with single-agent review

When Claude writes a feature and then reviews it, both roles share the same context. The implementation decisions — the assumptions that were made, the shortcuts taken, the edge cases that were mentally noted and then not written down — remain active in the same model state. The reviewer starts knowing the author's intent, which makes it harder to see what the code actually does versus what the author meant it to do.

This is not a model failure. It is a structural problem: a reviewer with full context is less likely to find the gaps in that context. The fix is not a better prompt — it is isolation.

Raising the effort level of a single-agent review (more reasoning tokens, longer thinking time) helps find bugs within the author's frame of reference. A panel of independent agents finds bugs outside that frame — the ones the author genuinely could not see because their context did not include them.

What an adversarial panel is

An adversarial panel is a fan-out of N named subagents over a static target — typically a diff or a set of files — where each agent is given a distinct review mandate. The mandates are adversarial by design: each agent is instructed to find a specific class of failure and to report confidently rather than hedging.

Each subagent:
- Starts with a fresh context (no knowledge of the parent session or the other reviewers)
- Receives the same diff as input but a different system prompt
- Is instructed to assume the code is wrong until it can prove otherwise
- Reports findings with concrete evidence: file path, line number, proof of impact

The parent collects all N finding sets, deduplicates, ranks by severity, and produces a consolidated review. The key insight is that no individual agent needs to be comprehensive — it needs to be deep on its mandate. Breadth comes from the ensemble.

The visualizer shows several panel shapes. The review preset is closest to what this chapter describes: multiple agents reading the same input in parallel, converging on a ranked finding list.

A concrete panel: the dynamic roles case study

In one large RBAC implementation — dynamic roles across two repos, approximately 32 commits — an 8-agent review panel was dispatched before merge. The mandates covered: security logic, database migrations, API contract stability, error handling and process safety, frontend parity, permission matrix correctness, integration test coverage, and regression detection.

The panel caught 7 critical and 11 high-severity issues before the PR merged. Two findings stand out as illustrative. (Source: packet-E, F-16)

The JWT crash: A synchronous  call was placed inside an async  chain in a socket event handler. In JavaScript, a synchronous throw inside a  callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection, not a caught error. The production process was crashing approximately every 12 minutes — every time an invalid token hit that path. The error-handling reviewer caught it. The author had not caught it in testing because test tokens were always valid.

The stale action list: A constant  was hardcoded in the permissions module. When four new RBAC actions were added as part of the same feature, nobody updated the constant. The "Add role" button was silently hidden for all users, including super-admins. The permission matrix reviewer caught it by checking that all actions in the codebase appeared in the constant — a mechanical check that no human reviewer had run.

Neither finding would have been discovered by raising the effort level of a single reviewer. Both required an agent whose job was to look for exactly that failure class, starting from scratch.

Designing the mandates

The quality of a panel comes from its mandate design. A weak mandate is: "review this diff for bugs." A strong mandate is: "assume this diff contains a race condition. Find it. If you cannot find a race condition, check for synchronous throws in async handlers, unhandled promise rejections, and state mutations that are not atomic. Report the three most likely issues with file and line evidence."

Effective mandates share four properties:

Specific failure class — not "security" but "IDOR vulnerabilities in query parameters" or "unvalidated user-controlled input reaching a database query". Specificity narrows the search space and produces denser findings.

Adversarial prior — the agent assumes the bug exists and is hunting for evidence, not auditing with an open mind. "Find the race condition" produces different attention than "check if there are any race conditions".

Evidence requirement — findings without file/line/proof are noise. Requiring "reproduce the failure with a minimal calling sequence" forces the agent to verify its claim before reporting it.

Known failure class list — give each agent a ranked checklist of what to look for if its primary mandate comes up empty. This prevents agents from returning empty-handed on clean sections and wasting their token budget on vague observations.

The verify-before-claim discipline

Panel review only works if each agent verifies its claims before reporting them. An unverified finding is a guess. It wastes the integrator's time, erodes trust in the panel, and can cause correct code to be reverted.

The verify-before-claim discipline has a simple rule: an agent may not report a finding it cannot demonstrate. Demonstration means one of:

- Showing the code path that reaches the bug (trace from an entry point to the failure site)
- Writing a minimal reproduction test and running it
- Finding a test that should exist and does not
- Quoting two code locations that contradict each other

This is stricter than it sounds. Many apparent bugs turn out to be handled correctly elsewhere — the input is validated upstream, the database query is already wrapped in a transaction, the null case is caught by a caller the agent had not read. Require evidence before reporting.

A panel that generates 30 findings and 20 of them are false positives does not help — it creates review fatigue and trains the developer to ignore reports. Mandate evidence. Accept zero findings on a clean section as a valid outcome. A reviewer that says "I audited the migration path and found no unsafe ALTER operations" is providing signal, not failing its job.

The practical implementation: in the agent's system prompt, include an explicit step before reporting. Something like: "Before adding a finding to your report, trace the code path from the entry point to the failure. If the path does not exist, do not report it. If you are not certain, say you are not certain and explain what additional evidence would confirm it."

Choosing the right model per mandate

Not all mandates require the same model. A finding that requires tracing through 15 levels of async call chains and reasoning about JavaScript's promise semantics benefits from Sonnet-class reasoning. A finding that requires mechanically checking that every action string in a constant matches a grep output does not.

The audit remediation pipeline (packet-E, F-14) was explicit about this: Haiku handled the verification stage (does the diff cover all 123 findings? are all tests present?) because that is counting and pattern-matching. Sonnet handled planning, implementation, and final fixing because those require reasoning about correctness under edge conditions.

The cost difference is significant. Assigning a Sonnet to every mandate, including mechanical ones, multiplies panel cost without proportional quality gain. Assign based on the cognitive demand of the mandate, not as a blanket policy.

Panel topology: when to fan out vs. pipeline

Two distinct shapes serve different purposes.

Fan-out (parallel panel): all agents read the same diff simultaneously, produce independent findings, and return. The parent aggregates. Use this when you want maximum coverage of a static artifact and reviewer independence is the priority. This is the right shape for pre-merge review.

Pipeline (sequential stages): one agent's output becomes the next agent's input. Each stage refines or gates the previous. Use this when you need a quality ladder — implement, then verify, then adversarially review the verify step. The audit remediation pipeline was a pipeline: planner → implementer → verifier → adversarial reviewer → fixer. Each stage was bounded because it received a compact summary from the prior stage, not its full context. (Source: packet-E, F-14)

The two shapes can be combined. Run the quality pipeline to produce a well-tested implementation. Then run a fan-out panel over the final diff before merge. The pipeline ensures correctness; the panel ensures the implementation has no blind spots the author missed.

Practical setup: running a panel as a skill

The simplest way to run a repeatable panel is to encode it as a skill. The skill receives the PR number or diff path as an argument, dispatches the subagents, and returns the consolidated report. (Source: packet-A, §8)

Invoke with  before merging PR #247. The skill handles the orchestration; you review the ranked findings.

What panels do not replace

Panels are not a substitute for typed APIs, automated test suites, or static analysis. They are an additional layer that catches what those tools miss — the semantically correct but logically wrong code, the integration assumptions that were never written down, the edge case that only appears under a specific calling sequence.

Before dispatching a panel, run , , and your test suite. Panels are expensive. Spending them on type errors that the compiler would catch is waste. The panel's job is to find what the compiler and tests missed — not to replace them.

Think of the layers as a stack:

1. Type checker — catches type errors
2. Linter — catches style and obvious correctness issues
3. Test suite — catches regressions in covered paths
4. Panel review — catches reasoning errors, integration failures, and blind spots

Each layer is cheap relative to the one above it. Run cheap gates first.

Recap

Adversarial subagent panels work because reviewer isolation breaks the shared-context problem: each agent starts fresh, sees the diff without the author's assumptions, and applies its mandate without influence from the other reviewers. Fan-out topology gives breadth; adversarial mandates give depth; the verify-before-claim discipline keeps findings credible.

Design mandates around specific failure classes, not general quality. Assign model tier by cognitive demand. Require evidence before a finding is reportable. Treat zero findings on a clean section as signal, not failure.

The next chapter covers the hook system — how to wire these review panels, verification gates, and quality checks into your session lifecycle automatically, so they run without requiring you to remember to invoke them.
git-pr-cicd:
Git, PRs & CI/CD with Claude

Claude Code can drive your entire version-control workflow — staging changes, writing commit messages, opening pull requests, and watching CI — without you losing the thread of what changed or why. This chapter shows how to structure that handoff so you stay in control of your git history while Claude handles the mechanical work.

What the chapter covers

You will learn how Claude interacts with git through the  tool, which guardrails keep commits safe, how to hook into the workflow for policy enforcement, and how to wire Claude into CI/CD pipelines so it can respond to build failures autonomously.

---

How Claude commits code

Claude has no native git tool. Every git operation — , , ,  — goes through the  tool, the same tool it uses for any shell command. That means Claude can run any git command your shell can, and the same permission rules apply. (Source: packet-A, §2)

The built-in git workflow instructions (controlled by  in ) prompt Claude to follow a sensible commit sequence:

1. Read the working tree state (, ).
2. Draft a commit message that describes intent, not mechanics.
3. Stage only relevant files — not everything, not secrets.
4. Commit, then report the SHA.

This sequence is advisory, not enforced. If you want something stronger — a specific commit-message format, a branch naming convention, an authorship check — you need a hook.

The  permission mode for CI

In interactive sessions, Claude prompts you before running  or  unless you have added them to your allow list. In CI/CD pipelines you typically want unattended operation. Set  and enumerate exactly which git and  commands are permitted:

Any Bash command not on the allow list is denied automatically — Claude cannot run it, even if it tries. This is the correct posture for unattended pipelines. (Source: packet-A, §3)

---

Enforcing commit policy with a PreToolUse hook

The most powerful integration point for git is the  hook on . It fires before every shell command executes, receives the full command string, and can block the command by exiting with code .

A practical example: enforcing commit author identity and banning AI attribution strings.

Wire this into your global settings so it applies to every project:

The  field pre-filters so the script only runs on  calls — not on every Bash command. (Source: packet-A, §5)

A hook that exits  is treated as success (Claude reads its stdout for optional JSON instructions). A hook that exits  blocks the tool call entirely and surfaces the script's stderr as the error message. Any other exit code shows stderr but does not block. Get this right or commits will slip through on script errors.

---

Writing commit messages that age well

Claude defaults to describing what changed mechanically ("add null check to user.ts"). You can push it toward intent-first messages with a standing instruction in your  or system prompt:

Claude reads  on every session start and treats it as a standing constraint. It is re-injected on every request but prompt-cached after the first, so there is no incremental token cost for this instruction across commits in the same session. (Source: packet-A, §12)

---

Opening and reviewing pull requests

Claude can open pull requests through the  CLI (GitHub's official tool). A typical sequence:

Claude will:

1. Run  to see what commits will land.
2. Run  to understand the full diff.
3. Draft a title under 70 characters and a body with a summary and test plan.
4. Run .
5. Report the PR URL.

The quality of the PR description depends directly on the quality of your commit messages. Good commits → good PR body. If your commits are mechanical, the PR body will be too.

Claude as a pre-merge reviewer

Before merging, you can ask Claude to review the diff for issues:

Claude will read the diff, check the changed files in context, and produce findings. This works best when you give it a scope: "correctness only", "security", "API contract", "test coverage". An open-ended review produces a lot of noise.

For larger PRs, the  skill (if installed) dispatches multiple review sub-agents in parallel, each covering a different quality dimension, and aggregates results. This is the pattern that catches the bugs that slip through a single-pass review — the kind that requires simultaneously holding the auth layer, the DB query, and the API contract in mind. (Source: packet-E, F-28, F-16)

---

CI/CD integration

Claude becomes especially useful when wired into a CI pipeline — not just to run commands, but to react to failures autonomously.

The basic integration pattern

In a GitHub Actions workflow this looks like:

A few things to get right here:

- * — without this, Claude will block waiting for a terminal prompt that no human will see.
-  — enumerate exactly what Claude may do. In a CI context,  should only be allowed if you want Claude to push back to the branch automatically.
-  — cap the loop so a stuck run does not consume infinite tokens. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Watching a build with Monitor

The  tool runs a command in the background and feeds each output line back to Claude as it arrives. This is the right tool when you want Claude to watch a long-running process and react to specific output patterns:

Claude issues a  call, receives lines as they stream, and can call other tools between line arrivals — or simply wait until the relevant pattern appears. This is how you wire Claude to react to deploy logs without polling. (Source: packet-A, §2)
