---

Keeping Claude out of production branches

The most important governance boundary in any git workflow is who can push to production branches. Claude should not have that permission by default.

A practical layered approach:

1. Branch protection on // — require pull requests, block direct push at the platform level.
2. Allow rules in  that permit  only to feature branch prefixes (, ).
3. A  hook that inspects the push target and blocks any push to  or .

The hook runs client-side; branch protection enforces the same rule server-side. Defense in depth: neither alone is sufficient.

---

A complete per-branch workflow

Putting it together, here is the structure that works for sustained feature development with Claude:

The shorter your prompts can be while still producing the right output, the more scalable your workflow is. A well-maintained CLAUDE.md that covers branch conventions, commit format, test requirements, and architecture constraints means you can open a session with "implement feature X" and get correct commits — because all the "how" lives in the standing document, not the prompt. (Source: packet-E, F-20, F-33)

---

Recap

- Claude runs all git operations through  — no native git tool exists, which means the same permission rules and hooks apply.
- Use  mode with an explicit allow list for CI/CD pipelines; avoid  unless the runner is fully isolated.
- A  hook on  is the right enforcement point for commit policy: author identity, message format, branch protection.
- The  tool lets Claude watch live build output and react to log events without polling.
- A well-maintained  with branch and commit conventions is worth more than a detailed per-prompt instruction — it applies to every session automatically.

Next:** Chapter "Hooks & Automation" goes deeper into the full 30-event hook system — how to build automated quality gates, session-start context injection, and multi-step pipelines that run without any human in the loop.
offload-every-stage:
Offloading every stage of dev

Software development has seven distinct phases — explore, design, plan, write tests, implement, review, and ship — and Claude can carry meaningful load in each one. This chapter shows you how to hand off each stage deliberately, which model tier and tool to reach for, and how to stitch the stages into a repeatable pipeline that lets you stay at the level of decisions rather than keystrokes.

The seven-stage map

Most guides treat Claude as a code-completion tool that happens to write longer completions. That undersells it badly. The stages before coding — exploration, design, planning — and the stages after — review and shipping — are where Claude's leverage is highest, because those are exactly the stages humans are most likely to skip or rush.

The rest of this chapter walks each stage in order. For each one: what to hand off, how to prompt it, and what to keep for yourself.

Stage 1 — Explore

Before writing a line of code you need to understand the shape of what already exists. This is the stage engineers most often skip when under time pressure, and where Claude pays back the most.

The built-in  subagent (powered by a fast, cheap model) is built exactly for this: read-only codebase search, no CLAUDE.md loading, optimized for speed. You do not invoke it directly — Claude spins it up automatically when it needs to gather facts before acting.

What you do control is the framing of your prompt. A good exploration prompt names the surface area to investigate and the question you need answered:

This produces a focused answer, not a tour of the codebase. Claude uses  (which respects ) to find callers,  to inspect them, and returns a structured summary — not a dump of every file.

Press  twice in the CLI to enter plan mode. In this mode Claude explores freely — reads, greps, traces call graphs — but cannot write or edit files. Use it to audit your assumptions before you commit to an implementation direction. When the plan looks right, exit plan mode and let Claude execute. (Source: packet-A, §3)

What to keep for yourself

Domain knowledge that is not in the codebase. Claude can read files; it cannot read the meeting where you learned the third-party API has a 60-second timeout in production. Put that in the prompt.

Stage 2 — Design

Design is the stage where you choose between approaches. It is collaborative by nature: you bring constraints, Claude brings options and trade-offs.

The prompt shape that works best is an explicit invitation to enumerate, not a directive to decide:

Claude will enumerate the options — rooms per user (already available), presence-table polling, a separate pub-sub service — with concrete trade-offs for each. Your job is to read the trade-offs, apply the constraints Claude cannot see (budget, team size, timeline), and choose.

After you choose, use a narrowing turn:

This second turn converts the selected option into a design document — prose that can feed directly into stage 3.

Using  for structured design review

The  slash command puts Claude into plan mode and switches it to the built-in  subagent — a research-first mode that reads the codebase before committing to a direction. Issue  before a complex prompt and Claude will explore, then present a plan for your approval before touching any file. This is the correct entry point for significant architectural changes. (Source: packet-A, §6)

Stage 3 — Plan

A plan is a design translated into an ordered, dependency-aware task list. It is the artifact that makes the implementation stage autonomous.

The critical property of a good plan: each task is atomic enough that completing it leaves the codebase in a valid state. A task like "add WebSocket support" is not atomic. "Add  to the express server and confirm  still returns 200" is atomic.

Ask Claude to produce the plan in a numbered list with explicit dependencies:

Spec and plan documents have a short half-life — they are useful during the implementation sprint and outdated the moment the code ships. Store them outside your git repo (a sibling directory that is not a git repository works well) so you are never tempted to commit them. The architecture doc is the long-lived record; update that instead. (Source: packet-E, F-29)

Once the plan is approved — by you, not by Claude — you have a task list you can feed back to Claude one item at a time, or dispatch in parallel to subagents when the tasks operate on disjoint files.

Stage 4 — TDD (write tests first)

With a plan in hand, the correct next step is to write the failing tests before writing any implementation. This is not optional ceremony — it is what makes the implementation stage safe to offload.

The widget above shows the Red → Green → Refactor cycle. Notice the Agent contribution bar: Red and Green are high-automation phases where a cheap model carries most of the cognitive load. Refactor is lower — structural judgement still tilts human.

For each task in your plan, the Red phase prompt is narrow:

The constraint "do not create the implementation" is load-bearing. Without it, an eager model will implement and test in one pass, skipping the red phase entirely and losing the specification benefit.

A real security audit remediation that covered 123 findings used exactly this structure per domain batch: a Sonnet-tier model wrote tests first, a cheap model ran the verification gate (test count, diff scope, no regressions), and only then did implementation proceed. The cheap model at the gate is deliberate — verification is a mechanical yes/no question that does not need deep reasoning, and running it cheaply lets you afford to gate every increment. (Source: packet-E, F-14)

Stage 5 — Implement

With red tests in place, the Green phase is the most mechanical stage of the pipeline: make the tests pass with the minimal implementation.

The phrase "do not add untested logic" prevents gold-plating. Claude tends to implement slightly more than is needed; this constraint keeps the diff reviewable.

Matching model tier to phase

Not every stage needs the most capable model. The pattern that emerges from sustained production use: (Source: packet-E, F-14)

| Phase | Tier | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Explore | Haiku (built-in Explore agent) | Read-only; speed matters |
| Design | Sonnet or higher | Trade-off analysis benefits from deeper reasoning |
| Plan | Sonnet | Dependency ordering is moderately complex |
| Red tests | Sonnet or cheap | Spec-to-test is structured; cheap is fine for simple specs |
| Green implementation | Sonnet or cheap | Mechanical for well-defined tests |
| Verification gate | Haiku | Yes/no gate; cheapest correct option |
| Refactor | Sonnet or higher | Structural judgement; worth the extra capacity |
| Review | Sonnet (multiple agents) | Parallel; each agent focused on one dimension |

Running a capable model at every stage is like paying a senior engineer to count lines of code. Match the model to the difficulty of the reasoning required at that stage.

Keeping context clean across stages

Each implementation task should run in its own worktree. Claude Code stores session history per working directory, so a worktree at  has its own session — its intermediate tool outputs, file reads, and failed attempts do not accumulate in your main project session. When the task is done, the worktree's history stays there; your main session receives a one-paragraph summary. (Source: packet-E, F-10; packet-A, §7)

The right mental model: the worktree is the implementation agent's sandbox. The main checkout is where you review and integrate.

Stage 6 — Review

The review stage is where parallelism pays its highest dividend. A single linear code review misses things — not because reviewers are careless, but because different quality dimensions require different attention modes. Security thinking and readability thinking do not co-exist well in a single pass.

The pattern that works: dispatch multiple subagents in parallel, each with a different review focus and a disjoint concern.

After all four return, a final Sonnet-tier agent triages the findings by severity and identifies any overlaps or contradictions.

An 8-agent review pass on a large RBAC feature caught 7 critical and 11 high-severity issues before merge — including a synchronous JWT verification call inside an async socket handler that caused process crashes in production, and a hardcoded action list that silently dropped four new RBAC actions from the UI. Neither finding was caught by the automated test suite, because both were architectural issues that only a targeted human-mode review would surface. (Source: packet-E, F-16)

Keep the review and fix stages separate. A review agent that also applies fixes conflates two different reasoning tasks and produces worse output at both. Let the review agents produce findings, then start a new implementation pass to address them — one finding at a time, back through the TDD cycle if the fix is non-trivial.

The verification gate between review and merge

Before merging, run a cheap agent as a final gate:

Exit code 2 from a hook blocks the merge. The same semantics apply to a cheap agent checking the result: yes/no questions, mechanical verification, exit code for pass/fail. (Source: packet-A, §5)

Stage 7 — Ship

Shipping is a sequence: open PR, run CI, merge, watch the deploy, verify the live environment. All of it is delegatable as a goal:

The key word is goal. The prompt does not list steps — it names the end state. Claude infers the steps from the CLAUDE.md, which should document your deploy workflow, your CI commands, and how to verify a successful deploy. (Source: packet-E, F-33)

Invest in the CLAUDE.md and you write shorter prompts forever. A 400-line CLAUDE.md means a 20-word "ship it" prompt contains everything Claude needs to act correctly. That ratio — long standing document, short per-session prompt — is the pattern that makes autonomous shipping safe. (Source: packet-E, F-20)

When a stage takes multiple sessions — or when you hand off to a fresh context — the memory system is what prevents you from re-explaining work already done. The remember pattern (automated PostToolUse extraction into dated logs) means "continue from where you left off" is a complete instruction. The session picks up from the last extracted summary, not from your recollection of what happened three sessions ago. (Source: packet-E, F-06, F-21)

Putting it together — a single-feature pipeline

Here is how the seven stages look end to end for a realistic feature (adding per-user push notifications to a CRM):

Total human time: specification (stages 1–3), approval at each gate, and review of findings. Automated time: everything in between.

What you never hand off

Three things stay yours regardless of how capable the pipeline becomes:

Acceptance criteria. Claude can translate a spec into tests. It cannot author the spec. The specification of what "done" means — in observable, testable terms — is the engineer's irreducible contribution.

Trade-off calls under hidden constraints. Design trade-offs that depend on information not in the codebase — political constraints, budget decisions, future roadmap commitments — cannot be delegated to a model. Name those constraints explicitly in the design prompt, or the design will optimize for the wrong objective.

Final merge authorization. The review stage catches a lot. It does not catch everything. A human reads the final diff and signs off. That signature is not ceremony; it is accountability.

Recap

Every development stage — explore, design, plan, TDD, implement, review, ship — admits meaningful delegation. The leverage is highest at the stages engineers most often skip: exploration before coding, review before merging, verification before shipping. Match model tier to reasoning difficulty: cheap models for mechanical gates, capable models for trade-off analysis and structural refactoring. Keep context clean with worktrees and session memory. Invest in a long, accurate CLAUDE.md and your per-prompt complexity drops to near zero.

The next chapter covers dynamic workflows — JavaScript scripts that move orchestration logic entirely out of Claude's context window, enabling coordination at a scale where even the thin parent context described here would become unwieldy.
api-agent-sdk:
The Claude API & Agent SDK

This chapter explains how to call the Claude API directly and how to embed the full Claude Code agent loop inside your own applications using the Agent SDK. By the end you will understand the message-loop mechanics, the SDK's entry points in TypeScript and Python, and the practical decisions — tool sets, permission modes, hook callbacks, cost guards — that determine whether an embedded agent behaves reliably in production.

Why the API alone is not enough

The raw Claude API (Anthropic's Messages endpoint) is a single-turn request-response interface. You send a list of messages; the model returns one response. That is sufficient for many tasks: summarization, classification, simple Q&A. It is not sufficient for coding agents, file-editing workflows, or anything that requires the model to call tools, read the results, and then continue reasoning.

The Agent SDK solves this by embedding the same loop that Claude Code runs internally — the multi-turn cycle of model call → tool dispatch → result injection → repeat — in a library you can import directly. You get every built-in tool (Read, Edit, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch, and more), session management, cost tracking, hook callbacks, and MCP server support, without shelling out to the  binary.

The Anthropic Messages API (at ) is a stateless HTTP endpoint. The Agent SDK ( for TypeScript,  for Python) is a library that wraps that endpoint in a stateful agent loop. They are related but distinct. This chapter is about the SDK. If you need the raw HTTP surface — for streaming, tool definitions, or non-agent use cases — the  skill covers that in full.

The agent loop — what actually runs

Understanding what the SDK does under the hood is the foundation for using it well. The loop is a turn-based cycle:

The only runtime state is an append-only message array. Each complete cycle — model response plus tool execution — is one turn. The loop terminates when Claude produces a response with no tool call requests. At that point the SDK emits a  with subtypes: , , , , or . (Source: packet-A, §1)

One important parallelism rule: read-only tools (, , , and read-only MCP tools) can run concurrently within a single turn. State-modifying tools (, , ) run sequentially. Custom tools default to sequential unless you annotate them with . The SDK manages this automatically. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Installing and calling the SDK

The primary entry point is  — an async iterator in TypeScript, an async generator in Python.

 counts only tool-use turns, not the final text-only turn. Without either limit the loop runs indefinitely — hazardous for open-ended prompts. Set both whenever you embed an agent in a server or CI pipeline. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Loading project context

By default the SDK runs with no project context — no CLAUDE.md, no settings, no hooks. Pass  to load  (including hooks, allowed tools, and any CLAUDE.md files) from the current directory:

This is the difference between an agent that knows your project conventions and one that works blind. For most real projects, this option is non-negotiable.

Permission modes

The SDK exposes six permission modes. The right choice depends on your trust context:

| Mode | Behaviour | When to use |
|---|---|---|
|  | Prompts for every potentially dangerous operation | Interactive prototyping |
|  | Auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands | Semi-automated workflows |
|  | Read-only; file edits always prompt | Exploration and planning passes |
|  | Never prompts; everything not in allow list is denied | CI/CD pipelines |
|  | Model classifier approves or denies each call | TypeScript SDK; balanced autonomy |
|  | Skips all permission checks | Isolated containers only; never run as root |

In CI,  with a narrow  allowlist is the right combination: the agent cannot do anything outside the list, and there are no prompts to interrupt the run. (Source: packet-A, §3)

If you run an agent with  in a long-lived process with network access, a malicious prompt could instruct it to exfiltrate files or make arbitrary HTTP calls. Use this mode only inside disposable, isolated environments — Docker containers with no external access, ephemeral CI runners, or sandboxed VMs. The SDK enforces one hard constraint: it refuses to run in bypass mode as root on Unix.

Hook callbacks — in-process guardrails

Hooks in the SDK are callback functions, not shell scripts. They run in your application process with no token cost, and they can read or modify what the agent is about to do before it does it.

The most important hook for production use is . It fires before every tool call and can block the call by returning a deny decision:

 lets you observe or modify what the agent sees after a tool runs — useful for scrubbing sensitive output before it enters the model's context window:

The complete event taxonomy from the SDK covers 30 named hook events spanning session lifecycle, prompt handling, tool execution, subagent coordination, file changes, and notifications. The key events for production hardening are  (block dangerous calls),  (scrub output),  (inject follow-up context), and  (gate sub-agent results). (Source: packet-A, §5)

Spawning sub-agents from within the SDK

The  tool is available in SDK sessions just as it is in interactive sessions. Claude can spawn named sub-agents — isolated agent contexts with their own tool sets, models, and system prompts — and collect their results:

Sub-agents added in version 2.1.172 can themselves spawn sub-agents, up to five levels deep. Each level is an isolated context — only the final summary returns to the parent, not intermediate tool outputs. This isolation is what makes hierarchical delegation safe: a sub-agent's exploratory file reads do not fill the parent's context window. (Source: packet-B, §4)

In a multi-agent pipeline, assign a cheaper, faster model to mechanical sub-agents — verification gates, file linting, test running — and reserve the more capable model for planning and synthesis. The  field in sub-agent frontmatter () controls this per agent type. The cost difference compounds across hundreds of sub-agent invocations. (Source: packet-E, F-14)

Cost and session management

Two fields on every  call prevent runaway spend:

-  — caps the number of tool-use rounds. A tight codebase task rarely needs more than 20.

The  in each  lets you resume a session in a later call — the model picks up with the full context intact. This is how you implement multi-turn agents that persist across HTTP requests or process restarts:

Sessions accumulate tokens rapidly with file-heavy tasks — a large  call can cost thousands of tokens. Context compaction ( in settings) summarises older history automatically when the window fills. The SDK emits a   when compaction occurs; you can hook  and  to log or inspect the boundary. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Connecting MCP servers

MCP servers extend the agent's tool surface beyond the built-in set. Pass them directly in the  option:

A minimal production pattern

Pulling the pieces together, here is a self-contained pattern that is safe to deploy in a server context:

Effort and thinking depth

The  option () controls how many thinking tokens the model uses per turn. Higher effort produces better results on complex reasoning tasks at higher cost. For mechanical tasks — running lint, collecting file paths, executing tests —  is usually sufficient. For planning, architecture review, or code synthesis,  or  is worth the cost. (Source: packet-A, §1)

Recap

The Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's multi-turn loop in your application. The loop runs until Claude produces a response with no tool calls; each turn dispatches tools in parallel (read-only) or sequentially (write), injects results, and feeds back to the model.  is the entry point;  and  are the safety guards you should always set.  loads your CLAUDE.md and settings so the agent knows your codebase conventions. browser-ide-extensions:
Browser & IDE extensions

Claude Code lives in your terminal, but some workflows are better served by meeting Claude where work already happens — in a browser tab or inside your editor. This chapter maps the two extension surfaces (Claude in Chrome and the IDE integrations), explains what each one can and cannot do, and gives you the decision heuristic for choosing which surface fits a given task.

The surface landscape

Before going deep on either extension, it helps to see how the surfaces relate to the CLI and to each other.

All three surfaces call the same underlying Claude models. What differs is the context each surface can see and the actions it can take. The CLI has the widest action surface (every built-in tool). Extensions have narrower, domain-specific action sets but zero setup friction for their target environment.

If you need to reach a tool that is not available in an extension — running a shell command, spawning a subagent, or calling an MCP server — the CLI is the right surface. Extensions are optimised for their lane, not as replacements for the full agent loop.

Claude in Chrome

The Claude in Chrome extension puts Claude inside your existing browser session. It can see, read, and interact with pages you have open without needing to open a new browser instance or configure a separate Playwright server.

What it can do

The extension exposes a set of tools that the model can call within a conversation:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
|  | Open a URL in a new tab or the current tab |
|  | Return the parsed content of the active page |
|  | Extract the plain text of a page |
|  | Locate elements by selector, text, or ARIA role |
|  | Fill form fields |
|  | Click, type, scroll — direct mouse/keyboard control |
|  | Execute JavaScript in the active page context |
|  | Pull the browser console log |
|  | Inspect network requests made by the page |
|  | Upload files into an open file input |
|  | Record a GIF of browser actions for documentation |

The key distinction from a headless Playwright setup is that the extension operates in your existing authenticated session. You do not need to log in again, handle OAuth flows programmatically, or set up cookies. If you are already signed into your staging environment, the extension inherits that session.

When it shines

Manual QA and bug reproduction. Describe a user journey in plain language; the extension navigates, fills forms, reads the result, and reports back. Because it reads the console log and network requests, it can report a failing API call or a JavaScript error that a human reviewer might miss.

Scraping pages behind a login. You are authenticated, so the extension can read content that a headless browser would need credentials to reach.

Documenting UI flows. The  tool records a sequence of browser interactions as an animated GIF — useful for issue reports, onboarding guides, or PR descriptions.

Debugging frontend issues interactively. Point Claude at a page that is behaving strangely, ask it to read the console, check the network requests for the relevant call, and inspect the DOM — all without leaving the conversation.

Limitations to keep in mind

The extension can only interact with tabs in the browser it is connected to. It cannot reach your filesystem, run shell commands, or call MCP servers that are configured in your CLI session. Cross-origin iframe content is subject to standard browser security restrictions — the extension cannot read inside a third-party iframe any more than your own JavaScript can.

The extension requires site-level permissions to be configured before it can execute tool calls on a given domain. Grant these in the extension's settings for each origin you want Claude to automate. This is a one-time step per site, not per conversation.

A representative workflow

You are tracking down a bug where the checkout page shows the wrong item count after applying a coupon code. Here is what a Claude-in-Chrome session looks like:

1. Navigate to the checkout page with items in the cart.
2. Apply a coupon code using  and  (click submit).
3. Read the page with  to check the displayed count.
4. Read the console with  to see if any errors fired.
5. Read the network request to  with  to see the server response.
6. Report: the server returned the correct count; the rendering component read from stale local state.

This whole sequence runs in one conversation. The finding is specific and reproducible.

IDE extensions

The IDE extensions (VS Code and JetBrains family) bring Claude into the editor itself. The integration is tighter than a browser extension because your editor already knows your project — it has the file tree, the language server, the open buffers, and the diff.

What the VS Code extension adds

The VS Code integration (available via the Claude Code extension in the marketplace) adds three things to a standard Claude Code session:

Side Panel. A persistent panel in the editor UI where you can converse with Claude without leaving VS Code. The panel has full access to the same agent loop as the CLI — it is not a stripped-down chat widget.

Inline completions. As you type, Claude can offer completions that are aware of the file you are editing, the surrounding code, and the project conventions in your . These are opt-in and respect the same permission model as the rest of the tool.

Editor context forwarding. When you open a conversation from inside VS Code, the extension automatically includes the currently open file, the selection, and any diagnostics (type errors, linter warnings) from the language server. You do not have to paste code into the chat; the editor hands it over.

The LSP advantage

Claude Code's  tool connects to language servers for code intelligence — jump to definition, find references, type error enumeration, call hierarchies. The official LSP plugins in the marketplace (one per language) require the language server binary to be installed separately, but once set up, the  tool runs automatically after each file edit and reports type errors back to Claude without a separate build step.[^lsp-source]

This is the most significant capability gap between using Claude Code in a raw terminal versus using it inside a project with a configured language server. In a terminal session, Claude must run  or  as a Bash call. With , the language server feed is live: edit, get errors, fix, repeat — without explicit build commands.

[^lsp-source]: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md — last verified 2026-06-21.

JetBrains

The JetBrains plugin (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, and the rest of the family) follows the same pattern: Side Panel for conversation, editor context forwarding for the active file and selection, and access to the full agent loop. JetBrains IDEs have their own language intelligence layer that is independent of the LSP plugin system, so the  tool integration works differently — check the plugin's own documentation for current support.

Choosing between the terminal and an IDE extension

Neither surface is strictly better. The choice depends on what you are doing in a given session.

| Situation | Preferred surface |
|---|---|
| Large multi-file refactor with type feedback | IDE extension (LSP active, inline context) |
| Running a workflow or spawning subagents | CLI (full tool surface, no IDE overhead) |
| Debugging a web page, scraping, or QA | Claude in Chrome |
| Writing a hook or customising settings | CLI or IDE — either works |
| Quick single-file edit while already in the editor | IDE extension |
| Headless / CI / scripted automation | CLI or Agent SDK |

The IDE extension reduces friction for editor-native work. The CLI gives you everything. The browser extension covers what neither of the others can reach.

The full tool surface (interactive reference)

The widget below lets you explore all built-in Claude Code tools, filterable by surface area and permission requirements. Use it to confirm which tools are available before planning a workflow on a particular surface.

When you move to a browser or IDE extension, you are working with a subset of this surface. The extension's own tools (browser actions, editor context) supplement it, but the 38 CLI tools do not all transfer — only the ones the extension exposes through its own host adapter.

Picking your surface

Three questions narrow the choice quickly:

1. Where does the data live? In a browser tab (use Chrome extension), in the filesystem or a shell (use CLI), in editor buffers with type feedback (use IDE extension).
2. Do you need shell access or MCP tools? If yes, the CLI is the only path.
3. Are you authenticated somewhere in the browser? If the target is behind a login you already have, the Chrome extension saves the credential-handling work.

In practice most power users run the CLI as their primary surface and reach for an extension when the task naturally lives in that environment. The extensions are not alternatives to the CLI; they are accelerators for the domain they occupy.

Recap and next

Browser and IDE extensions extend Claude's reach into environments where the CLI is not the natural tool. Claude in Chrome automates authenticated browser sessions, reads the DOM and network, and can document UI flows as GIFs. IDE extensions thread Claude into your editor's language intelligence, reduce context-copying friction, and make the  tool's live type feedback practical. The CLI remains the surface with the widest tool coverage and the one you reach for when orchestration, hooks, or MCP servers are in play.

Next up: plugins and the marketplace — how Anthropic's plugin system bundles skills, agents, MCP servers, and hooks into installable units, and how to evaluate what is worth installing.
headless-cli:
Headless / CLI automation

Most Claude Code chapters assume you are sitting at a terminal, watching the agent think. This one does not. You will learn how to drive Claude Code non-interactively — from shell scripts, CI pipelines, and programmatic wrappers — so that the same agent loop that works in your editor can also run unattended in a GitHub Actions job, a nightly cron task, or a custom build tool.

Why headless matters

The interactive Claude Code experience is powerful, but it is also synchronous: you wait, it thinks, you approve, it acts. Headless mode breaks that dependency. When Claude runs without a terminal, it can:

- Generate and apply code changes as part of a CI pipeline that no human needs to babysit
- Run automated review, linting, or migration passes on every pull request
- Be invoked from shell scripts as a composable step — the way you would call  or 
- Drive a custom application through the Agent SDK, where your code controls the loop entirely

The two main paths are the  flag on the CLI (for quick scripting) and the Agent SDK (for deeper integration). Both expose the same agent loop; they just differ in how you talk to it.

The  flag: one-shot non-interactive mode

Passing  (or ) to  puts it into print mode — it takes a prompt, runs the agent loop, prints the final output to stdout, and exits. No TTY required.

The flag works in any script context where you would normally call a subprocess. Exit code  means success; non-zero means the agent loop errored.

Controlling what is allowed

In non-interactive mode, Claude cannot ask you for permission mid-run. You have two options:

The CLI refuses to run this as root on Unix, which is the right default. Use it only inside isolated containers or disposable VMs — never on a workstation or a shared runner with real credentials.

With , Claude will delete files, overwrite configs, and run arbitrary shell commands without asking. Scope it tightly: run in a container that mounts only the files it should touch, and revoke credentials it does not need.

Capping cost and turns

Headless jobs can run indefinitely if you give them an open-ended prompt. Two guardrails help:

-  — stop after N tool-use round trips. Without this, a confused agent can loop until it hits an API error or drains a budget.
-  — override the model for one invocation from the environment, useful for using a cheaper model on routine tasks.

When  fires, the SDK emits a  with subtype  and the CLI exits with a non-zero code — which your script can detect.

You can pipe content into  by combining it with shell here-strings or process substitution:

Claude Code reads stdin when it is not a TTY and combines it with the  prompt. This lets you build pipelines that feed dynamic context without constructing large command-line strings.

The permission mode you choose determines whether the job can be interrupted by a prompt. For CI you almost always want :

Using the Agent SDK

For anything more complex than a single prompt — multi-turn sessions, structured output, custom tool handling, programmatic result parsing — the Agent SDK is the right tool. It embeds the full agent loop in your application without requiring the CLI to be installed.

Lockfile and dependency hygiene

If your workflow also calls  inside Bash tool calls, make sure both lockfiles are committed. An  that cannot find a package will fail before the agent loop even starts — not Claude's fault, but easy to miss in a headless context where there is no human to read the error.

Environment variables worth knowing

Using the  flag

Session continuity and the  flag

Debugging headless runs

When a headless job silently produces wrong output, the usual culprits are:

1. A tool that needed permission was silently denied — check that  covers every tool the prompt requires. Add  temporarily to confirm this is the issue, then tighten.

Recap

Running Claude Code headlessly comes down to three choices: the  flag for shell scripting, the Agent SDK for programmatic integration, and  plus permission mode to control what the agent can touch. mcp-use-build:
MCP — using servers & building your own

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets Claude reach beyond its built-in tools and talk to any external system — databases, APIs, design tools, CI platforms — through a common interface. By the end of this chapter you will know how to connect an existing MCP server to Claude Code, how to build a minimal server of your own, and how to think about what belongs in a server versus what belongs in a hook or skill.

---

What MCP is and why it exists

Claude's built-in tools (, , , and so on) are a closed set. If you want Claude to query your Postgres database, pull a Jira ticket, or post a Slack message, there is no built-in tool for that. MCP is the answer.

An MCP server is a small process — local or remote — that exposes tools, resources, and prompts over a standardized JSON-RPC protocol. Claude Code discovers those tools at session start and treats them as first-class peers of its built-in tool set. From Claude's perspective, calling  is identical to calling .

MCP was donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025 and has since been adopted by ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot — making it the closest thing the industry has to a neutral integration layer for AI agents. (Source: packet-B, §2.1)

Claude Code does not load every MCP tool's schema at session start. Instead it uses the  tool to fetch schemas on demand. This keeps the context window from filling with hundreds of rarely-used tool definitions. On Vertex AI or non-first-party base URLs, deferred loading is disabled and all schemas load upfront. (Source: packet-A, §14)

---

The MCP ecosystem today

The number of available MCP servers has grown rapidly since the protocol launched. Multiple registries track the public supply:

The widget above lets you filter by type and use case. Toggle "New / featured only" to see what has shipped recently. The official MCP reference servers (maintained by Anthropic at ) number seven: fetch, filesystem, git, memory, time, sequential-thinking, and everything (a test harness). Many vendor-maintained servers — GitHub, Supabase, Linear, Figma, Stripe, Cloudflare — now ship as first-party integrations. (Source: packet-B, §2.3–2.4)

---

Connecting an MCP server in Claude Code

There are two ways to wire a server into Claude Code: a project-level  file (checked in, shared with your team) or an entry in  (user or managed scope). For most team scenarios,  is the right choice.

Using

When Claude Code opens in this directory it will offer to connect these servers. Approve once; future sessions auto-connect without prompting if  is set in your . (Source: packet-A, §14)

Environment variable references like  are expanded from the session environment — put secrets in your shell profile or CI secrets, never in the JSON file itself.

Using an official plugin

Many of the most popular MCP servers ship as Claude Code plugins, which bundle the server configuration alongside skills and hooks. Installing from the official marketplace is a single command:

Plugins handle the  wiring automatically and add a scoped namespace (e.g. ) that you can reference in permission rules. (Source: packet-B, §1.3)

Approving MCP tools via permission rules

MCP tools surface in permission rules and hook matchers as . To auto-approve all tools from a specific server without approving every individual tool:

The pattern  (contains  and ) is treated as a JavaScript regex and matches every tool from the memory server. The pattern  (letters and underscores only) is an exact string match. (Source: packet-A, §5 — hook matcher pattern rules apply identically in permission rules)

---

Verifying a connected server

Run  to list all connected MCP servers, their status, and their exposed tools. A healthy output looks like:

If a server shows as disconnected, check:
1. The binary/package specified in  is installed and on .
2. Environment variables referenced in  are set in the current shell.
3. The server process did not crash — run the command manually in a terminal to see its startup output.

---

Building a minimal MCP server

Building a server is more approachable than it looks. The official TypeScript SDK () handles the protocol layer; you write the tools. A working server is under 60 lines. (Source: packet-B, §6.1 — )

A worked example: a project-status server

Imagine you want Claude to check the status of your deploys from within a session — without exposing full shell access. A purpose-built MCP server with a single tool is cleaner than a broad  permission.

Wire it into your project's :

Now Claude can call  or  without needing shell access to  or  from a permissive  rule.

What a tool definition must provide

Every tool needs three things:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Name | Identifier used in tool calls (, no spaces) |
| Description | What Claude reads to decide when to call this tool — be specific |
| Input schema | Zod schema (TypeScript) or JSON Schema — all inputs validated before your handler runs |

The description is the most important field for usability. Claude decides whether to call a tool based on it. "Returns the currently running image SHA for a given service" is concrete and unambiguous. "Gets deploy info" is not.

Transport choices

MCP supports two transport mechanisms:

Stdio (as above) — the server process starts as a child of Claude Code, communicating over stdin/stdout. Simplest for local tools; zero networking, zero auth.

HTTP with SSE — the server runs as a persistent process (or remote service) and Claude connects over HTTP. Required for shared or remote servers; supports OAuth 2.0 for authentication. This is how hosted integrations like Supabase and Linear operate.

For local tooling, stdio is almost always the right starting point.

---

Exposing resources and prompts

Tools are the most common MCP primitive, but the protocol also supports resources and prompts.

Resources are read-only data sources with stable URIs — think of them as files or API endpoints that Claude can browse and read without invoking a tool. The  and  built-in tools handle resource access on Claude's end. Resources are useful for exposing documentation, configuration files, or reference data that does not need a round-trip interaction.

Prompts are server-defined prompt templates that users can invoke as slash commands. They appear in Claude Code as . Prompts are the right choice for canned workflows — "generate a migration plan", "summarize the last week of issues" — where the server can inject live data into a structured prompt before Claude sees it.

---

MCP transport flow

---

When to build an MCP server vs using Bash

MCP servers add process-management overhead and require maintenance. They are the right tool when:

- You want to expose a well-typed interface rather than raw shell access —  is safer than .
- The logic needs to be shared across projects or teammates — a checked-in  means everyone on the team gets the same tools without configuring anything.
- You are exposing a remote or shared service — HTTP+SSE transport lets a single server instance serve multiple Claude sessions.
- The integration requires authentication that should not be typed into prompts — the server handles auth internally; Claude never sees credentials.

Stick with  when the operation is one-off, project-specific, and the shell command is already constrained by your permission rules. A  allow rule is often sufficient for solo use.

Before writing a server, check whether an official plugin already covers your integration.  gives you a complete, maintained GitHub MCP server in seconds. Build your own only when the integration does not exist or needs custom logic that a generic server cannot provide. (Source: packet-B, §1.3)

---

Enterprise authorization

For team deployments, MCP servers that require OAuth (Supabase, Linear, Atlassian, Figma, and others) previously meant every developer had to complete an OAuth consent flow individually. Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA), which reached stable status in June 2026, replaces this with zero-touch IdP-delegated auth. Admins configure the connection once via their identity provider (Okta is the first supported IdP); team members get access automatically when Claude Code is launched. (Source: packet-B, §2.5)

EMA applies to Team and Enterprise plans. Configuration in Claude also applies to Claude Code automatically.

---

Recap

- MCP is the open protocol that lets Claude call external systems through typed tools, resources, and prompts. It is platform-neutral and now governed by the Linux Foundation.
- Connect servers via  (project-shared) or  (user/managed). Official plugins bundle the wiring for the most popular integrations.
- MCP tools appear in permission rules and hook matchers as . Regex patterns let you approve an entire server in one rule.
- Building a server requires only the official SDK and a tool definition — name, description, Zod schema, and handler. Stdio transport is the simplest starting point.
- Choose MCP over  when you need typed safety, team sharing, remote deployment, or credential isolation. For quick local operations, a scoped  allow rule is often enough.

Next: Chapter "Hooks deep dive" examines the full 30-event lifecycle — , , , , and the less obvious events — with concrete patterns for automated quality gates, session-start context injection, and policy enforcement that runs without human review.
plugins-marketplaces:
Plugins & marketplaces

Claude Code ships with a plugin system, two official marketplaces, and access to a sprawling MCP ecosystem. This chapter shows you how to install and evaluate plugins, navigate the marketplaces, and wire in MCP servers — so you can expand Claude's default surface without accumulating dead weight in every session.

---

The plugin model: what a plugin actually is

A plugin is a versioned directory (or  archive) with a manifest at . Inside that directory you can bundle any combination of:

- Skills — slash commands backed by markdown instruction files
- Agents — custom sub-agents with their own tool restrictions and model selection
- Hooks — lifecycle scripts (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, etc.)
- MCP server configs — pre-configured  wired up and ready
- LSP server configs — language-server integrations
- Background monitors — shell commands whose stdout lines are delivered to Claude as notifications
- Binaries — a  directory added to your PATH for the session

The manifest  field becomes the namespace for every skill in the plugin. A skill called  in a plugin named  is invoked as . This scoping prevents collisions when you have dozens of plugins installed. (Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins)

Installation scopes

Plugins can be installed at three scopes:

| Scope | Where it's written | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
|  |  | You, in every project |
|  |  | Everyone who checks out the repo |
|  | Per-user per-repo override | You, in this repo only |

The  scope is the right choice when you want your whole team to get the same  or  behaviour. The  scope is right for personal preferences — , your preferred LSP, or security tooling you always want active.

As of v2.1.143, the in-app Discover tab shows a Context cost estimate (tokens per turn) for each plugin. A "Will install" component preview landed in v2.1.145. A plugin that adds three MCP servers plus two monitors may balloon your context even when you're not actively using its skills. Read the preview, then decide.
(Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/discover-plugins)

---

The two official marketplaces

skills-use-write:
Skills — using & writing

Skills are Claude Code's mechanism for packaging repeatable expertise into a single slash command. This chapter shows you how to find skills worth installing, how to invoke them effectively, and — crucially — how to author your own so that team conventions, project launch recipes, and personal workflows survive from session to session without you re-explaining them.

What makes a skill different from CLAUDE.md

Before diving into usage, it is worth being precise about how skills relate to the project instructions file most Claude Code users already know.

 is eagerly loaded — its full content lands in every request, whether or not it is relevant. That is fine for standing rules ("always use , never commit "), but it is wasteful for step-by-step procedures that you only need occasionally.

A skill is lazily loaded. Its  body is invisible to Claude until the skill is invoked. This keeps your base context small and your per-request cost low. Skills are also namespace-isolated: two skills with the same name in different scopes do not collide — the closest wins.

Claude Code's skill format is based on the agentskills.io open standard, which means skills you write for Claude Code can (in principle) be understood by other tools that adopt the same specification. Claude Code adds its own extensions — dynamic context injection, subagent execution, tool restrictions — on top of the base format.

The mental model:

| Mechanism | Loaded | Best for |
|---|---|---|
|  | Every request | Standing rules, project conventions, must-knows |
| Skill | On invocation only | Procedures, recipes, step-by-step workflows |
| Custom output style | Session start only | Communication register (terse, educational, etc.) |
| Hook | On lifecycle events | Enforcement, side effects, context injection |

Finding skills to use

Bundled skills (always available)

Claude Code ships a set of bundled skills that are pre-installed and require no setup:

-  — structured diff analysis at configurable depth
-  — systematic fault isolation
-  — infers how to launch your project from , , or 
-  — runs the app and observes real behaviour to confirm a fix
-  — fans out a task across many files in parallel
-  — multi-source web research with adversarial cross-checking
-  — repeats a prompt or skill on an interval

These cover the most common repeatable tasks out of the box. Start here before looking elsewhere.

If your project has a , it shadows the bundled . This is intentional — project-specific launch recipes are more accurate than the generic inference logic.

The plugin marketplace

Most skills worth installing arrive via plugins. A plugin is a versioned bundle that can contain skills, agents, hooks, and MCP server configs in a single installable unit.

Anthropic maintains two marketplaces:

- Official (): curated by Anthropic, auto-registered on first interactive launch. Browse at  or inside Claude Code at .
- Community (): third-party, review-gated submissions. Add it with .

|  |  — 7-phase guided feature workflow |

|  |  — audits and improves your CLAUDE.md |

Hand-rolled skills in your project

Check  in any repository you join. Teams that work with Claude Code tend to accumulate skills over time — deployment recipes, migration runners, release checklists. Read those files before creating duplicates.

How invocation works

Invoke a skill with a slash command:

Writing your own skills

When to write a skill

A skill earns its keep when you find yourself typing the same multi-step instructions more than once. Good candidates:

- Project launch sequences ()
- Release checklists (merge, tag, update changelog, notify)
- Code review checklists that your team actually enforces
- Deployment runbooks with conditional steps

The anatomy of a skill file

A skill is a folder containing a single  file:

The  list restricts which tools Claude may use while running this skill. Keeping it tight reduces the blast radius of a misbehaving step.

automate-daily-tasks:
Automating daily repetitive tasks

You spend some fraction of every workday on tasks that feel like work but are not really thinking: collecting the same information from the same places, reformatting it, and sending it somewhere else. This chapter gives you a practical mindset for spotting that friction, and a concrete toolkit — Claude, n8n, and Zapier MCP — for making it disappear. By the end you will have automated at least one real task and a framework for finding the next ten.

The first skill: noticing what is actually repetitive

Most people miss obvious automation targets because repetitive tasks spread across a workday rather than arriving in a block. The signal is not volume — it is the absence of decision.

Ask yourself: When I do this task, am I making a judgment call, or am I just moving information?

Moving information — copy a Slack message into a Google Sheet, pull yesterday's numbers into a report, send the same briefing email every Monday — is almost always automatable. Making a judgment call — deciding which leads are worth pursuing, drafting a nuanced response to a customer complaint — generally requires you.

A practical way to surface candidates is to keep a "friction log" for one week. Every time you do something that makes you think "I've done this exact thing before," write it down. After a week, look for clusters: the same app pair appearing more than twice, the same time of day, the same trigger event. Those clusters are your automation backlog.

The popular advice says: if a task takes less than two minutes, just do it. For automation, that advice is backwards. A 90-second task done 20 times a day is 30 minutes of context-switching, and context-switching is expensive. The right filter is: does this task recur? If yes, it is worth a look regardless of how short it is.

A mental model: Event → Condition → Action

Every repeatable task you automate has the same underlying shape. Something happens (an event), you check whether something is true (a condition), and then you do something (an action). The academic name for this is Event-Condition-Action (ECA) architecture, and it maps directly to how every automation platform is built.[^eca]

[^eca]: The ECA pattern as a formal model for personal automation is documented in: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.00583

Event: something that happens in the world — a new email arrives, a calendar event starts in 30 minutes, a form is submitted, a new row appears in a spreadsheet, a webhook fires.

Condition: an optional filter that gates the action — "only if the email is from a domain I care about," "only if the priority column says High," "only if it is a weekday."

Action: what you want done — send a message, create a calendar event, append to a sheet, call an API, post to Slack.

Once you frame a task this way, picking the right automation tool becomes straightforward.

Choosing the right tool

The three tools you will reach for most often occupy distinct niches. They are complementary, not competing.

| Tool | Best fit | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| Claude (direct) | One-off tasks, ad-hoc information work, tasks where the output needs judgment | Time in your conversation |
| Zapier / Zapier MCP | Connecting apps you already use, no-code, broad coverage (9,000+ apps) | Tasks from your Zapier plan quota |
| n8n | High-volume schedules, multi-step logic, AI-native workflows, full control | Self-hosted: infrastructure only (~$3–10/mo); Cloud: from €24/mo per run quota[^n8n-pricing] |

[^n8n-pricing]: n8n Cloud pricing as of 2026-06-21: https://n8n.io/pricing/ — Cloud Starter €24/month for 2,500 executions; self-hosted Community Edition is free with unlimited executions.

The decision tree above helps you pick the right mechanism. When in doubt, start with the simplest option that covers your use case and graduate to a more powerful tool only when you hit a real limit.

Your first automation: the daily briefing

The best first automation is one that pays off every single day. A morning briefing — pulling your calendar, open tasks, and relevant emails into a single message before you start work — is ideal. It has a clear trigger (a time), a fixed set of data sources, and a useful output.

Here is what it looks like expressed as ECA:

- Event: weekdays at 7:30 AM
- Condition: none (always run)
- Actions: fetch today's calendar events → fetch high-priority tasks → fetch unread emails from key senders → summarise with AI → send to yourself via email or Slack

In n8n, this maps to a Schedule Trigger node wired to Google Calendar, Google Sheets (or Todoist), Gmail, an AI node, and a send node. The community template library has several ready-to-use variants of this pattern — template #6133 (Todoist + Google Calendar + GPT-4o → Gmail) and template #4385 (Gmail + Calendar → daily brief) are good starting points.[^briefing-templates]

[^briefing-templates]: n8n community templates: https://n8n.io/workflows/6133-automated-daily-briefing-with-todoist-google-calendar-and-gpt-4o-via-gmail/ and https://n8n.io/workflows/4385-ai-powered-calendar-and-meeting-digest-with-gmail-and-gpt-4oclaude-daily-brief/

A minimal version you can build right now

If you have a Zapier account, you can build a simplified version without writing any code:

1. Trigger: Schedule — every weekday at your preferred start time.
2. Action 1: Google Calendar — get today's events.
3. Action 2: Gmail — get unread emails (filtered to important senders or labels).
4. Action 3: Claude or ChatGPT (via Zapier's AI actions) — summarise both into three bullet points per category.
5. Action 4: Gmail or Slack — send the summary to yourself.

Zapier MCP (mcp.zapier.com) is a remote MCP server that gives Claude access to 9,000+ apps as tools it can call directly — no Zap builder required. You paste a server URL into Claude's MCP settings, add the tools you want, and then a single chat prompt like "pull my calendar for today and send me a briefing" executes across apps. Each tool call costs two tasks from your Zapier quota.[^zapier-mcp-pricing] Think of Zaps as scheduled, trigger-based automation and MCP as giving your AI "hands" for ad-hoc action — the two complement each other.[^zapier-mcp-design]

[^zapier-mcp-pricing]: Zapier MCP task billing: https://www.goodcall.com/voice-ai/zapier-mcp — each MCP tool call costs two tasks from your plan's task quota.
[^zapier-mcp-design]: Zapier's own framing of Zaps vs MCP: https://zapier.com/blog/zapier-mcp-guide/

Levelling up: scheduled workflows in n8n

Once you are comfortable with simple trigger → action pairs, you will hit tasks that need branching logic, retries, or multi-step data transformation. n8n is built for exactly this.

Anatomy of an n8n scheduled workflow

n8n uses standard 5-field cron expressions.  runs at 8:30 AM on weekdays.  runs daily at 9 AM. You can also use the visual picker if you prefer.[^n8n-cron]

[^n8n-cron]: n8n Schedule Trigger node reference: https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger/ — cron format verified 2026-06-21.

n8n's self-hosted default timezone is America/NewYork. If you are in a different timezone and do not set it explicitly in Workflow Settings, your scheduled runs will fire at unexpected local times. Always set the workflow timezone, not just the instance timezone.[^n8n-tz]

[^n8n-tz]: Timezone gotcha documented at: https://aiworkflowsautomation.com/n8n-scheduling-tutorial-master-cron-jobs-triggers-for-workflow-automation/

Naming discipline

When you have a dozen workflows, "Workflow 3" is useless. A descriptive name like "Daily Sales Report – 9 AM Weekdays" or "Gmail Digest → Slack – Every Morning" tells you the trigger, the data, and the output at a glance. Treat workflow names like commit messages: future-you is the audience.[^naming]

[^naming]: Naming convention best practice from: https://aiworkflowsautomation.com/n8n-scheduling-tutorial-master-cron-jobs-triggers-for-workflow-automation/

The mindset: automate the process, not the mess

There is a trap waiting for new automators: building a workflow around a broken process. If you spend 20 minutes every morning fighting with a chaotic inbox, automating that chaos does not fix it — it scales it.[^broken-process]

[^broken-process]: "Automation does not fix broken processes; it scales them" — https://www.synergyonline.com/post/process-automation-best-practices-driving-business-efficiency-and-growth

Before building, spend ten minutes making the manual version clean and repeatable. Can you do it once without any confusion? If yes, automate it. If not, fix the process first.

This also means starting small. Build one automation, run it for a week, and verify it actually saves time before building five more. A phased approach — one automation validated before the next begins — is the professional standard even in enterprise automation programs.[^phased]

[^phased]: Phased automation rollout guidance: https://www.synergyonline.com/post/process-automation-best-practices-driving-business-efficiency-and-growth

If your workflow takes longer to run than the interval between runs, you get concurrent executions competing for the same resources. A daily workflow that takes 45 minutes is fine. A 15-minute workflow triggered every 5 minutes is a problem. Either lengthen the interval or add a concurrency limit in n8n's workflow settings to prevent the pileup.[^concurrency]

[^concurrency]: n8n concurrency control: https://docs.n8n.io/hosting/scaling/concurrency-control/

Five more quick wins to add to your backlog

Once your daily briefing is running, here are high-ROI automations that follow the same pattern:

1. Lead triage: New form submission → AI scores/classifies → routed to the right person via Slack. Replaces: checking a shared inbox and manually assigning.

2. Meeting prep brief: Calendar trigger (30 min before event) → pull attendee emails from CRM → AI generates context summary → sent to your phone. Replaces: scrambling for context two minutes before a call.

3. Weekly report draft: Friday 4 PM → pull metrics from Sheets/analytics → AI drafts summary → saved to Drive as a draft. Replaces: staring at a blank doc every Friday afternoon.

4. Email-to-task sync: New email with label "action-required" → parse due date and task name with AI → create task in Todoist or Linear. Replaces: manually re-entering information from email into your task manager.

5. File intake pipeline: New file uploaded to a shared Drive folder → extract text → append metadata to a tracking Sheet → notify relevant Slack channel. Replaces: manually logging received documents.

Each of these is a different ECA triple. Each is buildable in an afternoon once you have authenticated your integrations.

Recap

Spotting automation opportunities is a skill you develop by paying attention to the absence of decision in your own work. The ECA model — Event, Condition, Action — gives you a shared vocabulary for describing any repeatable task. Claude handles ad-hoc information work; Zapier and Zapier MCP give you breadth across thousands of apps; n8n gives you control, scheduling, and AI-native logic for workflows that run on their own.

Start with your daily briefing. Run it for a week. Then work through your friction log one item at a time. The compounding effect of even a handful of well-built automations is significant — and unlike most productivity improvements, these ones keep paying you back every day without any further effort.

Next:** the following chapter covers connecting Claude directly to external services using MCP — the underlying protocol that makes Zapier MCP and n8n's AI agent nodes possible, and how to wire up your own integrations.
n8n-gsuite:
n8n + GSuite patterns

n8n's visual workflow builder and Google Workspace's deep API surface are a natural fit: every Gmail message, Drive file, Sheets row, and Calendar event becomes a trigger or action you can orchestrate in minutes. By the end of this chapter you will know how to authenticate all four Google services in n8n, how to wire Claude into each of them, and how to assemble those pieces into durable multi-service automations.

---

How Google auth works in n8n

Before touching any workflow, get credentials right — everything downstream depends on it.

n8n offers three credential types for Google services:

| Credential type | Best for | Shared across nodes? |
|---|---|---|
| Google OAuth2 (single service) | Personal Gmail, Drive, Sheets, Calendar | One credential per product |
| Google OAuth2 (generic) | Broad-scope access when one cred covers several products | Yes |
| Service Account | Server-to-server, no human login | Yes, but with a sharp constraint (below) |

For most automators, the OAuth2 route is the right call. You create an OAuth2 credential in n8n, paste in the Client ID and Secret from a Google Cloud project you own, and complete the consent flow once. n8n stores the token encrypted under your  and refreshes it automatically.

Google changed Service Account permissions: accounts created after 15 April 2025 can only access Shared Drives, not personal My Drive. If your automation needs to read or write files in a personal Drive, use OAuth2. Service Accounts remain valid for Workspace-wide deployments with domain-wide delegation configured by a super admin. (Source: packet-D, §3.5)

All four Google nodes — Gmail, Sheets, Drive, Calendar — share the same credential family. Set up one OAuth2 credential per Google product and reuse it across every workflow that needs that service.

---

Gmail — trigger on email, send with intelligence

The Gmail Trigger

The Gmail Trigger polls your inbox at a configurable interval and fires a workflow execution for each matching message. Common patterns:

- Watch a specific label (e.g. ) and fire on arrival
- Filter by sender or subject keyword
- Combine with a label operation to mark processed messages, so re-runs skip them

Message operations

The Gmail node covers the full message lifecycle: send, reply, get, get-list, delete, mark read/unread, and add/remove labels. Replies preserve thread context — pass the  from the trigger output and n8n keeps the conversation intact.

Attachments on replies work through the standard n8n binary data pattern: a preceding node (HTTP Request, Drive Download, etc.) puts a file into the item's binary fields, and you reference that field name in the Gmail node's "Attachment Field Name" setting.

Wiring Claude into Gmail

The most valuable pattern is AI triage: Gmail receives the email, Claude reads it, decides what kind of response it needs, and either drafts a reply for human review or sends it automatically based on the classification.

The confidence gate is important. Let Claude handle the high-certainty cases automatically and surface the ambiguous ones to a Sheets log that a human checks once a day. This keeps the automation useful without removing oversight on edge cases.

---

Google Sheets — your automation's state layer

Sheets fills a role that surprises many newcomers: it is not just a data source but a mutable state store that non-technical teammates can inspect and edit directly. In n8n automations this makes it the ideal log, queue, and config surface.

Core operations

| Operation | What it does |
|---|---|
| Append Row | Add a new row at the end |
| Append or Update (upsert) | Update a matching row or insert if not found |
| Get Row(s) | Read rows; filter by column value |
| Lookup Row | Find first match; set "Return All Matches" for multiple results |
| Update Row | Change specific cells by row number |
| Delete Row | Remove a row by number |

The Sheets Lookup Row operation returns only the first matching row unless you explicitly set "Filter Has Multiple Matches" to "Return All Matches". Missing this setting is the most common reason a lookup-based workflow silently drops data. (Source: packet-D, §3.2)

The Sheets Trigger

The Google Sheets Trigger watches a sheet for changes — new rows or updates — and fires the workflow immediately. This makes Sheets a lightweight inbound queue: a form submission, a Zapier zap, or a human adding a row all become workflow triggers.

Pattern: interview scheduling pipeline

n8n's community template library includes an interview scheduling workflow (template #5001) that shows multi-service orchestration cleanly: read candidates from Sheets, create Calendar events, send personalized Gmail confirmations, then log outcomes back to the same sheet. The shape of that pattern reappears in dozens of real automations:

Each step is independently testable, and the Sheets log gives you a full audit trail without building a database.

---

Google Drive — file events as workflow triggers

Drive is the entry point for document-centric automations: a new PDF triggers a processing workflow, a folder upload kicks off a review cycle, or a changed file reruns an analysis.

Trigger events

The Google Drive Trigger listens for:

- File Created — new file lands in a watched folder
- File Updated — an existing file changes
- File Created or Updated — either of the above
- Folder Created — a subfolder appears
- File Deleted — removal event

File operations

Once triggered, the Drive node can: upload, download, move, copy, share, list, update metadata, or create a file from a text string. The Download operation returns binary data that subsequent nodes (Claude, a Sheets append, an email attachment) can consume directly.

Pattern: document intake and analysis

This pattern handles incoming contracts, invoices, reports, or any document type where the value is in the extracted content rather than the file itself.

---

Google Calendar — time as a trigger and output

Calendar sits at both ends of workflows: it produces events that trigger automations (meeting starting in 30 minutes — prepare briefing) and receives events created by other services (a Sheets row becomes a calendar block).

Trigger modes

The Google Calendar Trigger offers three modes:

- New event created — fires when any event is added
- Event updated — fires on changes to an existing event
- Event starting — fires a configurable lead time before an event begins (useful for pre-meeting briefings)

Event operations

Create, get, update, and delete are all available. The update operation supports two attendee management strategies: append (add new attendees without removing existing ones) or replace (set the attendee list to exactly what you specify).

Pattern: daily briefing before your first meeting

One of the most practically useful automations combines Calendar's "event starting" trigger with Gmail and Claude:

The community template library includes a workflow (template #4385) that does exactly this with Gmail and Claude. The key design decision is the lead time: 30 minutes is enough to read the brief before joining; 5 minutes is too short to be useful. (Source: packet-D, §8.3)

---

Composing multi-service workflows

Individual service connections become powerful when chained. The common challenge is keeping chains readable and maintainable as they grow.

The morning briefing pattern

A daily briefing that combines Calendar, Gmail, and Claude is a high-value workflow that most people can set up in under an hour. The shape is:

A few things to get right:

- Set timezone explicitly. n8n's self-hosted default is ; if you are not in that zone, set the workflow timezone in Workflow Settings or your scheduled trigger will fire at the wrong time. (Source: packet-D, §2.1)
- Handle the Merge stall. If Calendar returns zero events, the Merge node waits indefinitely. Add a fallback item on the Calendar branch for days with no events. (Source: packet-D, §10)
- Use HTML for the email body. Claude can output structured HTML; Gmail renders it natively. A plain-text digest is harder to scan quickly.

Bulk event creation from Sheets

The reverse direction — Sheets driving Calendar — is equally useful for scheduling interviews, recurring reminders, or content publish dates. Read all rows from a Sheets range, loop with an n8n Split In Batches node, and create one Calendar event per row. n8n bills per workflow execution, not per node call, so a 100-row batch costs one execution. (Source: packet-D, §1.2)

Claude as the reasoning layer

In every pattern above, Claude's role is consistent: it reads unstructured inputs (email bodies, document text, event descriptions) and produces structured outputs (classifications, summaries, draft text, extracted fields) that downstream nodes can act on deterministically.

The practical approach is to put Claude between the data source and the action node, and to treat Claude's output as JSON when you need to branch on it:

Constraining Claude's output format with a system prompt, then parsing it with a Code node, gives you reliable branching without fragile string-matching.

Community n8n practitioners note that Claude tends to follow system prompt format instructions more consistently than some other models, which makes it well-suited to the structured-output role in automation branches. (Source: packet-D, §4.1)

---

Error handling for GSuite workflows

Google APIs return rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) and transient failures. A workflow that does not handle these will silently drop data.

Retry on transient errors. Enable "Retry on Fail" on Gmail, Sheets, Drive, and Calendar nodes, and set retry intervals to increase with each attempt (1 s, 2 s, 4 s). This handles the majority of 429s and momentary outages without manual intervention. (Source: packet-D, §6)

Dead-letter rows for bad data. If a Sheets lookup fails because a row is malformed, route the bad item to a dedicated error sheet rather than stopping the whole workflow. The main path continues; the error sheet becomes a human-review queue.

Name your workflows descriptively.  and  are immediately meaningful when you are debugging at midnight.  is not. (Source: packet-D, §8.4)

---

Sharp edges to know before you ship

| Issue | Detail |
|---|---|
| Service Account My Drive access | Accounts created after April 2025 cannot access personal My Drive — use OAuth2 instead. |
| Merge node with empty branches | A branch that produces zero items causes Merge to stall indefinitely. Add a fallback No-Op item. |
| Self-hosted timezone default | Defaults to . Always set timezone explicitly in Workflow Settings. |
| Inactive workflow toggle | A workflow with the toggle off never runs scheduled triggers, even if the schedule would otherwise fire. |
| Concurrency and manual test runs | Manual executions bypass concurrency limits. Always test at realistic throughput before relying on concurrency settings. (Source: packet-D, §10) |

---

Recap and what's next

You now have the wiring patterns for all four major GSuite services in n8n: Gmail for email in/out, Sheets as a mutable state layer and trigger surface, Drive for file-event pipelines, and Calendar for time-based triggers and event creation. Claude threads through all of them as the reasoning layer that turns unstructured data into structured decisions downstream nodes can act on.

The next chapter covers scheduling and background automation — how n8n's cron triggers, loop patterns, and sub-workflows let you build a personal automation system that runs reliably around the clock without manual intervention.
personal-automation-system:
Building a personal automation system

You have individual automations — a scheduled digest here, a webhook there, a Claude skill you invoke manually. This chapter shows how to wire those pieces into a coherent whole: a tiered, resilient, self-monitoring system that runs unattended and grows with you without becoming a maintenance burden.

---

Why a system, not a collection

A collection of workflows breaks down at two predictable points: when one workflow's output needs to feed another, and when something fails silently. A system prevents both by applying three ideas from the start.

Layered triggers. Some things should run on a schedule (morning brief, weekly reports). Some should fire on events (new email, Drive file uploaded). Some should respond to your commands in real time (ad-hoc Claude + Zapier MCP calls). A system has all three layers, and each layer has its own tool choice.

Shared data surface. Isolated workflows can't cooperate. A Google Sheet, a Notion database, or even a simple JSON file that every workflow can read and write turns a collection into a network. One workflow writes status; another reads it to decide whether to proceed.

Explicit error paths. Automation does not fix broken processes — it scales them.[^eca] Before adding a workflow, verify that the underlying process is clear. Once it runs, route failures somewhere visible or the system lies to you through silence.

[^eca]: Source: "If the underlying workflow lacks clarity or efficiency, automation will simply scale those limitations." — Synergy Online, Process Automation Best Practices, https://www.synergyonline.com/post/process-automation-best-practices-driving-business-efficiency-and-growth

---

The three-tier architecture

Tier 1 — Scheduled workflows

n8n's Schedule Trigger node handles time-based work. It supports cron expressions ( = weekdays at 8:30 AM), plain intervals, and human-friendly modes (daily, weekly, monthly).[^sched] The workflow toggle must be on for the trigger to fire — inactive workflows silently skip their schedule.

A practical starting stack:

| Workflow | Trigger | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Morning brief |  | Calendar events + Todoist tasks → GPT/Claude summary → Gmail HTML |
| Email digest |  | Gmail inbox → AI summarize → delivery to your read-later inbox |
| Weekly report |  | Pull Sheet metrics → format → send to yourself |

[^sched]: n8n Schedule Trigger docs: https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger/

If you run n8n on a home server (Raspberry Pi 4 or similar), a reboot or power cut means scheduled jobs that fire during the downtime are silently skipped — they do not catch up. Cloud-hosted n8n avoids this. If you self-host, a simple uptime monitor (UptimeRobot free tier, a cron that pings a health endpoint) gives you visibility into gaps before they compound.[^selfhost]

[^selfhost]: Source: https://aiworkflowsautomation.com/n8n-scheduling-tutorial-master-cron-jobs-triggers-in-workflow-automation/

Tier 2 — Event-driven workflows

Webhooks and trigger nodes handle real-time events:

- Gmail Trigger polls for messages matching a label or filter on a configurable interval and fires when one arrives.
- Google Drive Trigger fires on File Created, File Updated, or Folder Created events.
- Google Sheets Trigger fires when rows are added or changed — useful for data-entry-driven pipelines.
- Webhook Trigger gives any external service a URL to POST to; the workflow fires instantly with the incoming payload.

A concrete example: Gmail receives a message you label "meeting-request". The trigger fires, a Google Gemini or Claude node extracts the proposed time and attendees, and a Calendar node creates the event — all without you opening a tab.[^cal] n8n community template #7340 demonstrates this exact flow.

[^cal]: n8n workflow #7340: https://n8n.io/workflows/7340-create-google-calendar-events-from-labeled-gmail-emails-with-google-gemini-ai/

Tier 3 — On-demand via Zapier MCP

Scheduled and event-driven tiers handle known patterns. For everything else — "pull the Zendesk ticket, check Stripe, draft a reply, send it" — Zapier MCP gives Claude real-time hands across 9,000+ apps.[^zmcp]

The mental model: Zaps are scheduled automation; MCP calls are what your AI does when you ask it to take action right now. The two are complementary.[^zcomp]

Setup takes under five minutes:
1. Go to , create a server, copy the server URL.
2. Paste it into Claude Code's MCP settings (or your ).
3. Search and add the actions you want (Gmail Send, HubSpot Contact Create, Notion Page Update, etc.).
4. In Claude Code, Zapier actions appear as .
